text:
Transfer rule: If chained percent changes compare different bases, then convert each relation to multiplicative factors from the same reference before combining.
Error pattern: I treated “more than” and “less than” as additive percentage arithmetic instead of base-dependent scaling.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite statements as equations like new = old × factor, substitute to one variable, and verify the final ratio is plausible relative to each factor.
Use when: This applies to multi-step percent comparison problems linking three quantities with phrases like “more than,” “less than,” “of,” or “is what percent of.”
Boundary: Ignore this for direct single-base percent questions or when absolute amounts are given and no chained comparison is needed.

Transfer rule: If distinct items are placed into distinct containers with no capacity limits, then count independent choices per item and multiply, rather than using distribution formulas that constrain totals.
Error pattern: Confused unrestricted item-to-box assignments with partitioning/composition reasoning that subtracts or omits valid cases.
Diagnostic check: List one item and verify it has the full number of container choices regardless of earlier placements; if every item passes, compute choices^(number of items).
Use when: Apply this for problems with different objects, different boxes, unlimited occupancy, and no extra restrictions like nonempty boxes.
Boundary: Ignore this when objects are identical, boxes are identical, capacities exist, or conditions link choices across items.

Transfer rule: If a product comes from repeated item weights, then factor it into primes and map exponents to item counts before choosing.
Error pattern: I matched options from rough magnitude or incomplete factoring instead of enforcing all exponent constraints from every item type.
Diagnostic check: Compute the prime-power form of the total product and solve the resulting count equations; verify each count is a nonnegative integer.
Use when: A problem gives fixed multiplicative contributions per object and asks how many of one type appear in a partial collection.
Boundary: Ignore this when totals are additive, approximate, or item values are not fixed independent factors.

Transfer rule: If a ratio involves perimeter and one side, then write the perimeter formula directly and solve algebraically before using area.
Error pattern: Introduced unrelated geometry and extra variables instead of exploiting the given rectangle relationships.
Diagnostic check: Let width = w; compute perimeter from the ratio, set 2(l + w) equal to that expression, isolate l in terms of w, then verify lw matches the area.
Use when: A rectangle problem gives a ratio involving perimeter and a side plus an area or another side relation.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the figure is not a rectangle or when the ratio concerns diagonal, semiperimeter, or another quantity.

Transfer rule: If a trip covers equal distances at different speeds, then compute average speed from total distance divided by total time, not by averaging the speeds.
Error pattern: Success came from using a weighted-by-time approach instead of an intuitive but invalid simple mean.
Diagnostic check: Set distance chunks equal, compute each chunk’s time as distance/speed, add times, then divide total distance by that sum.
Use when: This applies to multi-stage motion problems where segment distances are given and speeds differ across segments.
Boundary: Ignore this when durations are equal or when acceleration/traffic effects make speed nonconstant within a segment.

Transfer rule: If profit percent and absolute profit are both given with an extra cost tied to base cost, then set total investment = base cost + extra cost before equating profit.
Error pattern: Treated profit percent as relating only to the purchase price and mixed selling-price relationships, instead of using total cost basis consistently.
Diagnostic check: Define variables, write investment, selling price, and profit in one equation chain, then verify that percent profit equals absolute profit divided by total investment.
Use when: Word problems include repairs, overhead, or add-on expenses plus both a profit rate and a profit amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent is explicitly on selling price, discount, commission, or another stated reference amount.

Transfer rule: If a delayed meeting shifts by a known distance on a same-direction route, then equate relative closing distance over the delay, not one traveler’s solo distance.
Error pattern: Treated the delay as giving the faster traveler the full extra interval while ignoring that both travelers keep moving during that interval.
Diagnostic check: Define positions at the normal meeting and the delayed meeting, write each traveler’s distance change over the delay, and verify the meeting-point shift matches the difference of those changes.
Use when: Relative-motion word problems involve lateness, changed meeting location, and both objects moving along one line in the same direction.
Boundary: Ignore when one object is stationary, directions change, or the event is not a shifted meeting-time/meeting-point comparison.

Transfer rule: If two integers’ product and greatest common divisor are given, then compute the least common multiple as product ÷ greatest common divisor exactly once.
Error pattern: Replaced a standard identity with invented prime-factor logic after already deriving a valid result.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write gcd × lcm = product; substitute the given values, perform one division, and verify the result times the gcd reproduces the product.
Use when: A problem gives two whole numbers indirectly through their product plus gcd or asks for gcd/lcm of two integers.
Boundary: Ignore when there are more than two numbers or when the relation is not about integer gcd/lcm.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and go in opposite directions, then add their speeds and multiply by elapsed time.
Error pattern: Confusing opposite-direction separation with a difference-based or one-person distance calculation.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “separation rate = sum or difference?” and verify directions; opposite means sum, same means difference.
Use when: Any distance-between-two-objects problem where both start from a common point or known positions and move simultaneously.
Boundary: Ignore this when motion is not along one line, start times differ, speeds vary, or the question asks an individual distance rather than separation.

Transfer rule: If two quantities are each given as percentages of the same base, then write both as fractions of that base and divide to get one as a percent of the other.
Error pattern: Success came from using a shared-reference ratio instead of combining percentages multiplicatively.
Diagnostic check: Let the common base equal 100; compute the two quantities from their given rates, then verify the target percent equals 100 × first ÷ second.
Use when: Apply this to percent-of-percent comparison problems where multiple values are defined relative to one common quantity.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages refer to different bases or when the relationship is additive, not comparative.

Transfer rule: If a percent gain or loss is given on a known base price, then compute amount = base × (1 ± rate) and choose only the exact matching option.
Error pattern: Abandoning a correct calculation because of an option-scan mistake and then selecting a “closest” choice.
Diagnostic check: After computing, pause and compare the result digit-for-digit against every option; if one matches exactly, stop and pick it.
Use when: Basic percentage, profit/loss, discount, tax, markup, or simple interest questions with multiple-choice answers.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly asks for an estimate, nearest value, or says the options may be approximate.

Transfer rule: If a simple-interest problem says the time in years equals the rate percent, then set t = r and use SI = P·r²/100.  
Error pattern: Linearizing a relationship that becomes quadratic when one quantity is defined to equal another.  
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write the formula symbolically, substitute the equality condition, and verify whether solving requires a square root.  
Use when: Principal, interest, rate, and time are given or linked, especially with phrases like “as many years as the rate” or other self-referential equalities.  
Boundary: Ignore this when compounding is involved, units differ, or time is not explicitly tied to the numeric value of the rate.

Transfer rule: If asked for the minimum in an overlap-of-sets count, then use the complement form: required overlap ≥ sum(all set sizes) − (number of sets−1)×universe.
Error pattern: I undercounted by not applying the general lower-bound inclusion–exclusion formula consistently across all categories.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute the lower bound twice: once with inclusion–exclusion, once by placing all “missing” people outside the target overlap; both totals must match.
Use when: This applies to finite-population problems giving several group totals and asking how many must belong to all groups.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for an exact overlap without enough constraints, or when groups are not all subsets of the same universe.

Transfer rule: If an equation equals zero and factors into a product, then set each factor separately to zero and list only those roots.
Error pattern: Invented extra values by manipulating factors after factoring instead of applying the zero-product property directly.
Diagnostic check: After factoring, write each factor = 0, solve each one, then substitute every candidate back into the original equation and reject any unsupported value.
Use when: A polynomial equation is set equal to zero, especially quadratics with a common factor or easy factorization.
Boundary: Ignore this when the equation is not written as product = 0 or when operations could introduce domain restrictions requiring other methods.

Transfer rule: If a pay problem gives earnings for worked days and a penalty for idle days over a fixed total, then define both day counts, write one total-days equation and one net-pay equation, and solve simultaneously.
Error pattern: I likely guessed from partial arithmetic instead of modeling both categories consistently.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, substitute your day counts into total days and compute net pay as earnings minus idle penalty; confirm both match exactly.
Use when: Apply this to word problems with per-day gain, per-day loss, and a stated overall period or total amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the amounts are not linear per day, or when penalties/bonuses depend on thresholds, rates, or missing totals.

Transfer rule: If a ratio changes after adding to one group, then set original counts as common multiples of the ratio parts and write the updated-ratio equation before choosing.
Error pattern: Treated a ratio word problem as guesswork or scale-matching without enforcing consistency between the original and changed situations.
Diagnostic check: Let counts be a·k and b·k; apply the stated change, cross-multiply the two fractions, solve for k, and verify both ratios exactly.
Use when: A problem gives an initial part-to-part ratio and then a small adjustment changes that ratio.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is not a ratio update, or when totals/proportions are given directly without a before-and-after constraint.

Transfer rule: If a value “bears the same ratio” to another as one fraction does to a second, then set x/base = frac1/frac2 and compute x = base × frac1 ÷ frac2.
Error pattern: Mis-translating proportional language or doing fraction arithmetic in the wrong order leads to a nearby but incorrect option.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the statement as an equation, replace each ratio with a division symbol, then verify by plugging your result back into both sides.
Use when: A word problem compares two ratios, especially involving fractions of fractions or old-style proportion wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is additive, comparative without equality of ratios, or explicitly asks for a reciprocal or inverse.

Transfer rule: If a question scales a bundle of items at the same rates, then scale the total bundle cost by the common factor instead of splitting costs without enough information.
Error pattern: Treated a combined-cost statement as separate item prices and then guessed from choices when the arithmetic conflicted.
Diagnostic check: Compare requested quantities to given quantities; if each category is multiplied by the same fraction, apply that fraction to the total and verify no individual prices were assumed.
Use when: Total cost is given for a mixture, and the new mixture preserves the same composition ratio.
Boundary: Ignore this when quantities change by different factors or when separate unit prices are actually provided.

Transfer rule: If a percent increase under simple interest is given, then set rt equal to that increase in decimal form and solve t = increase/rate.
Error pattern: Mixed up simple and compound interest and used irrelevant doubling/log rules instead of the linear simple-interest model.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the governing formula; if the problem says simple interest, verify the gain after t years is P·r·t and compare it directly to the stated percent gain.
Use when: Relevant for time-to-target questions with annual simple interest, percent growth, and multiple-choice year options.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when interest is compounded, rates vary over time, or fees/payments alter the balance path.

Transfer rule: If counting subsets of an odd-sized set with a size cap at the midpoint, then pair each subset with its complement and take half of all subsets.
Error pattern: I treated “at most the lower half” as including all subsets, missing the complement symmetry that splits counts evenly.
Diagnostic check: Compute total subsets, verify the set size is odd, and confirm every subset below the midpoint pairs uniquely with one above it, with no equal-size middle case.
Use when: The problem asks for counts of subsets bounded by size in a set whose total size is one less than an even number.
Boundary: Ignore this when the set size is even, the bound is not the midpoint threshold, or extra subset restrictions break complement pairing.

Transfer rule: If a covering problem gives room dimensions, tile dimensions, and unit price, then compute counts from area or side-by-side fit first, then multiply by price once.
Error pattern: Mixed up quantity of pieces with total cost by skipping or misapplying the unit-count step.
Diagnostic check: Calculate room area ÷ tile area; independently check tiles along length × tiles along width; confirm both counts match before pricing.
Use when: Rectangles are covered by equal rectangular or square pieces with exact dimensions and a per-piece cost.
Boundary: Ignore when there is waste, partial tiles, non-rectangular regions, overlap, or pricing is by area rather than by piece.

Transfer rule: If two quantities have ratio a:b and both get the same additive change, then set them as ak and bk and solve (ak+c)/(bk+c)=new ratio before checking choices.
Error pattern: Treated an additive ratio-change problem like a proportional scaling shortcut, skipping the shared-base variable setup.
Diagnostic check: Cross-multiply the updated-ratio equation, solve for k, then verify by adding the common increase back to both values and recomputing the ratio exactly.
Use when: Initial values are given only by a ratio, both receive the same fixed increase or decrease, and a new ratio is provided.
Boundary: Ignore when the change is multiplicative/percentage-based or the amounts added to the two quantities are different.

Transfer rule: If an average changes after adding one score, then convert each average to a total and subtract to find the added score.
Error pattern: I relied on an intuitive increase and skipped the weighted-total calculation, causing a mismatch between group sizes.
Diagnostic check: Compute old total = old average × old count and new total = new average × new count; verify their difference equals one plausible score.
Use when: This applies to average/mean problems where a person, item, or data point is added or removed from a set.
Boundary: Ignore this when counts stay fixed and the task compares averages only, or when the change is not caused by adding/removing data.

Transfer rule: If coin counts are given in a ratio but coin values differ, then convert ratio parts into total monetary value before solving for counts.
Error pattern: Treated a ratio of quantities as if it directly matched money totals, ignoring unequal unit values.
Diagnostic check: Let counts be k times the ratio; compute total value from denomination×count for each type, solve for k, then verify the target count.
Use when: A problem mixes item counts, ratios, and different per-item values or weights under one total.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ratio already refers to values/totals in common units, not to numbers of items.

Transfer rule: If a calendar question gives one date’s weekday, then anchor that date and count forward/backward by exact day offsets to locate target weekdays and dates.
Error pattern: Unstructured, assumption-based calendar reasoning can wander into contradictions even when the final choice happens to be right.
Diagnostic check: Write the given date as a fixed anchor, derive the nearest occurrence of the needed weekday, then add whole weeks for the nth occurrence and only afterward apply extra-day shifts.
Use when: This applies to month-date problems involving weekdays, nth weekday occurrences, or “k days after/before” wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when dates depend on month length, cross-month transitions, or extra constraints not captured by simple weekday offsets.

Transfer rule: If two growth descriptions look similar, then compute each with its own formula from the same principal before comparing.  
Error pattern: Confusing simple annual growth with compounded annual growth and overapplying the percentage across years.  
Diagnostic check: Write both update equations explicitly, expand year by year, and verify one adds equal yearly gains while the other multiplies by the growth factor each year.  
Use when: Rates are given over multiple periods and wording mixes “annual interest,” “for two years,” and “compounded annually” or similar terms.  
Boundary: Ignore this when both investments use the same compounding convention or the question does not compare multi-period growth rules.

Transfer rule: If one chosen role is distinguished from an otherwise unordered group, then count by selecting the full involved set and assigning the special role, not by ordering everyone unless the count is equivalent.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a mixed selection-assignment structure where one position matters and the rest do not.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write the process as two stages, mark which slots are labeled, then verify the count matches “choose group × choose distinguished member” or an equivalent form.
Use when: A problem asks for a subset plus a leader, captain, chair, winner, or other single tagged person from the chosen subset.
Boundary: Ignore this when every position is distinct or when no chosen member has a special label.

Transfer rule: If one quantity added from one variable equals a stated percent increase of another, then write a direct equation between the two percentage amounts before forming any ratio.
Error pattern: Mismatched base quantities—treating percentages as if they refer to the same whole or flipping the ratio after solving.
Diagnostic check: Let the first and second quantities be x and y; set (given percent of x) = (given percent of y), solve for y/x, then verify by substitution.
Use when: Percentage-comparison word problems where an amount from one quantity causes a percent change in another quantity.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages are successive on one base, involve totals/differences, or extra conditions make a single equation insufficient.

Transfer rule: If a word problem compares two contribution schemes, then write both totals algebraically and subtract them before using options.
Error pattern: I mixed entities and variables, treating totals or contributions as the count instead of keeping one symbol for the number of students.
Diagnostic check: Define n as student count, compute scenario1 and scenario2 from roles, simplify scenario2−scenario1, and verify units stay “rupees” versus “people.”
Use when: Apply this to linear setup problems with the same participants under two payment rules and a stated increase or decrease between totals.
Boundary: Ignore this when options are reached by direct counting, or when the change is non-algebraic, conditional, or involves multiple unknown groups.

Transfer rule: If a rectangle gives one side and a diagonal, then find the missing side with the Pythagorean theorem and multiply the two sides for area.
Error pattern: Misapplied a shape property and then guessed from the choices instead of validating with a geometric relation.
Diagnostic check: Draw the rectangle’s right triangle, label side-diagonal-side, test whether known values satisfy a^2+b^2=d^2, then compute area and compare units.
Use when: A quadrilateral problem involves rectangles, diagonals, side lengths, or asks for area from partial dimensions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the figure is not right-angled, dimensions are not side-diagonal-side, or the task is not about geometric measurement.

Transfer rule: If choosing a subset with no roles, then model it with combinations, using symmetry to replace k by the smaller of k and n−k.
Error pattern: Misapplied counting formula or arithmetic in evaluating a binomial coefficient for an unordered selection.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify order is irrelevant, write C(n,k)=n!/[k!(n−k)!], simplify by cancellation, and confirm C(n,k)=C(n,n−k).
Use when: The task asks how many groups, teams, or subcommittees can be selected from a larger set without assigning positions.
Boundary: Ignore when selections involve order, distinct roles, repetition, or sequential arrangements; then use permutations or other counting methods.

Transfer rule: If a total commission comes from a percent of each item across many identical items, then divide total commission by item count, then divide by the commission rate to get price per item.
Error pattern: I skipped the per-item normalization step and treated the percentage relation too coarsely, inflating the result.
Diagnostic check: Compute commission per item; verify that price × rate equals that amount and that multiplying back by the quantity reproduces the total commission.
Use when: This applies to word problems with percentages, repeated identical units, and a known aggregate payout or fee.
Boundary: Ignore this when items have different prices or rates, or when the percentage is applied to profit, cost, or another base instead of selling price.

Transfer rule: If a ratio mixture has one component added, then first convert the original ratio and total into actual amounts, update only the changed component, and rebuild the ratio.
Error pattern: Treating ratio manipulation abstractly without translating to quantities causes wrong updates after an additive change.
Diagnostic check: Compute original part value from total ÷ sum of ratio parts, find each component amount, add the stated increase, then compare by division or simplify.
Use when: Use this for mixture, concentration, or ratio problems where a total and component ratio are given and some amount is added or removed.
Boundary: Ignore this when the change is multiplicative, both components scale equally, or the question asks for a percentage rather than a new ratio.

Transfer rule: If a number must satisfy two remainder conditions, then combine them into one congruence modulo the least common multiple and count only values in the stated range.
Error pattern: Miscounting valid cases by spotting a pattern but not verifying every candidate within the interval.
Diagnostic check: List the arithmetic progression from one condition, test each term against the second condition, then confirm the total stays inside the digit-range endpoints.
Use when: The problem gives simultaneous divisibility/remainder constraints and asks for how many integers in a bounded interval satisfy them.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are about existence, algebraic expressions, or when the interval is unbounded or not integer-only.

Transfer rule: If round-trip travel times differ only by aiding/opposing current, then set equal distances and use rates \(1/t\) to isolate still-water speed.
Error pattern: Success came from translating times into additive/subtractive rates instead of averaging times or picking a midpoint.
Diagnostic check: Let distance be 1 unit; compute downstream rate and upstream rate, then verify still-water rate is their average and reproduces both times with current added/subtracted.
Use when: Apply to boat, wind, conveyor, or current problems where the same vehicle covers the same distance under opposite external effects.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ, speed changes between legs, or the external effect is not constant and symmetric.

Transfer rule: If equal square tiles cover a known total area with a known count, then compute one tile’s area by total ÷ count and take the square root, converting units afterward.
Error pattern: Treated area-per-tile as a linear measure or skipped the square-root step when moving from area to side length.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify side² × number of tiles = total area, with all units consistent between square units and length units.
Use when: The problem gives total covered area, identical square pieces, and asks for one side length or edge measure.
Boundary: Ignore when pieces are not square, dimensions are mixed/partial, spacing exists, or the asked quantity is area, perimeter, or count instead.

Transfer rule: If several workers have different time units, then convert each to one common rate, sum rates, and compute total time by dividing workload by the combined rate.
Error pattern: Mixed-unit arithmetic and inconsistent continuation after a partial total caused an impossible time estimate.
Diagnostic check: Recompute each person’s per-hour rate, verify the combined hourly output, then multiply your chosen time back to see whether it reaches the target.
Use when: This applies to joint-work or combined-rate questions with minutes and hours mixed across contributors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is not additive over time or when workers cannot act simultaneously at constant rates.

Transfer rule: If a boundary of fixed width is asked around a figure and only the perimeter is given, then compute area as perimeter × width unless extra dimensions are needed.
Error pattern: Confusing a narrow border-area problem with a full-area or side-finding problem, leading to unnecessary assumptions and inflated results.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify units by multiplying linear measure by boundary width; if this gives square units directly, compare that scale to the choices.
Use when: Problems mention fencing, bordering, edging, painting strips, or gardening around a shape with known perimeter and uniform small width.
Boundary: Ignore this when width is not uniform, corners require exact outer-minus-inner area, or enough dimensions are given to determine the whole area instead.

Transfer rule: If a boat/current problem compares equal-distance travel times, then set time ratio equal to inverse speed ratio and use upstream = still-water minus stream, downstream = still-water plus stream.
Error pattern: Mixed up direction formulas and wrote inconsistent equal-distance equations, then distrusted a valid result because of option-handling noise.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify two signs: upstream speed < still-water speed < downstream speed; then confirm longer time pairs with lower speed.
Use when: Rate-time-distance questions involve rivers, currents, upstream/downstream motion, or any equal-distance comparison between opposing effective speeds.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ, external factors change speed across trips, or the context is not additive/subtractive relative motion.

Transfer rule: If asked for percent increase/decrease, then compute change ÷ original amount × 100, using the earlier value as the base.
Error pattern: Mistaking the new total or the ratio of totals for the percentage change instead of comparing the difference to the starting amount.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write old, new, and change; verify the denominator is the old value, then estimate whether the result is closer to one-quarter, one-half, etc.
Use when: Relevant for word problems about growth, decline, markup, discounts, or year-over-year comparisons between two quantities.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for percent of a total, a simple ratio, or uses a different stated reference base.

Transfer rule: If one worker is x% more efficient, then multiply the original work rate by 1+x and divide the original time by that factor.
Error pattern: Mixed up rate and time, treating a percentage increase in efficiency as a direct change in completion days instead of an inverse one.
Diagnostic check: Set total work to 1 unit; compute old rate = 1/time, new rate = old rate×factor, then new time = 1/new rate.
Use when: The problem compares productivity, efficiency, speed, or work rates for the same fixed job across people or machines.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percentage applies to time itself, or when total work changes between scenarios.

Transfer rule: If a single new score changes the average by a stated amount after one more inning, then set old total as n·a and new total as n·a + score = (n+1)(a+change).
Error pattern: I treated the average-change statement loosely and jumped to an option instead of forming the before/after average equations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write variables for prior average and prior innings, build both total-runs equations, and verify the new score alone accounts for the total increase.
Use when: This applies to average-update problems where one added observation changes the mean by a fixed amount.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple observations are added at once or when totals/means are already directly given.

Transfer rule: If price changes by p and quantity bought becomes q of the original need, then compare spending with (1+p)×q against 1 before choosing increase/decrease.
Error pattern: Treated the quantity reduction as if it directly offset the price rise, instead of multiplying both effects to get net expenditure.
Diagnostic check: Set original price and required quantity to 100 each; compute old spend, new spend after the percentage changes, then convert the difference back to a percent.
Use when: A problem gives sequential percentage changes on price and amount purchased/consumed and asks for net spending change.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages refer to the same base quantity only, or when absolute amounts—not relative expenditure—are requested.

Transfer rule: If a word problem gives quotient and remainder, then first write dividend = divisor×quotient + remainder and isolate the requested variable algebraically.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating the division statement into the standard equation before touching the choices.
Diagnostic check: Verify your rearranged form by substituting it back into dividend = divisor×quotient + remainder and confirming it simplifies exactly.
Use when: Apply this for integer division, Euclidean algorithm, or any prompt relating dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder.
Boundary: Ignore this when division is not stated with a remainder relation or when variables represent nonstandard operations or constraints.

Transfer rule: If subgroup percentages must be combined, then use a weighted average from the group ratio before taking the complement.
Error pattern: I mixed percentage reasoning with rounded headcounts from an arbitrary small sample, distorting the total.
Diagnostic check: Convert the ratio into population shares, compute overall high-score share as share×rate for each subgroup, sum, then subtract from 100.
Use when: A population is split into categories with a given ratio and each category has its own success/failure percentage.
Boundary: Ignore this when actual subgroup counts are given and exact integer arithmetic is required without any weighted-percentage aggregation.

Transfer rule: If total time is given for two mixed-distance scenarios, then write two linear equations using segment time = distance/speed before computing any ratio.
Error pattern: I guessed segment times from the time difference instead of comparing the two scenarios algebraically to isolate reciprocal speeds.
Diagnostic check: Subtract the two full-trip equations so the unchanged total distance cancels, solve the remaining difference equation, then back-substitute and verify both totals.
Use when: This applies to journey/rate problems where the same total route is split differently between two transport modes across scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore this when only one scenario is given or when times depend on stops, acceleration, or other nonconstant-speed effects.

Transfer rule: If payment is split by unequal days and daily-rate ratios, then compute each person’s earning share as days × rate-unit before dividing the total.
Error pattern: I treated a ratio component too directly and skipped converting mixed time-and-rate data into total contribution units.
Diagnostic check: Make a mini table with each person’s days, rate units, and product; sum the products, then verify the target share equals total × target product / total products.
Use when: This applies to work, wage, cost, or profit-sharing problems combining time worked with per-day ratio information.
Boundary: Ignore this when shares are given directly, rates are equal, or the quantity is unrelated to additive contribution units.

Transfer rule: If quantities are removed in successive fractions, then work backward from the final remainder using inverse fractions at each step.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling sequential percentage/fraction changes multiplicatively instead of adding or subtracting fractions from the original.
Diagnostic check: Compute the leftover fraction after each stage, multiply them to get the total remaining share, and verify final remainder ÷ remaining share gives a whole number.
Use when: Apply this to multi-step “some part consumed/removed, then another part of the remainder” word problems.
Boundary: Ignore this when all fractions refer to the original total, or when absolute amounts replace remainder-based fractions.

Transfer rule: If counting digit arrangements under a divisibility suffix rule, then count valid last-three-digit patterns first and multiply by allowable leading-digit choices while enforcing the no-leading-zero constraint separately.
Error pattern: I likely treated place restrictions inconsistently, missing or double-counting cases where zero appears in the suffix versus the front.
Diagnostic check: List all valid suffixes from the given digit set, mark whether each uses zero, then compute front-position choices case-by-case and verify totals by disjoint counting.
Use when: Apply this for permutation-counting problems with distinct digits, a leading-digit restriction, and divisibility determined only by the final few digits.
Boundary: Ignore when repetition is allowed, divisibility depends on all digits, or leading zeros are permitted.

Transfer rule: If prices are linked by “x of A equals y of B,” then convert all values through unit ratios stepwise to the target item before using money.
Error pattern: Mistaking chain-equivalence problems by reversing a ratio, skipping unit normalization, or combining links without preserving direction.
Diagnostic check: Write each link as one-unit equations, substitute from the known-priced item backward, and verify every cancellation leaves only the target unit.
Use when: Multi-step barter/value comparisons connect several item types and only one final monetary value is given.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are additive totals, independent prices are provided directly, or no transitive equivalence chain exists.

Transfer rule: If an age statement says “was” or “will be” relative to now, then convert each person to a present-age expression first, shift both to the target time, then average.
Error pattern: Success comes from anchoring all ages to one timeline; failures usually mix past and future offsets or average before aligning times.
Diagnostic check: Write present age for each person, subtract or add the requested years to both, and verify every term references the same moment before combining.
Use when: Apply to age word problems with multiple people, different reference times, variables for offsets, and a requested mean at another time.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are not all ages on a common timeline or when the asked operation is not an arithmetic mean.

Transfer rule: If dimensions are chained by multipliers, then substitute all in terms of one variable and multiply every factor before solving.
Error pattern: Dropped a multiplier in the product, then used unsupported divisibility/nearest-option reasoning to force a choice.
Diagnostic check: Write the volume as coefficient × variable^3; recompute the coefficient from all stated ratios, solve exactly, then plug back to verify the given volume.
Use when: Applies to rectangular solids or similar setups where several dimensions are defined as multiples of one base dimension.
Boundary: Ignore when relationships are additive, involve non-volume formulas, or the question explicitly asks for estimation rather than exact algebra.

Transfer rule: If grouped profit rates are compared with a stated total difference, then equate the excess/shortfall from the weighted-average rate to that money difference before solving for unit cost.
Error pattern: Ignored the explicit difference condition and treated unequal group profits as exactly equal to the uniform-profit case.
Diagnostic check: Compute weighted average profit across groups; compare it to the hypothetical uniform rate, multiply the rate gap by total cost, and verify it matches the stated rupee difference.
Use when: A quantity is split into parts sold at different percentage gains/losses and another overall percentage scenario is compared by a fixed amount.
Boundary: Ignore when no absolute difference between scenarios is given or when unit costs vary across items.

Transfer rule: If a moving object passes a stationary point, then distance traveled equals only the object’s full length; compute speed = length ÷ time and convert units before matching choices.
Error pattern: I likely misapplied a speed formula or skipped the unit conversion from meters per second to the answer’s unit.
Diagnostic check: Write “relative distance = ?” first; for point-crossing set it to full length, calculate m/s, then multiply by 3.6 if choices look like km/h.
Use when: Length-time motion questions involve trains, platforms, poles, or people, especially “crosses/passes” wording with mixed distance and speed units.
Boundary: Ignore when both bodies move and relative speed is required, or when crossing a bridge/platform changes distance beyond the object’s length.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and you need when one is ahead by a certain number of laps, then use relative rate = faster rate − slower rate and solve gap ÷ relative rate, then convert units.
Error pattern: Confusing an individual completion rate with the rate at which the difference between their lap counts grows.
Diagnostic check: Compute the lap-gap growth per hour first; divide the target gap by that value; verify the resulting time makes the lap difference equal the target.
Use when: Two entities move on the same repeating path or task and the question asks about being ahead by some amount after starting together.
Boundary: Ignore this when start times differ, directions differ, or the question asks for a meeting/overtaking count instead of a gap size.

Transfer rule: If two mixture equations share two unknown volumes, then write both total-volume and total-content equations and solve simultaneously before checking choices.
Error pattern: I replaced algebra with unsupported trial values and ignored that both constraints determine a unique mixture.
Diagnostic check: Define variables for each component, compute target pure amount, solve the linear system, then verify the result reproduces both total volume and concentration.
Use when: Apply to blend, concentration, percent, ratio, or weighted-average problems where components combine into a stated total and target composition.
Boundary: Ignore when only an estimate/comparison is asked or when the relationship is non-additive, nonlinear, or lacks enough equations for unique volumes.

Transfer rule: If a counting question says “at least one” from two groups, then compute total selections and subtract the none-from-target-group complement exactly once.
Error pattern: Started with the correct complement method, then double-counted by re-adding a valid case and changing approach midstream without a set-based justification.
Diagnostic check: Write the target set and its complement in words; verify they are disjoint and exhaustive, then ensure every subtraction/addition term maps to one set only once.
Use when: Selection/counting problems involve combinations, two categories, and wording like “at least one,” “none,” or “not all.”
Boundary: Ignore when choices are ordered, categories overlap, or constraints are not expressible as a simple complement.

Transfer rule: If two speeds give two different arrival times for the same trip, then equate distances and solve start-time/travel-time before finding the needed speed.  
Error pattern: I jumped to an intuitive middle-or-higher speed instead of using constant-distance relationships between rate and time.  
Diagnostic check: Let the common departure time be t; write distance as speed × (arrival time − t) for each case, solve t, then compute required speed from the target arrival.  
Use when: This applies to fixed-distance travel problems with unchanged start point and multiple speed/arrival-time scenarios.  
Boundary: Ignore this when distance changes, departure times differ by case, or there are stops, breaks, or varying speeds within a trip.

Transfer rule: If counting unordered selections with an “at least one from group X” condition, then count all valid composition cases or use total minus excluded cases.
Error pattern: Tendency to mix ordered and unordered counting, invent duplicate corrections, and let arithmetic drift even when the final choice happens to be right.
Diagnostic check: List allowed group splits, compute each with combinations, then verify the sum matches total committees minus committees with none from the required group.
Use when: Selection/counting problems involve small groups, committees/teams, no order, and membership constraints like “at least one,” “exactly one,” or “none.”
Boundary: Ignore this when roles/order matter, repetitions are allowed, or outcomes are arranged rather than merely chosen.

Transfer rule: If one worker is stated to be “as fast as” another by a factor, then convert that factor into rates first and add rates, not times.
Error pattern: Confusing speed relationships with time relationships, especially assuming proportional changes in days instead of using work-per-day.
Diagnostic check: Set slower rate to 1 unit/day-equivalent, express the other from the wording, add rates, then verify combined time = 1 divided by total rate.
Use when: This applies to work-time, pipes, machines, or team-output problems where relative speed and solo completion time are given.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem gives direct combined rates/times already or includes changing productivity across different intervals.

Transfer rule: If a problem equates selling value of one quantity to cost value of another, then compare per-item rates by dividing each side by its quantity before finding profit/loss percent.
Error pattern: Treated total-price equality too directly and skipped converting to unit price, leading to a wrong percentage ratio.
Diagnostic check: Let total equality be q1×SP = q2×CP; compute SP/CP = q2/q1, then percent change = |1 − SP/CP| × 100, with sign from whether SP/CP is below or above 1.
Use when: Relevant in percentage profit-loss questions involving different counts, equal total amounts, or bulk-to-unit comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when unit rates are already given directly or when totals include extra charges, discounts, or mixed item types.

Transfer rule: If two quantities have a known sum and one exceeds the other by a fixed amount, then define variables and verify whether the prompt asks for a single quantity or an expression after combining conditions.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting a direct expression quickly, but the general risk is skipping a consistency check between sum-and-difference relationships and the requested target.
Diagnostic check: Let the smaller be s and the larger be s+d; substitute into the stated total, isolate s, and compare the result’s form with your choice.
Use when: Apply this on word problems about two related amounts linked by a total and a stated difference.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is multiplicative, ratio-based, or involves extra independent variables not tied to the two amounts.

Transfer rule: If two parts have a fixed fractional relationship and a known total, then express them as ratio units, sum the units, and divide the total by that sum.
Error pattern: Success came from converting a part-to-part fraction into a whole-part ratio instead of guessing from the choices.
Diagnostic check: Let the larger part be 1 unit and the smaller be the stated fraction; verify the two unit amounts add to the total before mapping back.
Use when: Apply this to cut, split, age, money, or length problems where one amount is a stated fraction of another and the total is given.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship compares both parts to the total, involves a difference, or changes over time.

Transfer rule: If a line is given by slope plus an intercept, then first convert each line into a complete equation before finding any intersection quantity.
Error pattern: I treated an intercept as if it remained true at the intersection and mixed features from different lines without solving the system.
Diagnostic check: Write both equations, substitute or set them equal, solve for the shared coordinates, then plug back into both equations to verify the same point.
Use when: Apply this on coordinate-geometry questions involving two lines, intercept descriptions, and any request about their intersection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task concerns only one line’s own intercept or asks for a property that does not require the intersection point.

Transfer rule: If a number is divisible by two given integers, then test the least common multiple of those integers, not larger common multiples.
Error pattern: Success came from combining divisibility conditions via prime factors instead of guessing from one condition alone.
Diagnostic check: Factor each divisor into primes, take the highest power of each prime across them, multiply, then verify any candidate is guaranteed by that product.
Use when: Apply this on divisibility or “must be a multiple of” questions involving two or more divisors.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions are not simultaneous divisibility facts or when extra constraints change what is guaranteed.

Transfer rule: If a quotient with variables is said to be an integer/prime, then first enforce divisibility and integrality before testing any listed statements.
Error pattern: Success came from checking number-form constraints early instead of inferring properties of the variables from the conclusion.
Diagnostic check: Write the expression as a divisibility condition, list all ways the denominator can divide the numerator factor, and see whether any case can yield the required integer type.
Use when: Apply this to algebraic multiple-choice questions where an expression involving variables must be an integer, prime, even/odd, or otherwise have a strict number-theory property.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is purely symbolic manipulation or when integrality/divisibility is explicitly guaranteed already.

Transfer rule: If average difference over n periods is given, then convert it to a total difference and compare it to the sum of known period-by-period differences.
Error pattern: Mixed averages with monthly values by reusing variables across periods and cancelling unmatched terms instead of tracking each month separately.
Diagnostic check: Write d1, d2, d3 for period differences, compute n×(average difference), and verify d1+d2+d3 equals that total before choosing.
Use when: Relevant in multi-period comparison problems involving averages, totals, and changing gaps between two quantities across periods.
Boundary: Ignore when periods have unequal weights, missing periods, or the mean relation is not arithmetic across the same set of periods.

Transfer rule: If a question changes the interest rate but gives only total simple interest, then first check whether the principal or original rate can be uniquely recovered before computing any increase.
Error pattern: Treated an absolute rate increase as directly proportional to known interest without verifying that enough variables were known.
Diagnostic check: Write SI = P×R×T/100; count unknowns after substituting given values, and if more than one independent unknown remains, reject any numeric increase.
Use when: Simple-interest word problems compare earnings under a changed rate, time, or principal and provide only one interest amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the missing quantity is explicitly given or can be derived from another independent relation.

Transfer rule: If a quadrilateral problem gives both diagonals and asks for rhombus area, then compute one-half times their product.
Error pattern: I misrecalled or confused the area formula, likely using an extra factor or a different shape’s rule.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the target formula symbolically and test with easy values; equal diagonals should match the square case.
Use when: Apply this for rhombi, kites, or any figure where area is derived directly from perpendicular diagonals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives side and height, base and altitude, or asks for perimeter or side length instead.

Transfer rule: If multiple repeating intervals must align again, then compute their least common multiple and add that duration once to the start time.
Error pattern: I confused repeated-change synchronization with some other aggregation, indicating a failure to translate the scenario into an LCM timing model.
Diagnostic check: Prime-factor each interval, take the highest power of each prime to form the common cycle, then verify that cycle is divisible by every interval before converting to clock time.
Use when: Apply this to “again together,” “simultaneously,” or recurring-event synchronization problems with fixed repeating periods.
Boundary: Ignore this when intervals are nonrepeating, conditional, drifting, offset by different starts, or the question asks for counts rather than next alignment time.

Transfer rule: If a selection must include specific members, then fix them first and count ways to choose the remaining slots from the remaining pool, over all possible teams.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the condition into combinations instead of treating choices as ordered or using unsupported probability shortcuts.
Diagnostic check: Compute favorable and total counts with combinations, cancel carefully, and verify the result is between 0 and 1 and decreases as more required members are imposed.
Use when: This applies to random committee or team selection without order, especially when certain named people must all be included.
Boundary: Ignore this when selections are sequential with changing probabilities, when order matters, or when members have unequal selection chances.

Transfer rule: If shares are bought at a premium/discount, then compute dividend from face value per share, not from purchase price or total amount invested.  
Error pattern: Confusing market cost with nominal share value when converting an investment amount into dividend income.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, calculate number of shares = total paid ÷ issue price per share, then annual dividend = number of shares × dividend rate × face value.  
Use when: This applies to stock/share questions giving face value, premium or discount, total investment, and a dividend percentage.  
Boundary: Ignore this when returns are based on yield, interest on invested amount, capital gain, or dividend is explicitly stated on market price.

Transfer rule: If an expression mixes parentheses, multiplication, subtraction, and absolute values, then simplify inside grouping symbols first, apply multiplication, and evaluate each absolute-value part separately before the final subtraction.
Error pattern: Likely sign/order-of-operations slip from compressing multiple arithmetic steps mentally.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the work as sequential snapshots: inner parentheses, scaled result, each subtraction, absolute values, final combine; verify every negative sign survives each step.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic expressions with nested grouping, a coefficient outside parentheses, and absolute-value bars around subexpressions.
Boundary: Ignore for problems driven mainly by algebraic identities, estimation, or conceptual interpretation rather than exact stepwise arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If comparing “what percent less” between taxed totals, then compute each final total first and divide the difference by the reference item’s final total.
Error pattern: Mixed up the base for the percent comparison after correctly noticing taxes change both amounts.
Diagnostic check: Write three expressions: first final cost, second final cost, and (reference − other) / reference; verify the denominator matches the item being compared against.
Use when: Two quantities each get different percent changes and the question asks how much less or more one final amount is than the other.
Boundary: Ignore when asked only for absolute difference, tax amount alone, or percent change from an item’s own original price.

Transfer rule: If counting selections of identical items across categories with at-least-one constraints, then subtract one from each category first and apply combinations as C(remaining+categories−1, categories−1).
Error pattern: Mixed up the stars-and-bars parameters, swapping the number of remaining items with the number of categories.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, define variables explicitly: remaining items r and categories k; verify the count uses r stars, k−1 separators, and total slots r+k−1.
Use when: Total quantity is fixed, order does not matter, categories are distinct, and minimum-per-category conditions appear.
Boundary: Ignore when items are distinguishable, order/sequence matters, or category limits/dependencies make basic stars-and-bars invalid.

Transfer rule: If partnership profits are divided by capital only, then convert one known partner’s profit share into the common profit-to-capital ratio, find any missing profit share from the total, and divide by that same ratio.  
Error pattern: Treated proportional distribution loosely and likely rounded or skipped reconstructing the full share breakdown before solving for the unknown capital.  
Diagnostic check: Compute rate = known share / known capital; compute remaining partner’s share = total profit minus other stated shares; then verify each share equals rate × capital exactly.  
Use when: A profit-sharing partnership problem gives total profit, at least one capital, and some partners’ profit shares.  
Boundary: Ignore if time, different ratios, salaries, interest, or unequal sharing rules alter profit allocation.

Transfer rule: If a point’s coordinate is written as an expression and lies on a graph, then substitute the given coordinate into the graph first, equate the matching coordinate expression, and only afterward solve for the variable.
Error pattern: Mixed up x- and y-coordinates and then treated an impossible intermediate value as if it were valid.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write “x = ___, y = ___,” plug only x into the function, compare the resulting y to the point’s y-expression, and verify the final variable makes both representations equal.
Use when: A point on a curve has one coordinate numeric and the other expressed with a variable or exponent.
Boundary: Ignore for problems without coordinate substitution or where both coordinates are independently specified.

Transfer rule: If a linear relation between two nonzero integers reduces to one variable being a fixed positive fraction of the other, then infer same sign and fixed ratio before judging order claims.  
Error pattern: I overtrusted a ratio-comparison statement and skipped checking whether sign cases change subtraction or ordering conclusions.  
Diagnostic check: First isolate one variable as k times the other; record whether 0<k<1 or k>1 and whether k is positive or negative, then test sign-sensitive claims with both positive and negative examples.  
Use when: The choices mix ratio, sign, “between,” product, or difference statements derived from a single linear equation.  
Boundary: Ignore this when extra constraints fix the sign or when the relation is nonlinear, absolute-value based, or not reducible to a constant multiple.

Transfer rule: If a percentage describes one part of a total count, then convert it to an equation before manipulating expressions like sums or ratios.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping words to variables correctly and treating the percent as part-to-whole, not as an added amount.
Diagnostic check: Write “part = rate × whole,” substitute the given variables, then simplify the target expression using that relation only.
Use when: This applies to word problems with percentages, counts, and variables tied by phrases like “out of,” “of the total,” or “is x%.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the percentage refers to change over time, conditional probability, or a different base than the stated total.

Transfer rule: If a divisor of a power expression is known from a congruence like base^n ≡ -1, then rewrite candidates using odd multiples of n and factor identities before deciding.
Error pattern: Success came from exploiting exponent structure, but avoid unsupported classifications or invalid algebraic rewrites of exponential forms.
Diagnostic check: Let t = base^n; verify t ≡ -1 modulo the divisor, then test each candidate by reducing its exponent relative to n and checking whether it becomes t^(odd) + 1 or another forced zero form.
Use when: Relevant for divisibility questions involving powers of the same base and a given relation of the form base^n ± 1.
Boundary: Ignore when candidates use different bases, added constants break pure-power forms, or no clean exponent multiple/remainder relation exists.

Transfer rule: If a price cut causes the loss to “increase by x%,” then treat x% as x% of cost price unless the statement explicitly says “of the previous loss.”
Error pattern: Misread a percent change in loss percentage as a percent of the earlier loss amount, causing the wrong equation structure.
Diagnostic check: Let cost be C; write both losses as C minus each selling price, subtract them, and verify the difference equals x/100 × C.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss questions with two selling prices and wording like “loss/profit increases or decreases by k%.”
Boundary: Ignore when the problem explicitly says the change is relative to the previous profit/loss amount or gives markup/discount percentages instead.

Transfer rule: If comparing recurring rates with different time units, then convert both to the same yearly basis before subtracting.
Error pattern: I mixed unequal periods and used an inconsistent annualization, causing a bad comparison.
Diagnostic check: Compute annual cost two ways: weekly rate × 52 and monthly rate × 12; verify both use full-year counts before finding savings.
Use when: Apply this on word problems with weekly, monthly, daily, or yearly prices asking for total cost or savings over a year.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem explicitly supplies an exact conversion between periods or asks only about a single period.

Transfer rule: If a word problem changes quantities by moving an amount, then write post-transfer amounts with ± on both containers before applying any ratio.
Error pattern: I matched ratios to original amounts and reversed/omitted transfer effects, creating equations from the wrong state.
Diagnostic check: For each scenario, make “after” expressions for both buckets, then verify conservation: one loses exactly what the other gains and totals stay equal.
Use when: Relevant in two-container transfer problems with sequential hypotheticals, especially when ratios are stated after the move.
Boundary: Ignore when ratios refer to unchanged starting amounts or when transfer/conservation is not the relationship being modeled.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives overlapping category counts and asks for “none,” then compute “at least one” with inclusion–exclusion and subtract from the total.
Error pattern: Missed or misapplied overlap accounting, causing double-counting or an incorrect subtraction from the overall group size.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write union = sum of singles − sum of pairwise overlaps + triple overlap; then verify each overlap is used once with the stated triple condition.
Use when: Relevant for survey/set/Venn problems with multiple groups, shared members, and a request for total in any group or in none.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are mutually exclusive, overlaps are impossible, or the question does not depend on combining set counts.

Transfer rule: If two item counts and a total value are given, then set one equation for total quantity and one for weighted price, or subtract the lower unit price from the average to get the higher-price fraction.
Error pattern: Chose an option without verifying it satisfies both constraints; failed to use the price gap and average-price check.
Diagnostic check: Compute total value divided by total items; compare that average to each unit price, then use (average − lower price)/(higher − lower price) × total items and verify both totals exactly.
Use when: Relevant for two-category mixture or sales-count problems with distinct unit prices, a combined count, and a combined revenue.
Boundary: Ignore when there are more than two categories, changing prices, taxes/discounts, or noninteger/approximate data.

Transfer rule: If an average changes when one value is added, then convert both averages to totals and subtract to get the added value.
Error pattern: Treated an average shift as a direct score guess instead of reconciling totals across different group sizes.
Diagnostic check: Compute old total = old average × old count and new total = new average × new count; the difference must equal the missing score.
Use when: A problem gives before-and-after averages with one added or removed person, item, or test result.
Boundary: Ignore when the average changes because multiple values change or when weights differ across members.

Transfer rule: If two ticket types have a known price gap, then compare total revenue to the all-higher-price baseline and convert the shortfall into counts before taking any difference.
Error pattern: I jumped from totals to a plausible option without anchoring the arithmetic to a baseline model.
Diagnostic check: Compute revenue assuming all tickets are the higher price; divide the shortfall by the price difference to get one group’s count, use the total to get the other, then subtract.
Use when: This applies to two-category count-and-total word problems with fixed prices or rates and a asked-for difference.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are more than two categories, variable pricing, discounts, or noninteger constraints.

Transfer rule: If an absolute value has the form |a − bn| with integer n, then compare a/b to nearby integers and test those nearest values only.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing a minimization over integers to nearest-integer distance, not from trying many cases.
Diagnostic check: Compute a/b, identify floor and ceiling, evaluate the expression at both, and choose the smaller absolute result.
Use when: The variable is restricted to integers and the target is the least value of a linear absolute expression.
Boundary: Ignore when the variable is unrestricted, multiple variables interact, or the expression is not linear in the integer variable.

Transfer rule: If one unknown is added to a set with a target average, then compute x = (target average × count) − sum(known values).
Error pattern: Success came from using the average-as-total relationship instead of guessing near the center or relying on option spacing.
Diagnostic check: Count items, multiply by the target average, add the known numbers once, and verify the difference restores the target average when substituted.
Use when: A problem gives several explicit values, exactly one missing value, and a stated average or mean.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are multiple unknowns, weighted groups, medians, or averages that change between groups without fixed counts.

Transfer rule: If a ratio of integers is given as a terminating decimal, then rewrite it as a reduced fraction and infer mandatory divisors from the reduced numerator.
Error pattern: I guessed from decimal closeness and option familiarity instead of converting exactly and using divisibility consequences.
Diagnostic check: Convert the decimal to a fraction over a power of 10, reduce by the gcd, and verify which answer choices must divide any multiple of the reduced numerator.
Use when: The problem gives integer variables linked by a decimal, percent, or ratio and asks what must be a factor or multiple.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is approximate, involves irrational values, or does not constrain numbers to integers.

Transfer rule: If arranging equal-sized groups with strict alternation in a row, then choose the starting-group pattern count and multiply by each group’s internal permutations.
Error pattern: Success pattern: translating a verbal constraint into structure first, then using multiplication instead of guessing from total unrestricted arrangements.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write the two possible alternating templates, place one group into its slots in all orders, the other group into remaining slots, then multiply.
Use when: Apply to lineup or seating problems with two categories, equal counts, and a hard alternation or slot-restriction condition.
Boundary: Ignore when counts differ, alternation is partial/circular, people are identical, or extra adjacency/position constraints change the template count.

Transfer rule: If a target mixture price lies between two component prices, then use alligation: cheaper:dearer = (dearer−mean):(mean−cheaper).
Error pattern: Reversed the ratio or matched option format without checking which ingredient each part represents.
Diagnostic check: Compute the two differences from the mean to each component, assign them crosswise, then verify the weighted average reproduces the target.
Use when: Two-price mixture problems ask for the mixing ratio needed to achieve a specified intermediate average cost or concentration.
Boundary: Ignore when there are more than two components, hidden quantities/constraints, or the ask is total amount rather than component-to-component ratio.

Transfer rule: If drawing from duplicated-value groups and asked for “at least one match,” then count the complement “all values distinct” first and subtract from 1.
Error pattern: Overcounted favorable hands or ignored dependence between draws; complement counting is cleaner when matches can occur in multiple overlapping ways.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute total combinations, then count selections with no repeated value by choosing distinct value-groups and one card from each; verify the result is less than 1 and exceeds the single-pair-only estimate.
Use when: Sampling several items without replacement from a deck or set containing repeated categories, especially when any repeated category qualifies.
Boundary: Ignore when draws are independent with replacement, or when the event is exactly k matches rather than at least one.

Transfer rule: If a parity question asks which option “must be true,” then test each option’s full statement against a small odd/even case before choosing.
Error pattern: I applied a valid parity fact but failed to verify option-level consistency with the exact answer format and key.
Diagnostic check: Let the premise force the base number’s parity, then evaluate every claimed consequence separately; reject any choice containing one false component.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice logic items about odd/even powers, squares, and statements joined by “and.”
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-ended proof, or when no answer choices need whole-option validation.

Transfer rule: If a number must keep the same digits under multiplication by several small integers, then test whether each product is a digit permutation of the original by comparing sorted digits or digit counts.
Error pattern: Success came from direct verification instead of relying on pattern recognition or guessing a famous cyclic number.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate, multiply by every required factor, reject any product with different length, then compare digit-frequency vectors to the original.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice or puzzle problems asking for invariant/rearranged digits after multiplication across a fixed range.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for algebraic proof, non-permutation properties, or allows added/removed digits or leading-zero reinterpretations.

Transfer rule: If an equation among positive integers simplifies to one variable equaling a sum of positive terms, then infer it is greater than each addend, not necessarily equal to either addend.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing first and separating “must be true” from statements that are merely possible.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite to simplest form, note positivity, then test each claim with one confirming deduction or one counterexample pattern.
Use when: Apply on algebraic multiple-choice items with integer constraints, especially after cancellation reveals additive structure.
Boundary: Ignore when terms can be zero/negative, or when operations like squaring, absolute value, or inequalities block direct sum-order reasoning.

Transfer rule: If a group/overall percentage problem mixes subgroup rates and a leftover count, then convert every statement into equations for totals, gifted, and non-gifted before choosing.
Error pattern: Treated one subgroup count as if it directly determined the target subgroup, without reconciling complementary counts across all people.
Diagnostic check: Compute total gifted and total non-gifted from the overall rate, subtract the given subgroup non-gifted to get the other subgroup non-gifted, then use that subgroup’s gift rate to verify.
Use when: Relevant for percentage word problems with two groups, an overall proportion, a subgroup proportion, and one subgroup remainder count.
Boundary: Ignore when choices can be determined by direct arithmetic with a single percentage and no interacting subgroup constraints.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and meet, then set equal time for both and express each distance as speed × common time before combining with any distance difference.
Error pattern: Treated a relative-motion setup loosely instead of converting the “extra distance” statement into an equation tied to the shared meeting time.
Diagnostic check: Let the common travel time be t; write both distances, subtract them to match the stated excess, solve for t, then add the distances and verify the difference condition.
Use when: Two objects move simultaneously until meeting and the prompt gives speeds plus how much farther one traveled than the other.
Boundary: Ignore this when start times differ, there are stops/turns, or the given comparison is about times rather than distances.

Transfer rule: If an integer divided by n is given as a decimal, then split the decimal into whole part and fractional part, and compute remainder = n × fractional part.
Error pattern: Treated the visible decimal ending as the remainder instead of converting the fractional quotient into units of the divisor.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify that quotient = integer part + remainder/divisor, and that the computed remainder is a whole number between 0 and divisor−1.
Use when: A problem gives division by a positive integer and expresses the result as a decimal or mixed number.
Boundary: Ignore this when the quotient is not exact information, the decimal is rounded, or the divisor is not fixed.

Transfer rule: If asked for the average of evenly spaced terms, then use the arithmetic-sequence mean: average = (first term + last term) / 2.
Error pattern: I treated a sequence-average question like a counting or single-term lookup instead of using structure across all terms.
Diagnostic check: List the first and last requested terms, verify equal spacing, compute their midpoint, and confirm it lies between them.
Use when: The problem asks for a mean of consecutive multiples, consecutive integers, or any uniformly spaced sequence.
Boundary: Ignore this when spacing is irregular, terms are weighted, or the set is not a complete arithmetic progression.

Transfer rule: If a problem compares averages of two related arithmetic sequences, then write each set explicitly and compute each mean from first-and-last terms before comparing.
Error pattern: Success came from structural decomposition: separating “first k terms” from “terms up to a bound” instead of merging similar wording.
Diagnostic check: Verify the second set’s count from the bound, list endpoints of both sets, compute both averages, then subtract and simplify.
Use when: Apply for averages of evenly spaced numbers, especially when one phrase describes a count and another describes a numerical cutoff.
Boundary: Ignore when the sets are not arithmetic progressions or when weighting/frequencies make endpoint averaging invalid.

Transfer rule: If a price is increased and then discounted, then multiply factors on cost (e.g., markup factor × discount factor) before converting back to profit percent.
Error pattern: Treated successive percentage changes as if they combine by simple subtraction or by an unsupported shortcut.
Diagnostic check: Assume cost = 100, compute listed price after markup, apply discount to that new price, then compare final selling price with 100.
Use when: A problem gives sequential percent changes on price, such as markup, discount, tax, commission, or rebate.
Boundary: Ignore when all percentages are explicitly on the same original base or when the question asks only for a single-step percent change.

Transfer rule: If a square of an integer is divisible by a composite, then factor the composite into primes and require the base to include each prime whose exponent in the square would otherwise be too small.
Error pattern: Treated divisibility of a square as if square roots or arbitrary factors determined the base; the right method is prime-exponent parity.
Diagnostic check: Prime-factor the divisor, compare each prime’s exponent with twice an integer exponent, and round each needed base exponent up to the smallest integer meeting the square’s requirement.
Use when: The prompt gives divisibility of a power, asks what must divide the base, and answer choices are products of small factors.
Boundary: Ignore for addition/subtraction divisibility, non-integer domains, or when the condition is about exact equality rather than divisibility.

Transfer rule: If two quantities have ratio a:b and equal increments change the ratio, then set them as ak and bk, form (ak+c)/(bk+c)=p/q, solve for k, and compare the resulting value to the listed choices before selecting.
Error pattern: Solved the algebra but failed the option-matching step, treating a computed value as if it were automatically present among choices.
Diagnostic check: After finding a numeric result, scan all options for an exact match; if none matches and a catch-all choice exists, select the catch-all.
Use when: Ratio-change word problems with equal additions or subtractions and multiple-choice answers including a fallback option.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are not exhaustive, units/rounding are unspecified, or the task is open-response.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem changes workers mid-process, then convert each stage into fractions of the whole and solve with rates, not elapsed-time intuition.
Error pattern: I treated the short joint-finishing time as if it directly implied the second worker’s solo time, skipping a rate equation.
Diagnostic check: Compute remaining fraction after stage one, divide by joint-stage time to get combined rate, then subtract the first worker’s known rate and invert.
Use when: Apply this to sequential work, pumps, pipes, or people where one agent starts alone and another joins later.
Boundary: Ignore when times refer to equal whole-job completion under constant teams with no stage changes.

Transfer rule: If combining purchases with different quantities, then compute one weighted average: total cost ÷ total items.
Error pattern: I used an unweighted or shortcut average of unit prices instead of aggregating quantities and costs first.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write two sums—overall quantity and overall spending—then divide; reject any choice not matching that quotient.
Use when: This applies to average rate or price questions built from multiple groups with unequal sizes or different per-unit costs.
Boundary: Ignore this when all groups have equal quantities, or when the question asks for a simple mean of listed rates rather than an overall average.

Transfer rule: If a set-counting problem gives totals for single categories, union, and full overlap, then use inclusion–exclusion with variables for exactly-one, exactly-two, and exactly-three before choosing.
Error pattern: Treated category totals as “only” counts and multiplied an overlap count by the number of pairs without justification.
Diagnostic check: Compute excess = (sum of category totals) − (union total); verify that excess equals (exactly-two total) + 2×(exactly-three total).
Use when: Percentages or counts involve several overlapping groups and ask for people/items in more than one group.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are disjoint, the data are already “exactly” counts, or pairwise overlaps are given directly.
