Diagnostic check: Write the cost formula for one complete container, multiply by 1, 2, 3 containers, and verify any proposed total by explicit arithmetic including reset charges.
Use when: Item cost depends on position within each package, batch, film, ride, or subscription cycle.
Boundary: Ignore when the marginal price does not reset across groups or when every item truly has the same unit price.

Transfer rule: If a problem preserves the same total while regrouping people, then first compute the total once and equate it to the required series total.
Error pattern: Mixed unrelated quantities and failed to conserve the fixed total before applying a summation model.
Diagnostic check: Write one equation for total participants from the first arrangement, then test candidate circle counts with n(n+1)/2 until it matches exactly.
Use when: Relevant in regrouping word problems that shift from equal-sized rows/columns to cumulative patterns like 1,2,3,...
Boundary: Ignore when totals can change between stages or when the later pattern is not a consecutive triangular buildup.

Transfer rule: If two scenarios cover the same distance with changed speed/time, then equate distance expressions using exact time conversion and solve algebraically before checking choices.
Error pattern: Converting mixed time to a rough decimal and then forcing an implausible rounded option caused arithmetic drift and unjustified answer selection.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite minutes as a fraction of an hour, cross-multiply to avoid rounded decimals, then verify the found speed reproduces identical distances in both scenarios.
Use when: Apply this to rate–time–distance questions where one quantity changes and the trip length stays constant across cases.
Boundary: Ignore this when distance is not fixed, or when the problem directly gives a proportion, average-speed shortcut, or requires separate journey segments.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem mixes minutes and km/h, then convert each time segment to hours before writing distance = speed × time for every segment.
Error pattern: Unit inconsistency and ad hoc adjustment after algebra can still land on the right option by luck, masking flawed setup.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify every term in the distance equation has units of kilometers and that segment times sum to the stated total.
Use when: The journey is split into multiple intervals with changing speeds, especially when times are given in minutes and speed in km/h.
Boundary: Ignore this when all quantities already share consistent units or the task is purely conceptual, not computational.

Transfer rule: If asked for distinct prime factors, then fully factor the number and add each unique prime once, ignoring exponents and composites.
Error pattern: Confusing prime-power decomposition with summing repeated factors or including nonprime pieces from the factorization.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the number as a product of primes only; circle unique primes, verify each is prime, then sum the circled set exactly once.
Use when: Relevant in questions about factorization, prime divisors, distinct factors, or sums/products built from unique prime components.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for all factors, counts with multiplicity, greatest common factors, or nonprime factor sums.

Transfer rule: If a selling price includes a markup of p% on cost, then compute cost as selling price ÷ (1 + p), not by subtracting p% of the selling price.
Error pattern: Treated the percentage as based on the final price instead of the original base, causing a base-rate reversal.
Diagnostic check: Write “selling = cost × (1 + p)” first, solve algebraically for cost, then multiply your result by (1 + p) to verify it returns the selling price.
Use when: Percent markup, margin, tax, discount reversal, or any problem asks for the original amount from a final amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent is explicitly defined on the final amount or no reverse-percent relationship is involved.

Transfer rule: If a tournament is single-elimination, then total matches equal total entrants minus one, because each match removes exactly one player.
Error pattern: I failed by not mapping the wording to the elimination invariant and instead guessing from options.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, count required eliminations to get one winner; verify one loss causes one elimination, so matches must equal that elimination count.
Use when: Apply this to bracket or knockout contests where losers cannot continue and the goal is a single champion.
Boundary: Ignore this when players can lose and still advance, when draws/replays occur, or when standings are based on round-robin points.

Transfer rule: If total text stays constant while line width changes, then compute new lines as old lines × old width ÷ new width.
Error pattern: Treated an inverse-size change loosely instead of conserving the total amount of content.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, calculate total characters from the original layout, divide by the new width, and confirm the direction: narrower lines must increase line count.
Use when: Layout, rate, density, or unit-conversion questions where one quantity is redistributed across different group sizes.
Boundary: Ignore when content changes, wrapping rules add/remove material, or the relationship is not simple conservation.

Transfer rule: If a fraction of a total is sold and a remainder count is given, then first recover the whole from the unsold fraction before computing revenue.
Error pattern: Treating the remaining count as sold count or skipping the whole-total reconstruction from part-to-whole information.
Diagnostic check: Let total be T; set unsold_fraction × T = remaining_count, solve T, then compute sold_fraction × T and multiply by unit price.
Use when: Word problems give a sold or unsold fraction, a leftover number of items, and ask for total money from sold items.
Boundary: Ignore when totals are already given directly or when item prices vary across groups requiring separate case totals.

Transfer rule: If one amount is stated as a fixed difference above another and a total is given, then assign the smaller amount a variable, express the larger as variable plus difference, and solve the sum equation.
Error pattern: I treated the difference as if it could be subtracted directly from the total without accounting for both people contributing to the total.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, substitute smaller = s and larger = s + d; verify total = 2s + d, then isolate s and compare with choices.
Use when: Relevant in algebra word problems involving two related quantities linked by “more than” or “less than” plus a combined total.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is multiplicative, ratio-based, or involves more than two quantities or changing amounts.

Transfer rule: If a line must be perpendicular to one line and share another line’s y-intercept, then use the negative reciprocal of the first slope and keep the second intercept unchanged.
Error pattern: Success came from separating slope and intercept constraints instead of mixing them from the same equation.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, extract both lines’ slopes/intercepts, compute the perpendicular slope, then verify candidate slope matches it and candidate constant term matches the required intercept.
Use when: Apply this on linear-equation multiple choice problems that combine a perpendicularity condition with a shared intercept or other single-parameter constraint.
Boundary: Ignore this when equations are not in slope-intercept form and you have not first converted them reliably.

Transfer rule: If variables are linked by chained equalities, then rewrite each variable directly in terms of the requested symbol before subtracting or combining.
Error pattern: Success came from correctly unpacking equality relationships instead of treating the chain as a single arithmetic expression.
Diagnostic check: Substitute a simple test value for the shared quantity, compute each variable, and verify your symbolic result matches the numeric difference.
Use when: Apply this on algebra questions with equalities like one variable equaling a multiple of another and also equaling a third form.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationships are independent equations requiring solving a system rather than simple substitution from a shared value.

Transfer rule: If each bet risks a fixed fraction of the current bankroll, then update multiplicatively per bet and combine identical outcomes as repeated factors.
Error pattern: Treated fractional wagering like additive gains/losses, double-counting wins instead of modeling bankroll evolution from the changing base.
Diagnostic check: Write the bankroll transform for one win and one loss, then verify that applying them in any order gives the same product.
Use when: The problem involves sequential bets, percentages or fractions of current money, and asks for a final amount after several wins/losses.
Boundary: Ignore this when stakes are fixed absolute amounts, payouts depend on external odds, or later bets are not based on current bankroll.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives two numbers’ HCF and LCM plus one number, then compute the other as (HCF × LCM) ÷ known number and verify integrality.
Error pattern: Success comes from recalling the product identity for two integers instead of guessing from option size or divisibility alone.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, multiply the known number by your candidate; it must equal HCF × LCM, and the gcd/lcm pair must match exactly.
Use when: Apply this for two-number integer problems involving gcd/hcf, lcm, and one missing value.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are more than two numbers, non-integers, or extra constraints that break the basic product identity alone.

Transfer rule: If set sizes are bounded and an overlap minimum is asked, then assign all flexible counts to other regions first and test whether the target overlap can be reduced to zero or one.
Error pattern: I jumped to a larger overlap without exhausting extreme allocations that satisfy all lower and upper bounds.
Diagnostic check: Draw a 3-set Venn with variables, place the fixed triple overlap, push each set to its nearest bound, and verify the target region under those extremal assignments.
Use when: This applies to inclusion-exclusion or Venn problems with ranges, fixed intersections, and a minimum/maximum overlap request.
Boundary: Ignore this when exact totals or additional pairwise constraints already determine the regions uniquely, making extremal shifting unnecessary.

Transfer rule: If several group-like percentages are all high and ask for the minimum in every group, then use lower bound = sum(percentages) − (number of groups − 1)×100.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing an inclusion–exclusion style overlap bound instead of averaging, multiplying, or guessing from closeness.
Diagnostic check: Add all given percentages, subtract the maximum excess above 100 shared across groups, and verify the result is within 0–100 and among the choices.
Use when: Apply for multiple-category preference/ownership questions with only overall percentages and a target of “all,” “common,” or “at least in every set.”
Boundary: Ignore when intersections, independence, actual counts, or exact overlap structure are provided; then this bound may be non-exact.

Transfer rule: If a total is split into taken and remaining with a stated difference, then define both parts algebraically from the same total before choosing.
Error pattern: I guessed from arithmetic intuition instead of enforcing a part-part-whole equation and the comparison statement exactly.
Diagnostic check: Let removed = x and remaining = total − x; substitute the verbal relation between them, solve, then verify both add to the total and satisfy the difference.
Use when: Apply this to word problems about an initial amount, an amount removed or used, and a sentence comparing the leftover to the removed amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when values are not complementary parts of one fixed total or the comparison is about ratios, rates, or percentages.

Transfer rule: If a whole amount is split into two parts and a transfer makes them equal, then set the initial difference of the parts equal to twice the transferred amount.
Error pattern: Misread a percentage relation to the total and failed to convert the balancing transfer into a difference equation before testing choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute one part from the stated percent of the total, get the other by subtraction, then verify that their difference equals 2 × transfer.
Use when: A full container is redistributed, one part is given as a percent less/more than the original, and a later transfer causes equality.
Boundary: Ignore when the transfer does not create equality or the percent is relative to another part rather than the original total.

Transfer rule: If motion is against a current, then use effective speed = still-water speed minus current speed, then compute time = distance / effective speed.
Error pattern: Confusing upstream speed with another rate formula or skipping the direction adjustment before calculating time.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the signed speed equation for the direction of travel and verify the resulting speed is slower than still-water speed but still positive.
Use when: Applies to river/current, wind, conveyor, or relative-motion problems where a mover’s base speed combines with an external flow.
Boundary: Ignore when no opposing/helping flow exists or when the given speed is already the net speed in the travel direction.

Transfer rule: If partners invest different multiples at different start times, then convert each to capital × active-months and split profit by that ratio.
Error pattern: I likely compared raw capitals or delayed starts incompletely instead of weighting each investment by its exact time in the business.
Diagnostic check: Set a common base amount x; compute each person’s month-weighted contribution, reduce the ratio, and verify all active months sum to a consistent 12-month window.
Use when: This applies to partnership, profit-sharing, or work-rate style questions where entry times and investment multiples both vary.
Boundary: Ignore this when shares are given directly, all investments begin together, or timing does not affect the payoff rule.

Transfer rule: If a process includes pauses after each completed segment, then count pauses as completed segments minus any final stop at the destination.
Error pattern: Miscounted repeated events and then accepted an option without validating units or arithmetic consistency.
Diagnostic check: Compute movement time and pause time separately, verify pause count with a segment timeline, then confirm total in the answer’s units.
Use when: Distance/rate problems include recurring breaks, fees, or delays triggered by each interval or milestone.
Boundary: Ignore when the stop explicitly occurs at the endpoint too, or when intervals are time-based rather than segment-completion based.

Transfer rule: If asked for the sum of consecutive integers from a first to a last value, then use average × count or the arithmetic-series formula before choosing.
Error pattern: Miscomputed a basic sequence total by guessing instead of applying a structured summation method.
Diagnostic check: Count terms inclusively, compute (first + last) / 2, multiply by the term count, then verify by pairing ends to get equal sums.
Use when: Relevant for ranges of consecutive whole numbers, especially inclusive endpoints and multiple-choice answers close together.
Boundary: Ignore for nonconsecutive sets, skipped intervals, weighted sums, or when the task is not a straightforward arithmetic series total.

Transfer rule: If simple interest equals the rate-number over the same number of years, then write SI = PRT/100 and isolate P before choosing.
Error pattern: Algebraic setup was fine in spirit, but variable cancellation and reciprocal handling were reversed.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the condition into SI = PRT/100, cancel the common factor carefully, and verify by plugging the resulting P back to recover the stated interest.
Use when: A percentage-rate-and-time simple-interest question asks for the principal in terms of the same variable or symbols.
Boundary: Ignore this when interest is compound, rates and times differ, or fees/instalments modify the basic SI formula.

Transfer rule: If a fill/drain problem gives solo fill time and net fill time, then compute leakage rate as solo fill rate minus net fill rate, then invert it for emptying time.
Error pattern: Confusing a net rate with the leak’s standalone rate and mixing time and rate operations.
Diagnostic check: Convert all times to “tank per hour,” verify solo rate = net rate + leak rate, then take reciprocal only after isolating the leak rate.
Use when: One agent fills, another drains, and the question asks for the drain alone from combined-performance data.
Boundary: Ignore when rates are not constant, capacities change, or the data are not about additive/subtractive work rates.

Transfer rule: If a number series has equal gaps between consecutive terms, then extend it by repeating that constant difference before considering other patterns.
Error pattern: I overlooked a simple first-order arithmetic progression and guessed a more complex rule without verifying consistency across all adjacent terms.
Diagnostic check: Compute at least the first three consecutive differences; if they match, apply that same gap to the last term and compare with choices.
Use when: This fits ordered numeric sequences where terms change steadily and the options include one value reached by a repeated add/subtract step.
Boundary: Ignore this when first differences vary systematically, ratios fit better, or digit-position transformations explain every term more cleanly.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is repeatedly changed by fractions, then treat each fraction as applying to the current amount unless the wording explicitly refers to the original.
Error pattern: Mixed whole-amount arithmetic with sequential fraction operations and failed to anchor the final target to the stated comparison amount.
Diagnostic check: Define start S, compute remaining amount step by step from S, compute target as S × (1 + percent increase), then subtract remaining from target using one common denominator.
Use when: Multi-step word problems involve fractions of a quantity, leftovers, spills, or “percent/fraction more than started” comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when changes are independent absolute amounts or when every fraction is explicitly of the original total.

Transfer rule: If asked for the chance that neither of two events happens, then compute 1 minus the union, with union = first + second − overlap.
Error pattern: Inclusion–exclusion/complement setup failure; treating “neither” as a direct subtraction without first forming the union.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the two-step template “union = p1 + p2 − both; neither = 1 − union” and verify the result is between 0 and 1.
Use when: Relevant for probability questions involving two events with individual chances and an overlap, especially wording like “at least one” or “neither.”
Boundary: Ignore for mutually exclusive counts without complements, conditional probability setups, or problems with more than two events unless the formula is expanded.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is “x% fewer” than a known amount, then multiply the original by (1 − x/100) before rounding.
Error pattern: Replaced a small percentage decrease with an excessively large drop, failing magnitude estimation after the percent calculation.
Diagnostic check: Estimate first: 5% is half of 10%, so subtract about one-twentieth of the original; verify the result stays close to the starting value.
Use when: Percent increase/decrease problems ask for a new value and then a rounded answer from multiple choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is applied repeatedly, to a different base, or when “fewer than” compares two unknown quantities.

Transfer rule: If two travel ranges use the same tank size and one mpg is a fixed amount less than the other, then set range/mpg equal for both and solve that equation.
Error pattern: Treated mpg and total range too directly, skipping the shared-capacity constraint that links the two situations.
Diagnostic check: Let higher efficiency be x and lower be x minus the stated difference; write equal tank capacities from each range, solve, then verify both capacities match.
Use when: A word problem compares distance per full tank, fuel efficiency, and a difference between efficiencies across two driving conditions.
Boundary: Ignore when fuel amounts differ, partial tanks are used, or no constant tank capacity is implied.

Transfer rule: If comparing counts of length n+1 and n arrangements without repetition from the same pool, then cancel the shared factors and keep only the extra multiplicative term.
Error pattern: Expanded full permutations correctly but failed to simplify the ratio by cancellation, causing an arithmetic mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Write both counts in product form, cross out identical leading factors, and verify the ratio equals the single leftover factor.
Use when: Counts involve ordered selections, no repeats, same source set, and lengths differ by exactly one.
Boundary: Ignore when repetition is allowed, order does not matter, or the two counts come from different pools or differ by more than one step.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is the result after a percent increase, then recover the original by dividing by 1 + rate, not by subtracting the percent from the final.
Error pattern: Treating percentage growth as an additive change from the new value instead of a multiplicative change from the old value.
Diagnostic check: Let prior = current / growth factor; then multiply prior by the growth factor and verify it reproduces the stated current exactly or within rounding.
Use when: The prompt gives a later amount and says it changed by a percent from an earlier amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent is of a different base, the change is a decrease, or the relationship is not direct single-step percent change.

Transfer rule: If two numbers share a given HCF and the remaining LCM factors are provided, then write the numbers as HCF×a and HCF×b with gcd(a,b)=1, using those factors as a and b.
Error pattern: Confusing factors of the LCM with extra factors of one number, instead of distributing them across the two coprime reduced numbers.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, divide both candidate numbers by the HCF; the quotients must be coprime, and their product must equal the non-HCF part of the LCM.
Use when: A problem gives an HCF plus leftover LCM factors and asks for the original numbers or the larger one.
Boundary: Ignore this when the numbers are not stated to share that HCF exactly, or when the LCM/HCF relationship is not the basis.

Transfer rule: If a rate question gives total distance over total time and distance per cycle, then compute per-time distance first and divide by distance per cycle.
Error pattern: Arithmetic and setup were correct, but the final choice contradicted the computed result due to answer-selection inconsistency.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write one equation with units, simplify to the target units, and verify the selected option matches that final numeric value.
Use when: Apply this to constant-speed, unit-rate, wheel/gears, rotations, or “per hour” problems requiring conversion from totals to rates.
Boundary: Ignore this when speed changes over time or when the asked quantity is not a simple distance-per-cycle rate.

Transfer rule: If a selection is split into independent category quotas, then compute combinations within each category and multiply the results.
Error pattern: I treated unordered selections like ordered picks, inflating the count by using permutations or sequential multiplication without dividing out order.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, ask: “Does swapping two chosen items within a category create a new outcome?” If no, use nCr for each category, not arrangements.
Use when: Apply this on grouped-choice counting problems with fixed numbers chosen from several distinct pools and no role labels for chosen items.
Boundary: Ignore this when chosen positions are labeled, order matters, or later choices depend on earlier selections.

Transfer rule: If seats are grouped and occupied group counts must all differ, then first assign the minimum distinct occupancies and subtract from the total before counting empty groups.
Error pattern: I chose an option without enforcing the distinctness constraint systematically; I treated capacity and occupancy too loosely.
Diagnostic check: List allowable distinct occupancies from zero up to capacity, build the smallest nonzero distinct set, sum it, and compare with the total people.
Use when: This applies to distribution problems with identical-capacity groups, a fixed total, and a requirement that occupied-group counts be all different.
Boundary: Ignore this when repeated occupancies are allowed, groups have unequal capacities, or the question is about arrangements rather than feasible occupancy counts.

Transfer rule: If exponential growth gives one time-to-multiple, then compare target multiples with exponent rules before estimating any rate.  
Error pattern: Success comes from using multiplicative scaling in compound growth instead of linear or rough rate approximation.  
Diagnostic check: Rewrite final/initial as powers of the known multiple; verify the needed factor equals the known factor times any extra factor, then add corresponding years.  
Use when: A quantity grows by a constant percentage per period and two target totals are both given relative to the same starting amount.  
Boundary: Ignore when growth is not compounded at a constant rate, or when contributions, withdrawals, or changing bases break pure exponential scaling.

Transfer rule: If comparing a sphere’s whole surface with a hemisphere’s whole surface, then include the hemisphere’s curved part plus its flat circular base before forming the ratio.
Error pattern: Omitted-component failure: treated a composite surface as only its curved area, producing an understated total.
Diagnostic check: Write each solid’s surface-area formula explicitly and mark every exposed face; verify the hemisphere count includes one circular base.
Use when: Relevant in geometry questions asking for total, whole, or exposed surface area of cut solids such as hemispheres, cylinders, cones, or prisms.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem asks only for curved/lateral area or when a base is absent, hidden, or explicitly excluded.

Transfer rule: If relative-position statements can both be true, then model the entities in a single ordered line and test the smallest arrangement first.
Error pattern: I jumped to adding counts independently instead of checking whether the same middle entity satisfies both observations.
Diagnostic check: Draw slots in a row, place one speaker, then verify whether another can have the opposite front/behind count without creating extra entities.
Use when: Apply this to counting riddles with “in front of,” “behind,” “between,” or mirrored statements from different speakers.
Boundary: Ignore this when statements refer to different groups, changing positions over time, or non-linear layouts.

Transfer rule: If people return together to a start point on a track, then compute the least common multiple of their lap times, including every participant named.
Error pattern: I used an incomplete set of cycle times, so the synchronization time fit only a subset rather than the whole group.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list all runners, count their lap times, and verify the common-return time is divisible by each listed time.
Use when: This applies to circular motion, repeated cycles, bells, shifts, or any “meet again at start/together” timing question.
Boundary: Ignore this when the meeting can occur away from the start or when speeds, starts, or directions are not fixed and identical in setup.

Transfer rule: If workers act sequentially on the same job, then convert each person’s time into work fractions, subtract completed fractions stepwise, and invert the leftover fraction done per given time.
Error pattern: I mixed days and work units, inventing arithmetic instead of tracking a single conserved quantity.
Diagnostic check: Set total work to 1; compute each stage’s completed fraction; verify fractions sum to 1 and only then convert the final worker’s rate into total time.
Use when: Use for time-and-work problems with handoffs, partial completion, or several workers contributing in separate intervals.
Boundary: Ignore when tasks are not identical, rates vary over time, or workers overlap with interaction effects.

Transfer rule: If a point’s coordinates are given on an unlabeled graph, then infer the hidden axes/origin from the drawing’s spacing and orientation before matching a candidate point.
Error pattern: Success came from using the visual layout rather than forcing an unsupported symmetry or algebraic rule from the coordinates alone.
Diagnostic check: Trace horizontal and vertical offsets from the known point to the candidate point, then verify those offsets match the sketch’s relative direction and distance.
Use when: A coordinate-plane diagram omits axes labels or origin, and one known point must anchor another point’s coordinates.
Boundary: Ignore this when the graph explicitly labels axes/origin or when a formula, not the picture, determines the point.

Transfer rule: If a price is sold at a discount on a stated price, then compute selling price as stated price × (1 − discount rate).
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the correct base quantity and applying percent decrease directly, rather than mixing up cost, markup, and discount.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What price is the discount applied to?” then multiply that amount by the remaining percent and verify the result is smaller.
Use when: Apply this for percentage discount questions involving listed, marked, or original price and a final selling amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when markup must be computed first or when discount is applied to a different base than the stated price.

Transfer rule: If a number is given by a remainder modulo n and then multiplied, then multiply the remainder and reduce modulo n; do not invent size-based cases.
Error pattern: Treated remainders as changing by ad hoc rules instead of using consistent modular arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the value as n*k + remainder, apply the operation, then strip off multiples of n and keep only the final residue.
Use when: A problem gives a remainder after division and asks for the remainder after addition, subtraction, or multiplication.
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut if the operation is not residue-preserving under the same modulus, such as ordinary division or comparisons of magnitude.

Transfer rule: If subgroup totals change by different percentages but the overall total after change is known, then set unknown subgroup counts, write both sum equations, and solve before comparing ratios.
Error pattern: Chose a plausible ratio by intuition instead of enforcing both the original-total and updated-total constraints simultaneously.
Diagnostic check: Let the two groups be x and y; verify x+y equals the first total and updated x and y equal the second total, then reduce x:y.
Use when: A mixture or population problem gives category-specific growth rates and both an initial combined total and a later combined total.
Boundary: Ignore when only one total is given or subgroup changes are identical, making direct ratio recovery impossible or unnecessary.

Transfer rule: If a rate is given per fixed base amount, then convert the total into that many bases and multiply once by the rate.
Error pattern: Mis-scaling a proportion by using the wrong number of groups or an extra zero; place-value/rate-conversion failure.
Diagnostic check: Compute total ÷ base unit, verify the quotient is reasonable, then multiply by the rate and estimate magnitude before choosing.
Use when: A word problem states “for every …” with large units like million or billion and asks for a total count.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is not proportional or when the given rate is already the total, percentage, or cumulative count.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives post-increase prices and asks for pre-increase values, then divide each final price by 1 plus its percent increase before adding.
Error pattern: Treated given amounts as original values and tried subtraction of the increase amount instead of reversing multiplicative percent change.
Diagnostic check: For each item, compute original = final/(1+r); then reapply the percentage increase to verify it returns the stated final amount.
Use when: The prompt states prices, wages, totals, etc. after percentage increases or decreases and asks for the before-change amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the given values are explicitly before-change amounts or when the percent is applied to the combined total rather than each part.

Transfer rule: If a target average over all weeks is given, then compute required future average as (target total for all weeks − current total) ÷ remaining weeks.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/setup drift after a correct first sum; mixing current-average adjustment with future-total calculation can produce impossible intermediate values.
Diagnostic check: Sum known weeks, compute target total as target average × total weeks, subtract to get needed combined future amount, then divide by remaining weeks and verify the 7-week average.
Use when: A word problem gives several past totals and asks what later average is needed to reach a specified overall average.
Boundary: Ignore when weights differ, periods are unequal, or the question asks for median, percent change, or one specific unknown value instead of a future average.

Transfer rule: If a trip has equal distances at two speeds, then use average speed = total distance ÷ total time, equivalently the harmonic mean 2ab/(a+b).
Error pattern: I treated the round trip like an arithmetic average of speeds or weighted the speeds incorrectly instead of averaging by time over equal distances.
Diagnostic check: Let each leg be distance d; compute times d/a and d/b, sum them, then divide 2d by that total and verify the result lies below the simple mean.
Use when: This applies to out-and-back journeys or any scenario with equal-distance segments traveled at different rates.
Boundary: Ignore this when segment times are equal, distances differ, or another quantity besides speed is being averaged.

Transfer rule: If counting digit strings with no repetition and a minimum length, then sum permutations for each allowed length from the minimum up to the total available digits.
Error pattern: I treated different lengths as multiplicative stages instead of mutually exclusive cases that must be added.
Diagnostic check: List every feasible length, write its count as a permutation of available symbols, and ask “add or multiply?”; use addition when one password has only one length.
Use when: The task counts arrangements from a fixed symbol set under uniqueness rules and allows several possible total lengths.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are made in sequential independent phases that all occur together, or when repetition is allowed.

Transfer rule: If rates and times change with leftover work, then define planned days as a variable and equate total work in both scenarios.
Error pattern: Mixing day counts and output rates informally, then rounding to fit options instead of solving the linear relationship exactly.
Diagnostic check: Write planned work = planned rate × d and actual completed work = actual rate × (d + extra days); include leftover separately and solve.
Use when: Relevant for work-rate, distance-rate-time, or production problems comparing an original plan with a delayed outcome and remaining amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the answer depends on estimation, discrete scheduling constraints beyond the model, or missing a consistent total-work equation.

Transfer rule: If profit and commission/discount are stated on different bases, then set net receipts from the marked amount equal to required selling price and solve exactly before checking options.
Error pattern: Arithmetic execution error followed by unjustified rounding to force a nearby option despite a precise linear equation.
Diagnostic check: Compute target receipt from cost first, write the single equation using multipliers, then reverse-calculate to verify the obtained marked amount reproduces that receipt exactly.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss, commission, discount, or markup questions where one percentage is on cost/selling price and another is on marked/list price.
Boundary: Ignore when all percentages share the same base or the problem explicitly instructs estimation or rounding.

Transfer rule: If every pair in a group interacts exactly once, then count unique pairs with n(n−1)/2 rather than multiplying per person directly.
Error pattern: Double-counting symmetric interactions by treating each person’s count as distinct instead of shared between two participants.
Diagnostic check: Compute total two ways—sum each person’s links, then divide by 2; verify it matches the combination formula for unordered pairs.
Use when: Relevant for handshake, friendship, connection, or edge-count problems where all members connect pairwise exactly once.
Boundary: Ignore when interactions are directional, repeated, missing for some pairs, or when self-interactions are allowed.

Transfer rule: If asked for a winner’s vote percentage, then add all candidates’ votes, divide the largest count by that total, and compare with nearby percent options.
Error pattern: Success came from using the full-part ratio method instead of estimating from a single pair or skipping the total.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the total includes every listed count, compute winner/total ≈ decimal, and confirm the chosen option matches after rounding.
Use when: This applies to election, survey, or category-share problems asking what percent of the whole the largest group received.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for margin, percentage points, growth rate, or a percent relative to another candidate rather than the total.

Transfer rule: If a simple-interest amount and time are given, then first compute the original rate from interest = amount minus principal, then apply only the stated rate increase to the same principal and time.
Error pattern: I matched an option without deriving the rate change systematically; I treated the new amount as a guess instead of recalculating from the base rate.
Diagnostic check: Compute original interest, divide by principal×time to get rate, add the increment, recompute interest, and verify amount = principal + new interest.
Use when: This applies to principal-amount-time questions involving simple interest and a changed rate.
Boundary: Ignore this when compounding, changing time/principal, or non-percentage adjustments are involved.

Transfer rule: If averages change after adding a fixed number of new performances, then convert averages to total-score equations and solve for the original count algebraically.
Error pattern: I guessed from average intuition instead of enforcing consistency between old total, added total, and new combined average.
Diagnostic check: Let original count be n; write old total = old average × n, added total = added average × added count, combined average = old average + stated increase; solve and verify integer n.
Use when: Apply to word problems about averages before and after extra games, tests, innings, or observations.
Boundary: Ignore when averages are weighted unequally, counts are unknown for multiple groups, or the change is not a simple combined-average update.

Transfer rule: If asked for the biggest measure that exactly measures several quantities, then compute their greatest common divisor, not any multiple.
Error pattern: Confused a “largest exact measuring unit” question with a common-multiple question; reversed divisor vs multiple reasoning.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test your candidate by dividing each quantity; all quotients must be whole numbers, and no larger listed unit should also divide all.
Use when: Apply this on packaging, tiling, grouping, or measuring problems asking for the greatest size/unit that fits several totals exactly.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a smallest common schedule/total, repeated coincidence, or any “minimum multiple” requirement.

Transfer rule: If partners invest for the same duration, then split profit in the ratio of their capitals and scale shares to the total profit.
Error pattern: Chose values without enforcing proportionality, effectively reversing or distorting the investment ratio.
Diagnostic check: Compute capital ratio, convert it to fraction shares, multiply by total profit, and verify the two amounts sum exactly to the stated profit.
Use when: A profit or loss must be divided among contributors whose invested amounts are given and time periods are equal.
Boundary: Ignore this when investment durations differ or when salaries, interest, prior withdrawals, or nonproportional rules affect sharing.

Transfer rule: If eating prey makes the eater become prey and others can then eat it, then analyze each agent’s incentive via parity/induction on predator count before choosing an outcome.
Error pattern: I matched a plausible end-state without checking whether any predator would rationally initiate the first eat under backward reasoning.
Diagnostic check: Test small cases in order (1, 2, 3 predators), record whether the first eater survives, derive the even/odd pattern, then verify the initial count against that pattern.
Use when: A puzzle has self-transforming consumption, repeated possible turns, and outcomes depend on whether any actor benefits from acting first.
Boundary: Ignore when actions are forced, simultaneous, random, or agents do not optimize self-preservation.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the percent sold from combined groups, then compute a weighted total: sold count in each group, sum sold, divide by sum of all items.
Error pattern: Mixing valid aggregate calculation with irrelevant manipulation after noticing option uncertainty; abandoning a correct method instead of trusting the checked result.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify units by writing “sold items / total items,” ensure the result is between the smallest and largest group sale rates, and stop if extra operations change the unit.
Use when: Totals are split across categories with different starting amounts and different percentages or rates.
Boundary: Ignore when all groups have equal starting sizes or the question asks for a simple average, not an overall rate.

Transfer rule: If a quantity-price problem gives one ratio and asks for another amount, then compute the unit rate first and scale once.
Error pattern: Treated a proportional relationship inconsistently, likely skipping the per-unit conversion and guessing among options.
Diagnostic check: Divide total cost by given quantity, multiply by target quantity, then verify the result preserves cost-per-unit equality.
Use when: Relevant for direct-proportion word problems involving prices, wages, speed, recipes, or any constant rate between two quantities.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is nonconstant, includes fixed fees, discounts, taxes, thresholds, or piecewise pricing.

Transfer rule: If counting possible diameters from points in/on a sphere, then first cap surface points using the percentage and pair only antipodal surface points.
Error pattern: Success came from reducing geometry to a matching/counting problem and enforcing all hidden constraints before evaluating choices.
Diagnostic check: Compute the greatest allowed number on the surface by flooring the percentage limit, then divide by two and floor again for the maximum number of diameter pairs.
Use when: A 3D geometry problem asks for the maximum number of diameters/chords under a restriction on how many points can lie on the boundary.
Boundary: Ignore when segments are not required to be diameters, boundary points are unrestricted, or points can coincide/non-antipodal endpoints are allowed.

Transfer rule: If a work problem gives completion times and a rate difference, then define total work as W, convert each time to rates as W/time, and solve algebraically before plugging values.
Error pattern: Treated a completion time like a page rate, mixing units and doing unsupported arithmetic with minutes, pages, and pages per minute.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write units on every quantity; verify each equation adds only rates to rates or multiplies rate × time = work.
Use when: Relevant for joint-work, machine-output, or printer/pump problems where total job size is unknown but times and relative speeds are given.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem directly gives absolute rates or asks only for a rate comparison without needing total work.

Transfer rule: If two movers start together and must meet at the start again, then convert both rates to the same lap-per-time unit and take the least common multiple of their lap times, not relative-speed catch-up.
Error pattern: Mixed units and treated a shared-start recurrence like an overtake problem, creating impossible lap counts and irrelevant differences.
Diagnostic check: Write each lap time in one unit, list the first few return-to-start times, and verify the chosen time is a common multiple; count the initial start as the first occurrence.
Use when: Two periodic motions on a loop begin together and the question asks for the next or second simultaneous return to a marked point.
Boundary: Ignore this when they start apart, move on different paths, or the meeting can happen anywhere, where relative position methods apply.

Transfer rule: If ages are linked by a fixed difference and a future ratio, then assign variables, write both equations for the same time point, and solve simultaneously.
Error pattern: I guessed from option plausibility instead of enforcing all stated constraints with algebra.
Diagnostic check: Let child = x and older person = x + gap; add the stated years to both, set the future multiple equation, solve, then verify both original and future conditions.
Use when: Apply on word problems involving present ages, age differences, and statements about future or past multiplicative relationships.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is not linear age arithmetic or when no consistent equation system is implied.

Transfer rule: If only solvent is removed from a mixture, then keep solute amount constant and recompute concentration as solute divided by the new total volume or mass.
Error pattern: Treated a concentration-change process as if the percentage stayed unchanged, ignoring that evaporation reduces the denominator only.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “solute before = solute after?”; if yes, calculate initial solute quantity and divide by final total quantity to verify the new percent.
Use when: Relevant in evaporation, dilution, concentration, mixing, boiling, drying, or replacement problems where one component changes while another stays fixed.
Boundary: Ignore when solute is also removed, added, reacts, precipitates, or when percent is defined on a different basis than the changing total.

Transfer rule: If multiple workers combine on one job, then convert each time to a work rate, add the rates, and invert once at the end.
Error pattern: Success comes from using rate-based reasoning instead of averaging times or picking a value between the individual times.
Diagnostic check: Assume one whole job; compute each worker’s fraction per hour, sum them, then verify the result is less than the slower time and no greater than the faster time.
Use when: Apply this to shared-work, fill-empty, travel-speed, or any problem where per-unit rates combine.
Boundary: Ignore this when tasks are sequential, workers interfere, or outputs are not additive.

Transfer rule: If a fraction is taken, then update the total remaining first and apply later fractions to that new remainder, not the original whole.
Error pattern: Fraction-of-a-remainder problems often fail by treating successive fractions as sharing the same base quantity.
Diagnostic check: Let the whole be 1; compute remaining after each step explicitly, and verify each fraction’s base before combining or subtracting.
Use when: Use this for sequential percentage or fraction changes, especially wording like “of the remaining,” “left,” or “after that.”
Boundary: Ignore this when all fractions are stated relative to the original whole or when quantities are independent, not sequential.

Transfer rule: If interest is compounded more than once per year, then convert the annual rate to rate-per-period and use principal × (1 + r/n)^(nt).
Error pattern: Treated a short, standard compounding setup as something requiring an inflated or mismatched calculation, ignoring scale and period consistency.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute the number of compounding periods, divide the annual rate by that count, apply the exponent, and verify the result is only moderately above the principal for one year.
Use when: Relevant for finance questions involving principal, annual rate, a time in years, and wording like monthly, quarterly, or half-yearly compounding.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem uses simple interest, continuous compounding, changing rates, deposits/withdrawals, or asks for interest instead of final amount.

Transfer rule: If a group’s average is given at an earlier time and a new member is added now, then first shift the original group’s total to the present before comparing with the new overall total.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking totals over time instead of mixing averages from different dates.
Diagnostic check: Compute old-group total from the earlier average, add elapsed years times original member count, then subtract from the current combined total; verify units are all “years of age now.”
Use when: Use for age/average word problems with time gaps, changing group size, or a person joining later.
Boundary: Ignore when all averages refer to the same date or when no membership change occurs.

Transfer rule: If a calendar-count problem asks for 53 occurrences in a 366-day year, then use 366 = 52 weeks + 2 days and count which weekdays get the two extras.
Error pattern: Lucky correctness from invalid arithmetic and mixing “number of weekdays” with “probability of start days” instead of using week-remainder structure.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, write year length as 52 weeks plus remainder, list the consecutive extra weekdays from the start day, and verify the target weekday is included exactly when intended.
Use when: Randomly selected year/day-of-week problems ask about extra occurrences of a weekday in leap or common years.
Boundary: Ignore when weekdays are not equally likely or when the selection process is not a uniformly random year/start weekday.

Transfer rule: If a mixture is diluted by adding only solvent, then keep solute amount constant and solve using initial solute = final concentration × final total volume.
Error pattern: Treated concentration change too intuitively instead of enforcing a conservation equation for the unchanged ingredient.
Diagnostic check: Compute solute first; then divide by target fraction to get required final volume; added solvent must equal final volume minus starting volume.
Use when: Percent concentration changes because pure solvent is added to a solution, with no solute removed or added.
Boundary: Ignore when the added substance contains solute, densities/weight-volume conversions matter, or volume is not additive.

Transfer rule: If distance and constant speed are given, then compute time = distance ÷ rate and keep units aligned.
Error pattern: Used the wrong operation or weak proportional reasoning, producing a too-small time from a larger distance.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, divide total distance by per-hour distance, then verify by multiplying the result back by the hourly rate.
Use when: Relevant in one-step rate, speed, work, or unit-rate multiple-choice questions with constant pace and direct scaling.
Boundary: Ignore when the rate changes over time, there are stops/segments, or values use different units that must be converted first.

Transfer rule: If asked for “at least one” in random selection, then compute the complement (“none”) and subtract from 1 using combinations.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing a simpler complement event instead of summing many overlapping favorable cases directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write both events, verify they are exact complements, then calculate total-ways and complement-ways with the same counting method.
Use when: Applies to without-replacement selection problems involving categories and phrases like “at least one,” “none,” “all,” or “not all.”
Boundary: Ignore when trials are dependent in a nonuniform way, the event is not a true complement, or outcomes are weighted/ordered inconsistently.

Transfer rule: If two items have the same selling price but opposite equal percent gain/loss, then compute each cost price separately from the common selling price before totaling.
Error pattern: Treating symmetric percentages as canceling on total price instead of recognizing gains and losses apply to different cost bases.
Diagnostic check: Convert sale price to cost using factors (for gain divide by 1+p, for loss divide by 1−p); add both costs and verify the total differs from simply doubling one base.
Use when: Equal selling prices are given with percentage profit on one item and percentage loss on another.
Boundary: Ignore when percentages apply to selling prices, or when both percentages affect the same original base.

Transfer rule: If output depends jointly on workers and days, then compute unit rate as total ÷ (workers × days) before scaling.
Error pattern: I broke proportional reasoning by dividing by only one factor, then added an unjustified adjustment step.
Diagnostic check: Verify dimensions cancel: length/(workers·days) × workers × days = length; also compare with baseline—more workers but far fewer days should yield less total output.
Use when: Apply on work-rate, production, construction, or similar direct-variation problems with interchangeable workers over time.
Boundary: Ignore when rates vary, teams are nonidentical, setup/fixed costs matter, or output is not proportional to workers and time.

Transfer rule: If a whole-trip average is given for changing rates, then compute total distance in segments and set overall average = total distance / total time.
Error pattern: I relied on intuition about averaging rates instead of forming the weighted-average equation with time weights.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, assign total time t, write segmented distance, divide by t, and verify the resulting average exactly matches the given overall rate.
Use when: Rates differ across time blocks or phases, and the question asks for total time, total distance, or combined average speed.
Boundary: Ignore this when all segments have the same rate or when distances, not times, are the direct weights.

Transfer rule: If a variable is constrained to be odd and an expression mixes powers, sums, or a reciprocal, then reduce each factor modulo 2 and check integer-ness before judging parity.
Error pattern: I treated parity term-by-term and missed that factoring can force an even product while a reciprocal-looking factor may still be an integer under the constraint.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite using parity-preserving identities, test whether every factor is integer for all allowed inputs, then mark any product with an unavoidable even factor as must-be-even.
Use when: Applies to multiple-choice parity questions with odd/even assumptions, polynomial factors, cancellations, or nonobvious integer factors.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not about guaranteed parity over all allowed values, or when domain/integer status is unspecified.

Transfer rule: If one quantity is x% more than another, then write larger = (1 + x/100)·smaller and invert to express smaller as a fraction of larger.
Error pattern: Reversing a percent-increase statement without converting through the multiplicative factor causes wrong reciprocal percentages.
Diagnostic check: Assign a simple base like 100 to the original smaller quantity, compute the larger, then divide back: smaller/larger × 100 should match your choice.
Use when: This applies to comparison problems involving “more than,” “less than,” or asking one quantity in terms of the other.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is an absolute difference, a change over time, or already directly gives the requested ratio.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is bought for a total amount, then find unit price by dividing total cost by total items before applying discounts and unit conversion.
Error pattern: Success came from chaining ratios and conversions stepwise instead of manipulating the final expression too early.
Diagnostic check: Compute item count carefully, then verify the sequence: unit price → discounted unit price → total for requested items → convert dollars to cents.
Use when: Relevant in word problems with grouped quantities, percentage discounts, and a final unit change such as dollars to cents.
Boundary: Ignore this when prices are not proportional per item or when fees, taxes, or mixed pricing break simple unit-rate scaling.

Transfer rule: If water content changes but only water is lost, then hold the non-water mass constant and solve from dry-matter percentages.
Error pattern: Treated the water percentage as directly scalable total weight, ignoring that percentages apply to different wholes after shrinkage.
Diagnostic check: Compute current dry mass first, then divide by the original dry-matter fraction; verify the same dry mass appears in both states.
Use when: A substance changes weight because moisture changes, especially in fruit, food drying, dehydration, or concentration scenarios.
Boundary: Ignore when solids are added/removed, multiple ingredients change, or the problem asks for a ratio unrelated to conserved dry mass.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem changes crew size after part of a job is done, then convert work to worker-days and compute remaining time from remaining worker-days ÷ new crew size.
Error pattern: I treated time and crew size too intuitively, skipping the conserved-quantity setup and losing the fractional result.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, calculate total worker-days from the completed fraction, infer full-job worker-days, subtract completed worker-days, then divide by the new number of workers.
Use when: This applies to shared-rate jobs with a known fraction completed, constant individual rates, and a later change in team size.
Boundary: Ignore this when workers have different rates, rates vary over time, or the task is not proportional to worker-days.

Transfer rule: If pieces per item are given, then convert to cuts per item as pieces minus one before using a cutting rate.
Error pattern: Treated pieces as equal to cuts, causing a systematic overcount in rate-to-output problems with segmented objects.
Diagnostic check: Compute cuts needed for one finished item; multiply by your item count and verify it matches total cuts from rate × time.
Use when: A task involves cutting, slicing, or partitioning whole objects into a stated number of pieces at a given cuts-per-time rate.
Boundary: Ignore when pieces are produced by non-sequential methods or when the rate already refers to completed items rather than individual cuts.

Transfer rule: If a mixture has total amount and target unit price, then set total value = (target unit price)×(total amount) before solving component equations.
Error pattern: Confused unit rate with total cost, causing a value equation that ignored the total quantity.
Diagnostic check: Verify every term’s units; each money equation term must be currency, and substituting your quantities should reproduce both the total amount and target average price.
Use when: Combining two priced components into a fixed-size mixture, weighted average, alloy, solution, or blend problem.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks only for a ratio, percent, or comparison without a fixed total quantity or value equation.

Transfer rule: If totals differ only because each person adds the same extra amount, then divide the total increase by the per-person increase to get the number of people.
Error pattern: I ignored the direct linear relationship between uniform per-person change and overall change, likely guessing from the original total instead.
Diagnostic check: Compute (new total − original total) ÷ extra per person; ensure units match and the result is a whole count before choosing.
Use when: This applies to equal-contribution, equal-share, or fixed increment/decrement problems comparing two total amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when contributions are unequal, the headcount changes, or percentages/compound changes alter the total nonlinearly.

Transfer rule: If several cylinders share one circumference and only curved area is asked, then find the common radius from the perimeter and sum lateral areas as circumference × total height.
Error pattern: Mixed up surface-area formulas by adding base terms or mishandling the arithmetic-series sum of heights.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute common circumference, list all heights, add them once, then verify the unit is area and no bases are included.
Use when: A set of cylinders or prisms has repeated cross-section information and asks for combined exterior area excluding some faces.
Boundary: Ignore this when radii vary, diameters are given inconsistently, or total surface area explicitly includes end caps.

Transfer rule: If category totals overlap and some people can belong to multiple categories, then use inclusion–exclusion by subtracting overcounts from the sum of category totals.
Error pattern: Treated overlapping counts as nearly additive and adjusted incompletely, missing that “exactly two” and “all three” contribute different multiplicities.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, assign weights: single-like = 1 count, exactly-two = 2 counts, all-three = 3 counts; verify total likes sum equals category totals.
Use when: Relevant for survey/set-counting problems with multiple groups, overlaps, “exactly,” “at least one,” and a requested total population.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are disjoint, or when the question asks for overlap sizes directly rather than the union total.

Transfer rule: If one item has a special price and the rest are sold only in bundles, then subtract the special item’s cost first and convert the remaining money using the fixed bundle size.
Error pattern: Confusing price-per-bundle with items-per-bundle and patching arithmetic after an invalid setup.
Diagnostic check: Compute leftover cost after special pricing, verify it is an exact multiple of the bundle price, then total items = special-item count + (multiple × items per bundle).
Use when: A word problem mixes a one-time exception with later purchases restricted to grouped units.
Boundary: Ignore when all items share one unit price or bundles are optional rather than required.

Transfer rule: If a problem asks for cylinder volume, then compute base area × height using πr²h before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the standard geometric formula directly instead of estimating or mixing area and volume formulas.
Diagnostic check: Write the formula, square the radius explicitly, multiply by height, then verify the unit is cubic before selecting.
Use when: This applies to solid-geometry questions about cylinders where radius and height are given and answers are numerical.
Boundary: Ignore this when the shape is not a cylinder or when the question asks for surface area, circumference, or another measure.

Transfer rule: If a commission/payment schedule changes after a threshold, then split the total into fixed part up to the threshold plus variable part beyond it.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling a piecewise linear total instead of applying one rate to all units.
Diagnostic check: Compute the threshold-total first, compare it with the given total, and divide only the remainder by the post-threshold per-unit amount.
Use when: A word problem has tiered rates, brackets, or “first N items at one rate, after that another rate.”
Boundary: Ignore this when a single constant rate applies throughout or rates compound multiplicatively rather than by units.

Transfer rule: If categories cover everyone and overlaps are asked, then use inclusion–exclusion with variables for exactly one, two, and three before choosing.
Error pattern: I guessed from options after algebra broke, instead of validating the setup with a counting identity.
Diagnostic check: Compute total category memberships; subtract the covered population and twice the all-category overlap; the remainder must equal the exactly-two total and be nonnegative.
Use when: Apply on percentage/count problems with overlapping groups, especially “at least one,” totals for each group, and a stated all-groups intersection.
Boundary: Ignore when groups are disjoint, not exhaustive, or when the question concerns a specific pairwise overlap rather than the combined exactly-two count.

Transfer rule: If a subset is given as a fraction of the whole, then convert that fraction into an exact item count before using averages.  
Error pattern: Misapplied fraction-to-count conversion and then rounded an unjustified intermediate result to fit choices.  
Diagnostic check: Compute whole total = overall average × total count; subset count = fraction × total count; subset total = subset average × subset count; remainder average = (whole total − subset total) ÷ remaining count.  
Use when: A problem gives an overall average, a subgroup average, and asks for the average of the remaining items.  
Boundary: Ignore when counts are unknown, the subgroup overlaps others, or weights/frequencies differ across items.

Transfer rule: If a number sequence looks irregular, then compute first differences and second differences before matching any repeated-looking term.
Error pattern: I fixated on surface repetition and skipped testing the sequence’s change structure, leading to a tempting but unsupported choice.
Diagnostic check: Write consecutive gaps, then compare how those gaps change; accept an option only if it preserves the simplest consistent pattern across all terms.
Use when: Apply this to ordered numeric series, especially when one option repeats an existing term or when growth appears uneven rather than purely arithmetic.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is non-sequential, explicitly geometric by ratio, or governed by a stated external rule instead of inferred differences.

Transfer rule: If two quantities differ by a fixed amount and have different unit values, then define the smaller quantity as x, write the larger as x plus the difference, and form one revenue equation.
Error pattern: Chose a plausible option without fully translating both relationships into algebra and checking the total against the equation.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, substitute your proposed counts into both constraints: the difference condition and the total-value sum; reject any answer that fails either.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with two item types, distinct prices, a stated count difference, and a combined sales or cost total.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are linked by ratios, percentages, or changing rates instead of a fixed additive difference.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is described as “a fraction less than another amount,” then compute that reduction from the referenced amount, not from the whole.
Error pattern: Misread comparative fraction language and treated “less than what was spent” as subtracting from total savings instead of from the prior purchase.
Diagnostic check: Let total savings be 1; write the first spending as a fraction of 1, compute the second as (1 − stated reduction) × first spending, then add.
Use when: A word problem gives sequential amounts using phrases like “less than,” “more than,” or percentages/fractions relative to a previous amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when each amount is stated directly as a fraction of the original whole with no comparison to another amount.

Transfer rule: If two travelers cover the same distance at different speeds with a known time difference, then set distance divided by each speed as times and equate their difference to the given gap.
Error pattern: Turning a rate-time comparison into ad hoc arithmetic instead of writing both times from one shared unknown distance.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute d/small_rate minus d/large_rate symbolically; solve for distance and verify the resulting times differ by the stated amount.
Use when: Equal-distance motion problems give two speeds and specify how much longer one trip takes than the other.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ, rates change during travel, or the condition involves sums/ratios of times rather than a direct difference.

Transfer rule: If a rate is charged per fixed distance unit, then divide total distance by that unit, multiply by the per-unit charge, and add the starting fee once.
Error pattern: Treated the variable charge as if based on whole miles or mis-scaled the distance unit, causing an inflated total.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute “number of charge units = distance ÷ unit distance” and verify variable cost changes proportionally with a quick estimate.
Use when: Flat-fee-plus-increment word problems involving money, distance, time, weight, or any repeated billing block.
Boundary: Ignore when pricing uses caps, minimums, tiered brackets, rounding rules, or partial units are explicitly handled differently.

Transfer rule: If two objects move toward each other, then add their speeds and divide total combined length by crossing time before converting units.
Error pattern: I treated a relative-motion pass-by as if only one length or one speed mattered, causing an undercount.
Diagnostic check: Compute relative speed = sum of both lengths / time; if equal speeds, halve it for each object, then convert m/s to km/h by multiplying by 3.6.
Use when: This applies to train, car, runner, or conveyor problems involving complete crossing, opposite directions, and given lengths with time.
Boundary: Ignore this when motion is same-direction overtaking, partial overlap, unequal lengths not both relevant, or acceleration is involved.

Transfer rule: If two item types have known counts and prices with total quantity and revenue, then define variables and solve the simultaneous equations before checking choices.
Error pattern: Success came from structured algebraic setup instead of guessing from answer options or doing partial arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Write count and revenue equations, solve one variable by substitution/elimination, then verify both totals exactly match.
Use when: Relevant for two-category mixture, sales, ticket, coin, or inventory problems giving a total number and a total amount.
Boundary: Ignore when there are more than two categories, changing prices, discounts, taxes, or insufficient independent constraints.

Transfer rule: If counting permutations with exactly one correct placement, then choose the fixed item and require the remaining items form a derangement.
Error pattern: Mistook “one fixed point” for a rarer event by not enforcing/counting the leftover no-match arrangement correctly.
Diagnostic check: For n items, compute count as n × !(n−1), divide by n!, and verify by listing small leftover cases if unsure.
Use when: Random assignment or permutation problems ask for exactly one correct match, one person/item in the right place, or one fixed point.
Boundary: Ignore when matches are independent trials, placements are not all distinct, or the question asks for at least one or unrestricted numbers of matches.

Transfer rule: If an average is unchanged after time passes but one member is added, then equate total age increase of old members minus added years from the new member.
Error pattern: Success came from tracking totals instead of manipulating averages directly.
Diagnostic check: Convert each average to a total, advance only existing members by elapsed years, add the new person separately, then verify whether the present average matches.
Use when: A word problem compares averages at two times and family/group size changes because someone joins after the earlier time.
Boundary: Ignore when membership is fixed throughout or when departures/unknown ages make simple total-change accounting invalid.

Transfer rule: If one part is a fixed fraction of the other and the total is known, then represent the larger as whole ratio units, sum the units, and divide the total before choosing values.
Error pattern: Treated a fractional relationship like a direct pick from options instead of translating it into a part-to-part ratio and total-units model.
Diagnostic check: Let larger = 1 whole, smaller = stated fraction; compute total wholes, convert total length to one whole, then verify smaller plus larger equals the given total.
Use when: Total-and-parts word problems where one quantity is given as a fraction of another.
Boundary: Ignore when the fraction refers to the total, or when both pieces are independently specified by equations or differences.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a total from disjoint groups, then add all group counts directly before checking choices.
Error pattern: Miscomputed a simple aggregation and matched an option without verifying the arithmetic against the wording.
Diagnostic check: Write a mini-equation from the sentence, compute it once, then compare the result digit-for-digit with the selected option.
Use when: Relevant for basic counting, totals, category-combining, or any prompt phrased as “how many altogether/in total.”
Boundary: Ignore when groups overlap, items are excluded, or the task asks for a difference, ratio, or remaining amount instead.

Transfer rule: If a compound inequality gives an open interval, then rewrite it as an absolute-value form by using center = midpoint of endpoints and radius = half the interval width.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating between interval notation and distance-from-center; failure usually comes from using an endpoint or wrong half-width.
Diagnostic check: Compute midpoint and half-width, then verify the candidate is equivalent to “distance from midpoint is less than half-width” and reproduces both endpoints.
Use when: Apply this to choices involving absolute value, distance language, or symmetric bounds around a center.
Boundary: Ignore this when the interval is unbounded, one-sided, closed in a mismatched way, or the choices are not distance-based.

Transfer rule: If a total cost is split across items and then increased by a percentage, then first find unit cost by dividing total by quantity, then multiply by 1 + markup rate.
Error pattern: I applied the percentage to the total or rewrote the expression without simplifying the per-item base, mixing total-level and unit-level quantities.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute symbolically in two stages—unit cost, then marked-up unit price—and verify units remain “dollars per item,” not total dollars.
Use when: This fits word problems involving totals, equal items, and percent increase or decrease on each item.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent applies to the whole batch, fees are added separately, or items have unequal original costs.

Transfer rule: If earnings combine a fixed base and a per-unit rate, then write separate equations for each period and solve for units from the target total, not by doubling units or adding the base twice.
Error pattern: Treating a linear compensation model as proportional growth; mixing up fixed and variable parts when scaling from one month to another.
Diagnostic check: Compute prior units as (prior total − base) ÷ rate, compute target total explicitly, then solve (target total − base) ÷ rate and verify by substitution.
Use when: A word problem gives a constant amount plus a repeated-per-item amount and asks for a new count under a changed earnings goal.
Boundary: Ignore when the relationship is purely proportional, uses changing rates, or asks only for total earnings rather than required units.

Transfer rule: If profit shares depend on different joining times, then equate capital × active-time for each partner and solve the missing duration from the given ratio.
Error pattern: Success came from using weighted investment-time rather than comparing capitals alone or subtracting times in the wrong direction.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each partner’s money-months, set their ratio equal to the profit ratio, and verify the solved time lies within the business year.
Use when: Apply to partnership, investment, work-share, or profit-division questions where entrants join later or leave early.
Boundary: Ignore when shares are based on salaries, interest, equal partnership agreements, or any rule not proportional to capital-time.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives perimeter first, then convert perimeter to side length before finding area; never treat perimeter as area.
Error pattern: Mixed up related measures and then forced arithmetic, ignoring whether dimensions and units stayed consistent.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list each quantity with units, derive side from perimeter using the shape formula, recompute area, then verify length × width matches that area and perimeter uses 2(l+w).
Use when: Geometry word problems link perimeter, area, and side lengths across squares and rectangles.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when all needed dimensions are already given directly or no perimeter-to-area conversion is required.

Transfer rule: If converting a rate across distance and time units, then convert each unit explicitly and verify the net units match the question.
Error pattern: I changed one unit but failed to scale the time unit correctly, causing a large-factor underestimate.
Diagnostic check: Write the conversion chain with units; multiply by distance factor and by minutes-per-hour, then estimate whether the result should be much larger than the per-minute value.
Use when: Apply this to speed, density, price-per-unit, or any compound rate with two or more unit changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when units already match the target or the problem is purely conceptual, not a numeric conversion.

Transfer rule: If a growth problem has a fixed percent plus an additional percent each year, then combine them into one annual rate and compound over the stated years.
Error pattern: Success came from recognizing repeated percentage change as multiplicative growth, not by simple addition across years.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write annual multiplier = 1 + total yearly rate, raise it to the number of years, then subtract 1 and convert to percent.
