Use when: Apply this to population, investment, depreciation, or similar word problems with multiple yearly percentage changes acting in the same period.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are one-time adjustments, apply to different bases, or are explicitly simple-interest/non-compounding changes.

Transfer rule: If dividend is quoted on face value but return on investment is quoted on purchase price, then equate dividend per share to yield × market price, not to total invested amount directly.
Error pattern: Mixed up face value, dividend rate, yield, and share count by treating a percentage on nominal value as a percentage on purchase outlay.
Diagnostic check: Compute dividend per share from nominal share value first; then divide by the investment-return rate to get buying price per share; verify units stay “per share.”
Use when: Relevant in stock/share questions involving face value, dividend percent, and overall percent return or yield.
Boundary: Ignore when all percentages are explicitly based on the same base amount or when no nominal-versus-purchase distinction exists.

Transfer rule: If race margins are given over the same fixed distance, then convert each result into a speed ratio using winner’s covered distance when the loser finishes.
Error pattern: Success comes from chaining multiplicative speed ratios; failure comes from treating margins as additive differences across separate races.
Diagnostic check: Compute each pairwise ratio as full_distance : loser_distance_at_finish, multiply ratios along the chain, then convert the final ratio back into a margin over the full course.
Use when: Relevant for race, work-rate, or motion problems linking several head-to-head outcomes over an identical total distance.
Boundary: Ignore when distances, starting times, or finishing conditions differ, or when margins are given in time rather than remaining distance.

Transfer rule: If an equation asks for distinct integer pairs with symmetric exponents, then test integer-domain constraints by small cases and known parameterizations before inferring “infinite.”
Error pattern: Overgeneralized a real-number/logarithm argument to integers and skipped verifying claimed examples and domain restrictions.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the smallest distinct integer candidates; then use the standard form x^(1/x) or consecutive-integer pattern to see whether any integer pair actually satisfies the equation.
Use when: Relevant for equations of the form variable-in-exponent equals swapped-variable-in-exponent, especially when the question asks for a count of integer solutions.
Boundary: Ignore when variables are unrestricted reals/complex numbers or when the task is not about counting discrete solutions.

Transfer rule: If two agents complete the same fixed job in given times, then convert each time to a rate, subtract/add rates, and invert to recover the unknown time.
Error pattern: Treated a combined-work time as an individual-work time instead of using rate decomposition for a fixed workload.
Diagnostic check: Set workload = 1 job (or the stated fixed batch), compute rate_P and rate_total, verify rate_Q = rate_total − rate_P is positive, then take time_Q = 1/rate_Q.
Use when: A problem gives one worker’s solo time and a joint time for the same amount of work.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are not rates on the same fixed job or when workers’ rates vary over time.

Transfer rule: If coin counts are given in a ratio and total value is known, then set counts as ratio parts times k and build one value equation in smallest currency units.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a count ratio into algebra before comparing values, instead of mixing count ratios with value ratios.
Diagnostic check: Compute the value contributed by one full ratio bundle; divide the total value by that bundle value, then multiply the target coin’s ratio part by the quotient.
Use when: Apply this to mixture/count problems with several denominations, a total monetary value, and a count ratio across types.
Boundary: Ignore this when the ratio refers to values, weights, or probabilities rather than numbers of items, or when totals are not additive.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem scales both workers and time, then compute output = (items per worker-day) × workers × days from the baseline.
Error pattern: I treated the relationship as additive or pattern-matched choices instead of using a constant per-worker-per-day rate.
Diagnostic check: First reduce the given scenario to one worker for one day, then rebuild the target scenario and verify units cancel cleanly.
Use when: Apply this to production, work, filling, or weaving questions that give one group-time-output example and ask for another.
Boundary: Ignore this when rates change, workers interfere, setup costs matter, or the problem states nonlinearity or partial completion.

Transfer rule: If distinct items are each assigned independently to one of several distinct containers with no restrictions, then count choices per item and multiply: containers^(items).
Error pattern: Confused which set supplies the repeated independent choices, swapping “choices for each item” with “items per container.”
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write one sample assignment as item1→container?, item2→container?, ...; count decision points and options at each point.
Use when: The problem says different objects, different boxes/bins/groups, and any object may go to any container.
Boundary: Ignore this when objects are identical, containers have capacity/emptiness constraints, or order within containers matters.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for percent increase/decrease, then compute change ÷ original amount × 100 before matching choices.
Error pattern: I treated percent change like a ratio to the new amount or another incorrect base instead of the starting value.
Diagnostic check: Write three slots—original, new, change—and verify that percent × original = change numerically.
Use when: This applies to word problems about prices, populations, measurements, or counts changing from an initial value to a later value.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem asks for percent of a total, percent remaining, or uses a different stated reference base.

Transfer rule: If converting a position from one end to the other in an ordered list, then compute total minus given rank plus one.
Error pattern: I overcomplicated a one-step counting conversion and altered the result with unjustified extra adjustments.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test with a tiny list and verify the first position from one end maps to the full size from the other.
Use when: This applies to ranking, seating, lines, floors, or any problem asking for position from the opposite end.
Boundary: Ignore this when there are ties, missing positions, circular arrangements, or the reference point is not an endpoint.

Transfer rule: If total spending must stay constant and unit price changes by p%, then set new quantity = 1/(1+p) of old quantity and convert the drop to a percent.
Error pattern: I treated the needed reduction as a simple percent subtraction instead of using the inverse proportional change required by fixed expenditure.
Diagnostic check: Compute with a base case, like cost = 100 and quantity = 100 units; after the price change, solve the affordable new quantity and compare.
Use when: A word problem links price, quantity, and unchanged total cost, especially with “must be reduced/increased so expenditure remains same.”
Boundary: Ignore this when total expenditure also changes or when the relationship is not multiplicative inverse.

Transfer rule: If a quantity depends on dimensions altered by a fixed-width border, then verify whether area alone uniquely determines the border area before choosing any determination/impossibility option.
Error pattern: Treated non-uniqueness correctly but failed to distinguish equivalent-looking uncertainty choices by matching the test to the exam’s wording.
Diagnostic check: Parameterize several shapes with the given area, compute the inner-border area formula, and see whether different dimension pairs produce different costs.
Use when: Geometry or mensuration questions give total area plus a uniform strip/path but omit side lengths and ask for area or cost.
Boundary: Ignore when additional constraints fix dimensions uniquely or when all uncertainty options are explicitly synonymous.

Transfer rule: If a geometry question asks for a sphere’s total surface area, then compute 4πr² explicitly and estimate magnitude before matching choices.
Error pattern: Misapplied arithmetic or digit-order confusion turned a correct formula type into an implausible option.
Diagnostic check: Square the radius, multiply by 4, then by π≈22/7 or 3.14, and verify the result’s leading digits and place value.
Use when: Radius is given and answer choices are close permutations, reversals, or near-calculation distractors in mensuration problems.
Boundary: Ignore when the figure is not a sphere or when the problem asks for volume, curved area of another solid, or leaves π symbolic.

Transfer rule: If a task divides one item into equal pieces, then compute required cuts as pieces minus one before multiplying by time per cut.
Error pattern: Confusing the number of resulting segments with the number of cutting actions needed.
Diagnostic check: First find how many full pieces fit, then subtract 1 and compare that count to the action count you were about to use.
Use when: Lengths or quantities are partitioned into equal units and each cut, break, or split has a fixed time cost.
Boundary: Ignore when pieces are pre-separated, multiple pieces are cut at once, both ends need trimming, or setup/movement time is included.

Transfer rule: If distinct items go into identical groups, then count set partitions by occupancy patterns and divide out basket-label symmetry instead of using labeled-box assignments.
Error pattern: Treated identical containers as distinguishable, causing overcounting from permutation symmetry.
Diagnostic check: List possible nonempty size patterns summing to the item total, count allocations for each with combinations, and verify no two arrangements differ only by swapping baskets.
Use when: Distribution problems have different objects, containers are explicitly identical/unlabeled, and empty containers may be allowed.
Boundary: Ignore when containers are labeled/distinguishable or when a one-to-one placement model is explicitly requested.

Transfer rule: If two objects under the same lighting are compared, then set up a constant height-to-shadow ratio and solve by proportional scaling.
Error pattern: I treated the relation as additive or over-scaled instead of preserving the same multiplicative ratio between corresponding measures.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute shadow/height from the first object, apply it to the second, then verify both ratios match exactly.
Use when: This applies to word problems involving similar triangles, constant rates, or matched conditions linking two paired quantities.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions differ between cases or the relationship is explicitly nonproportional, nonlinear, or includes offsets.

Transfer rule: If a quantity changes by a fixed multiplicative factor each interval, then move backward by applying the inverse factor for whole intervals.
Error pattern: Overcomplicated exponential reasoning and invented extra intervals instead of using direct relative amounts between two nearby states.
Diagnostic check: Compare the target amount to the known amount, express that ratio as the growth factor or its reciprocal, then count only the needed intervals.
Use when: The problem gives one state at a specific time and asks for an earlier or later time under constant doubling, tripling, quadrupling, decay, or similar.
Boundary: Ignore this when growth is not constant per interval or when capacities, additions, or piecewise rates change the multiplicative pattern.

Transfer rule: If a two-at-a-time bridge problem asks for minimum total time, then compare the two standard shuttle plans for the two slowest and choose the smaller total.
Error pattern: Treating crossing times as divisible, inferable, or accumulative from unrelated counts instead of modeling complete trips and return constraints.
Diagnostic check: Sort times a≤b≤c≤d, compute plan1=(a+2b+d) and plan2=(2a+c+d) for moving the two slowest, then add the remaining base case explicitly.
Use when: Small bridge-and-torch puzzles where only one light/tool exists, at most two travel together, and a return trip is required.
Boundary: Ignore when times interact nonlinearly, capacities vary, more than two can travel, or the task is not minimizing total elapsed time.

Transfer rule: If a term is “factorial-like” plus a small offset, then test each offset against divisors already contained in the factorial-like product.
Error pattern: Success came from using inherited divisibility systematically instead of estimating primality from size or sparse checking.
Diagnostic check: Let N be the product term; for each candidate N+k with small k, check whether k shares a factor with N or directly divides N+k.
Use when: Applies to consecutive numbers near a product of the first several integers, especially when offsets are smaller than or among those factors.
Boundary: Ignore when the base expression is not a full product of consecutive integers or offsets are large enough that inherited divisibility is not immediate.

Transfer rule: If a yearly total is split equally by month, then first compute the planned amount for the elapsed months and compare actual spending to that subtotal.
Error pattern: I compared against the wrong benchmark by not scaling the monthly allocation to the number of months already passed.
Diagnostic check: Calculate monthly budget = annual total ÷ total months, then elapsed-plan = monthly budget × elapsed months, and verify variance = actual − elapsed-plan with sign.
Use when: A total budget or quota is evenly distributed across time periods and the question asks under/over status after some periods.
Boundary: Ignore this when allocations are uneven, prorated differently, or the comparison is to the full-year total rather than elapsed periods.

Transfer rule: If a rate problem gives downstream and upstream speeds, then compute still-water speed as their average and stream speed as half their difference.  
Error pattern: Algebra-check failure—after setting correct equations, the result was mis-solved and then altered by unsupported guesswork.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, add the two equations to isolate the base rate, subtract them to isolate the current, and substitute both values back into both original rate relations.  
Use when: Apply this to motion-in-a-current problems with one speed aided by flow and one opposed by flow.  
Boundary: Ignore this when speeds are not simple add/subtract combinations, such as varying current, unequal effort, or non-linear rate relations.

Transfer rule: If two group totals and the count in exactly one group are given, then set exactly-one = (group1 − both) + (group2 − both) and solve for overlap.
Error pattern: Misapplied overlap counting by not translating “only one” into the sum of the non-overlapping parts before solving.
Diagnostic check: Let x be overlap; compute the exactly-one total as group1 + group2 − 2x, solve, then verify each exclusive count is nonnegative.
Use when: Counts involve two categories with terms like “both,” “only,” “either,” overlap, or Venn-diagram style membership.
Boundary: Ignore when categories are not binary memberships or when totals involve three or more sets without reducing to a two-set relation.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s dimensions multiply across several face areas, then rewrite each face area in edge variables and multiply symbolically before mapping to a derived quantity.
Error pattern: I matched units and relationships by intuition instead of expanding expressions to compare powers of the same base dimensions.
Diagnostic check: Let the three meeting edges be x, y, z; compute face areas xy, yz, xz, multiply them, and compare the result to (xyz) and its powers.
Use when: This applies to geometry or measurement questions relating areas, volumes, and products of multiple dimensions in rectangular solids.
Boundary: Ignore this when figures are not orthogonal boxes or when given relationships already involve non-edge-based formulas.

Transfer rule: If an equation pits a polynomial in the variable against an exponential with the same variable, then test small integer values and compare growth to bracket all possibilities.
Error pattern: I overgeneralized from asymptotic growth and skipped checking exceptional small cases where equality can occur.
Diagnostic check: Evaluate consecutive nearby integers from the smallest meaningful domain values; if one side switches from larger to smaller, inspect that interval exhaustively for integer hits.
Use when: Relevant for discrete equations mixing powers of the variable with a fixed-base exponential, especially when answer choices ask for the count of integer solutions.
Boundary: Ignore when the domain is continuous, noninteger methods are required, or monotonicity/structure already proves impossibility without case checks.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives a product of item values and a count-equality condition, then model counts as exponents in prime factorization, not as sums or value equalities.
Error pattern: Mixed up product constraints with total-value equations, then guessed after invalid algebra; answer was right only by luck.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, rewrite each value into primes, match exponents on both sides, and verify every given count relation directly on the exponents.
Use when: Relevant for counting objects with fixed per-item values, especially when the total is multiplicative and some item counts are linked.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem asks for a sum, average, or total score rather than a product/composite factorization constraint.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then compute a weighted average using each group’s size before dividing by the total size.
Error pattern: Success came from weighting by counts instead of taking a simple mean of the group averages.
Diagnostic check: Convert each average to a group total, add totals, add group sizes, divide once, and verify the result lies between the smallest and largest group averages.
Use when: Relevant for mixture, class, batch, or subgroup average problems where groups have unequal sizes.
Boundary: Ignore when all groups have equal size or when the task asks for an unweighted mean of already comparable aggregates.

Transfer rule: If a new score changes an average after n prior entries, then set previous total = previous average × n and use (new total)/(n+1), not the score itself, to infer the new average.
Error pattern: Treated an average-increase statement like a direct shortcut and skipped forming the total-sum equation linking old and new averages.
Diagnostic check: Let prior average be x; write nx + added value = (n+1)(x + stated increase), solve, then verify the increase matches exactly.
Use when: A problem gives one new observation, the count of observations, and a stated change in average.
Boundary: Ignore when the average change is not tied to exactly one added data point or counts are ambiguous.

Transfer rule: If a discount and a profit are both stated, then set cost to 100, compute discounted selling price from profit, divide by the retained-price factor, and convert back to profit percent.
Error pattern: Mixed up percent, multiplier, and option scale; after getting a reasonable intermediate value, I transformed it incorrectly instead of matching the answer format.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify units twice: selling-price multiplier, then profit percent = (selling price − cost)/cost × 100; reject any result far outside the option scale.
Use when: Relevant in markup/discount/profit problems where one selling condition is observed and another is asked.
Boundary: Ignore when discounts apply sequentially to different bases or when profit is defined on selling price, not cost.

Transfer rule: If one object passes a point in time T and a longer obstacle at the same speed in time kT, then obstacle length = (k−1) × object length.
Error pattern: I mixed total-distance scaling with added-distance reasoning, failing to subtract the object’s own length from the longer pass.
Diagnostic check: Let speed be v; write distances for both cases, divide by v, and verify longer-case distance minus point-case distance equals only the obstacle length.
Use when: Relative motion problems keep speed unchanged but the passed target changes from a point/person to a finite-length platform/train.
Boundary: Ignore this when speeds differ, acceleration occurs, or both bodies move so a simple same-speed time ratio is invalid.

Transfer rule: If pay includes cash plus an item for a full period, then prorate the full-period total and equate it to the partial-period cash plus replacement item.
Error pattern: Treated a noncash component as unpaid/irrelevant instead of converting it into an unknown value within the same proportion.
Diagnostic check: Let the item value be x; write full compensation as cash + x, set partial-service share = partial cash + substitute item, and solve for x.
Use when: Compensation problems involve time worked, mixed payment forms, and one promised item being replaced by another at settlement.
Boundary: Ignore when payment is not proportional to time, includes bonuses/penalties, or the replacement is additional rather than substitutive.

Transfer rule: If one variable is guaranteed smaller than another and a multiplier is restricted to be nonnegative, then compare their products by checking the multiplier’s sign first.
Error pattern: I focused on a tempting transformed comparison and ignored the operation-preservation rule for inequalities under multiplication.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, test each option with sign-aware logic: does multiplying by the allowed factor always preserve, reverse, or collapse the inequality?
Use when: Integer inequality problems where one value is below a threshold, another above it, and expressions include multiplying both by the same constrained variable.
Boundary: Ignore when the multiplier can be negative or when the operation compared is not monotonic over the allowed signs.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then convert each group’s average to a total, add totals, and divide by the combined count.
Error pattern: Success pattern: treating averages as weighted by group size rather than simply comparing or informally blending them.
Diagnostic check: Compute each subtotal, verify the overall average lies between the group averages, and check it is closer to the larger group’s average.
Use when: One quantity is averaged over one set, another average is given for an additional set, and a combined average is asked.
Boundary: Ignore when all group sizes are equal or the task asks for a total/change instead of a pooled average.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what an ordered subset sum “could be” given a fixed mean, then convert mean to total and test each candidate against extremal constraints from positivity and ordering.
Error pattern: I treated a tempting large value as attainable without checking whether the remaining smaller terms could stay positive and no larger than the chosen top terms.
Diagnostic check: Let total = count×mean; set the target subset sum, compute the leftover sum, and verify those leftover terms can be positive and each not exceed the smallest chosen term.
Use when: Relevant for mean/total problems with sorted values, subset sums, and a “could be” feasibility question.
Boundary: Ignore when values need not be ordered, can be nonpositive without restriction, or the task asks for a mandatory value rather than feasibility.

Transfer rule: If asked for percent increase, then compute (new − old) / old × 100, using the original amount as the base.
Error pattern: Confusing increase ratio with the wrong denominator, causing an inflated percentage.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify the absolute change divided by the starting value gives a decimal that matches the option range.
Use when: Relevant for percent increase/decrease questions comparing a later amount to an earlier amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for percent of a total, percent difference, or change relative to the new amount.

Transfer rule: If workers share a constant rate on a fixed job, then keep total work constant by equating worker-days before solving.
Error pattern: I treated the relation intuitively instead of using inverse proportion, causing an overestimate when time decreased.
Diagnostic check: Compute total work as current workers × current days, divide by target days for required workers, then subtract the original team size.
Use when: This applies to fixed-work, equal-rate teamwork problems asking how many more or fewer people are needed for a new deadline.
Boundary: Ignore this when rates differ, productivity changes, work size is not fixed, or setup/overhead makes output non-linear.

Transfer rule: If a set’s average is no greater than every subset’s average, then test equal-value subsets and infer all elements are identical; then check what that forces for center measures.
Error pattern: Correctly spotting a strong equality condition but stopping before propagating its consequences to every listed statement.
Diagnostic check: Compare the whole-set mean to each one-element subset mean; if any element differs, one singleton violates the condition. If all match, verify median equals that common value.
Use when: A condition compares a set statistic with the same statistic on all subsets, especially for means and statements about equality or median.
Boundary: Ignore when subsets are restricted, weights differ, or the statistic is not preserved by all-equal data.

Transfer rule: If a pass-mark percentage and a shortfall from passing are given, then first compute the pass-mark score by adding the shortfall to the obtained score, then divide by the percentage as a decimal to get the total.
Error pattern: Treated a percentage condition loosely and skipped converting the verbal deficit into the actual passing-score equation.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write “obtained + deficit = passing score,” then verify that passing score ÷ total equals the stated percentage.
Use when: Relevant in exam-score, cutoff, profit-loss, or target problems mixing percentages with “short by” or “exceeds by” wording.
Boundary: Ignore when the percentage refers to a part other than the full total, or when multiple thresholds/weightings are involved.

Transfer rule: If a hypothetical swap changes several items by a fixed dollar amount and causes a stated percent change in the total, then set item-count × per-item change equal to percent × original total.
Error pattern: Mixing up “share of total” with “amount of change,” or inventing totals not given; the reliable pattern is direct change-equation setup.
Diagnostic check: Compute the per-item difference, multiply by the number switched, and verify that this dollar loss equals the stated fraction of the original total.
Use when: A word problem gives two prices or rates, changes some cases from one to the other, and states the resulting percent decrease/increase.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the percent refers to a subgroup, average, or new total rather than the original overall total.

Transfer rule: If a counting problem has independent selection stages with a restriction, then count each stage separately and multiply, instead of stopping after the first choice.
Error pattern: Undercounting by tracking the allowed groups but not the internal choices within each chosen group.
Diagnostic check: List the full decision sequence; for each step ask “after this choice, are there still multiple valid ways to finish?” If yes, include that factor.
Use when: Selection/counting tasks involve categories, pairs, families, or forbidden pairings, especially when you first choose source groups and then specific members.
Boundary: Ignore when choices are not independent, order matters in a different way, or later restrictions change earlier factor counts.

Transfer rule: If two quantities have an initial ratio and the same amount is added to both, then set them as common multiples of the ratio and write the new-ratio equation before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from translating ratio language into algebra instead of guessing from options or comparing raw differences.
Diagnostic check: Let the numbers be rk and sk; after the equal addition, cross-multiply the new ratio and verify the solved values reproduce both ratios.
Use when: Apply this to word problems involving two-part ratios, equal adjustments to each part, and a second ratio condition.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are unequal, multiplicative, or involve more than two quantities or extra constraints.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem gives solo and pair times, then convert each to rates, solve for the missing person by subtraction, and invert only at the end.
Error pattern: Mixing times with rates or skipping the isolate-and-invert step causes confident but wrong choices.
Diagnostic check: Set total work to 1; compute each given rate, derive the target rate symbolically, then verify all original pair equations before selecting an option.
Use when: Relevant in combined-work questions with phrases like “alone,” “together,” and multiple pairwise completion times.
Boundary: Ignore when workers’ rates vary over time, tasks are unequal, or the problem is not additive work-rate arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If a group’s average is given at an earlier time and membership changes now, then first advance the original members to the current time before adding the newcomer.
Error pattern: Mixed time frames—treated a past average as if it were current when comparing with a present-day group average.
Diagnostic check: Compute the original group’s current total by adding elapsed years × original headcount; then compare that total with the new current total.
Use when: A word problem mentions averages at different times, aging over years, and someone joining or leaving a group.
Boundary: Ignore when all averages refer to the same date or no time shift affects the original members.

Transfer rule: If asked for counts of perfect k-th powers in 1 through N, then count integers m with m^k ≤ N and use that count over N.
Error pattern: Replaced a structural definition with unrelated divisibility counting, confusing powers with multiples.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the actual k-th powers near the range limit and verify the next one exceeds N; compare this list count to your method.
Use when: The set is a consecutive integer interval and the target property is “perfect square,” “perfect cube,” or another exact power.
Boundary: Ignore this when the property is about divisibility, prime factors, residues, or a nonconsecutive sample space.

Transfer rule: If quantities in a ratio get different percentage changes, then multiply each ratio term by its own growth factor and simplify before matching choices.
Error pattern: Applied uneven percent updates incorrectly or skipped exact simplification, causing a near-miss ratio.
Diagnostic check: Compute transformed terms symbolically, clear decimals uniformly, then divide by any common factor and compare every position with the options.
Use when: A problem starts with a base ratio and applies distinct percentage increases or decreases to each part.
Boundary: Ignore when all parts receive the same percentage change, since the original ratio remains unchanged.

Transfer rule: If speed and time use different units, then convert to one system before multiplying.
Error pattern: Unit-conversion failure; treated a rate per hour as if it matched seconds, yielding a mismatched-distance result.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write units through the calculation so hours cancel with hours or seconds with seconds; verify the final unit is distance.
Use when: Rate–time–distance multiple-choice questions, especially with km/h, m/s, minutes, or seconds mixed together.
Boundary: Ignore this when all quantities already share compatible units or when the task is purely conceptual, not numerical.

Transfer rule: If a total comes from multiplying several averages/counts, then combine powers of ten first and choose the nearest order of magnitude before considering coefficients.
Error pattern: Undershot by many orders because I treated a multi-factor product as a much smaller scale and skipped magnitude aggregation.
Diagnostic check: Round each factor to 1-digit scientific notation, add exponents, multiply leading digits roughly, then verify the result’s digit count fits the chosen scale.
Use when: Totals are built from number of groups × average per group × average per item, especially in estimation or “closest power of ten” choices.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are added/subtracted instead of multiplied, or when exact arithmetic is required and powers-of-ten estimation is too coarse.

Transfer rule: If a one-step verbal equation is described, then write the equation symbolically and undo operations in exact reverse order before checking choices.
Error pattern: Converted or reversed operations incorrectly and skipped verifying that the chosen value reproduces the stated result.
Diagnostic check: Let the unknown be x; build the expression from the wording, solve by inverse operations, then substitute your candidate back into the original sentence to confirm the final value matches.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic word problems with a starting number followed by sequential operations like multiply, add/subtract, divide, or comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore for problems requiring estimation, geometric interpretation, or direct pattern recognition rather than solving a procedural equation.

Transfer rule: If a ratio changes after people leave in two stages, then assign variables to the post-change group counts and write equations from each stage before solving.
Error pattern: I guessed from one ratio and skipped enforcing both sequential constraints, causing an answer that fit partially but not the whole process.
Diagnostic check: Let later counts be x and y; translate each “leave” statement into reverse equations, solve both, and verify all counts stay nonnegative integers.
Use when: This applies to word problems with boys/girls, mixtures, or populations where removals occur and ratios are stated after each change.
Boundary: Ignore this when ratios compare unchanged totals, or when the problem is direct arithmetic with only one condition.

Transfer rule: If one amount is given as a percent of another and their total is known, then convert the statement to a ratio, sum ratio parts, and divide the total accordingly.
Error pattern: Success comes from translating percentage language into a part-to-part relationship before doing arithmetic, instead of guessing from totals.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite “is p% of” as multiplier or ratio; verify the combined ratio parts times the unit value reproduce the total exactly.
Use when: Apply this to total-sharing problems with two linked quantities stated by percentage, fraction, or “more/less than” wording.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages refer to change over time, separate bases, or when the given total excludes one component.

Transfer rule: If a word problem describes amounts after giving or receiving, then write equations using post-transfer balances with parentheses before simplifying.
Error pattern: I dropped transfer adjustments and switched from algebra to unjustified option chasing instead of solving the simultaneous equations cleanly.
Diagnostic check: For each condition, compute both people’s balances after the transfer, state the required ratio/equality, then substitute your candidate back into both original scenarios.
Use when: Apply this on two-person money, age, or object-transfer problems involving “left with,” “after giving,” and multiplicative comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the relationships are direct pre-transfer comparisons or when no state change occurs before the comparison.

Transfer rule: If a rhombus gives a side and one diagonal, then find the other diagonal from half-diagonals forming a right triangle, then use area = product of diagonals divided by two.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the shape to its perpendicular-bisecting diagonals instead of guessing from side-length formulas.
Diagnostic check: Halve the known diagonal, compute the missing half with the Pythagorean theorem using the side as hypotenuse, double it, then verify units and plug into the area formula.
Use when: A quadrilateral is a rhombus or kite with perpendicular diagonals, and side-plus-diagonal information is provided.
Boundary: Ignore when the figure is not guaranteed to have perpendicular bisecting diagonals or when another direct area formula is given.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s total surface area is given for a cube, then divide by 6 to get one face area, take its square root for edge length, and cube that edge.
Error pattern: Success comes from using the cube’s geometry formulas in sequence instead of guessing from nearby choices.
Diagnostic check: Verify units and run 6 × edge² = given surface area before using edge³ for volume.
Use when: This applies to cube problems that provide total area and ask for edge length, volume, or another dimension-based quantity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the solid is not a cube or when the given measure is lateral area, perimeter, or side area only.

Transfer rule: If an age statement compares future and past ages with a multiplier, then set one present-age variable and write both shifted expressions before choosing.
Error pattern: I matched an option by intuition instead of translating each time reference into an equation and solving systematically.
Diagnostic check: Let present age be x; form “future shift = multiplier × past shift,” solve, then substitute back into both time-shifted ages to verify.
Use when: Relevant in word problems involving one person’s age, multiple time offsets, and a proportional relationship between those ages.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem gives direct current ages or compares different people without requiring time-shift equations.

Transfer rule: If past ages are given in a ratio and a present total is given, then represent past ages as k-scaled parts, add the elapsed years to each person, and solve from the present total.
Error pattern: I matched a tempting option without enforcing consistency between the ratio time-shift and the total-sum equation.
Diagnostic check: Let past ages be a:b:c times k; compute present ages by adding the same offset to all three, then verify their sum equals the stated total before choosing.
Use when: Relevant for age problems with multiple people, a ratio at a different time, and a current or future total.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio already refers to present ages or when totals/relations are not linear age shifts.

Transfer rule: If a selling price is on future credit, then convert it to present cash value using the stated interest before comparing with cost.
Error pattern: I compared nominal future proceeds to cost and ignored time value, causing an overstated gain.
Diagnostic check: Compute present value of the credit amount for the given term and rate; then subtract purchase cost and compare that result with the chosen option.
Use when: A buy/sell or profit-loss question mixes cash price, credit price, delayed payment, or explicit simple annual interest.
Boundary: Ignore this when all prices are at the same time point or no financing/interest adjustment is specified.

Transfer rule: If two people start equal and then spend different amounts, then assign one variable to the starting amount and write each remaining amount before applying the comparison.
Error pattern: Success came from translating the verbal ratio between leftovers into an equation instead of comparing spending amounts directly.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify your setup gives equal starting values and that substituting the result makes one remainder the stated multiple of the other.
Use when: Apply this on word problems with equal initial quantities, different increases or decreases, and a multiplicative relationship between final amounts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship concerns totals spent, percentages, or unequal starting amounts.

Transfer rule: If markup or commission is stated as a percent of the final selling price, then define selling price as a variable and write cost + (rate)(selling price) = selling price before applying any discount.
Error pattern: Success comes from modeling percent-of-sale relationships algebraically instead of treating the percent as based on cost by habit.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify the base for each percent and solve the equation for the original selling price; then compute discounted revenue minus cost.
Use when: Rates are attached to selling price, retail price, revenue, or another quantity different from cost, especially with sequential markup and discount steps.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when every percentage is explicitly based on cost or when no chained percentage relationship is involved.

Transfer rule: If a total average is below every segment’s stated average, then first verify the setup is physically possible before doing algebra or choosing an option.
Error pattern: I accepted an impossible weighted-average situation and then matched an option instead of checking consistency.
Diagnostic check: Compare the claimed overall average to the minimum and maximum segment averages; if it lies outside that interval, flag contradiction and re-read for a hidden condition or typo.
Use when: This applies to rate, speed, price, density, or score problems combining parts into one overall average.
Boundary: Ignore this check when the overall quantity is not a weighted average of the parts or when some parts can be negative/reversing.

Transfer rule: If a selling price includes a stated profit percent, then compute cost as selling price ÷ (1 + profit rate), not by subtracting that percent from selling price.
Error pattern: Treated a markup percentage as a direct part of the final price rather than as a multiplier on the original base.
Diagnostic check: Write the relation SP = CP × factor; solve for CP; then plug back in and verify the resulting profit amount equals the stated percent of CP.
Use when: Percent gain/loss, markup/discount, or reverse-percentage questions ask for the original amount from a final amount.
Boundary: Ignore when the percent is explicitly taken on the final amount or when only approximate estimation is requested.

Transfer rule: If a word problem equates two operation sequences, then write both expressions with parentheses, set them equal, and isolate the variable by inverse operations.
Error pattern: Algebra setup was fine, but the solve phase had an arithmetic/distribution mistake after forming the correct equation.
Diagnostic check: Expand both sides, collect like terms, solve, then substitute the candidate back into both original verbal procedures to verify matching results.
Use when: Apply this on single-variable linear word problems describing different ordered operations on the same starting number.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relationship is not equality, involves multiple unknowns, or requires non-linear methods rather than straightforward linear isolation.

Transfer rule: If asked for a winner’s vote percentage, then first compute total votes and divide the largest vote count by that total before matching choices.
Error pattern: Selected a plausible option without verifying the ratio from the complete data; skipped the full aggregation step.
Diagnostic check: Identify the maximum count, sum all candidates’ counts, calculate max ÷ total × 100, and compare the result against options.
Use when: Relevant in multi-candidate election, survey, or share-of-total questions asking for the leading group’s percentage.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for margin, second-place share, or when totals/weights are already given differently.

Transfer rule: If converting a rate across distance and time units, then convert each unit stepwise before comparing choices.
Error pattern: Success came from systematic unit conversion instead of guessing from familiar-looking numbers.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the rate with conversion factors, cancel units, and verify the final units are distance per minute.
Use when: The problem gives speeds or rates in one unit system and asks for an equivalent rate in another time or distance unit.
Boundary: Ignore this when units already match the question or when no unit conversion is required.

Transfer rule: If a data-sufficiency age problem gives multiple relations, then test each pair by translating to equations and checking whether it yields a unique present age.
Error pattern: Success comes from evaluating sufficiency systematically; failure comes from jumping to all-statements-together or not verifying uniqueness and consistency.
Diagnostic check: For each statement pair, solve or simplify to the target age, then mark whether the result is one value, multiple values, or contradiction.
Use when: The question asks whether statements about ages, ratios, or time shifts are sufficient rather than asking only for a direct numerical solution.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices are plain numeric answers or when the task is not a sufficiency/uniqueness check.

Transfer rule: If current and future ratios are given, then set present ages as common multiples, convert any time unit first, and solve the resulting proportion equation.
Error pattern: I likely matched an option from rough intuition without enforcing both ratio conditions algebraically after the time shift.
Diagnostic check: Write ages as 5k and 4k, add the same future increment to both, cross-multiply the future ratio, and verify the solved age reproduces both ratios.
Use when: This applies to age, mixture, or quantity problems that compare a present ratio with a later ratio after equal additive change.
Boundary: Ignore this when ratios are between differences, percentages, or multiplicative growth rather than equal additions to both quantities.

Transfer rule: If a variable is in the denominator of a simple equation, then isolate it by multiplying both sides by that denominator and dividing by the other factor.  
Error pattern: Chose an option by weak intuition instead of performing the inverse-operation solve and verification.  
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as dividend = divisor × quotient, compute the missing divisor, then substitute it back into the original equation to confirm equality.  
Use when: A number is divided by an unknown, especially in one-step algebra or multiple-choice settings with tempting nearby values.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the unknown is not acting as the divisor or when additional terms, exponents, or multiple operations require broader algebra.

Transfer rule: If prices change by a constant amount across ordered levels, then model them as an arithmetic sequence and use total = count × average.
Error pattern: Misusing the common difference or endpoint count in an arithmetic-series setup, causing the final term to be off.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write first = last + (levels−1)×step, compute average of first and last, and verify count×average matches the given total.
Use when: A problem gives equally spaced tiers, one item from each tier, and a total cost or sum across all tiers.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are not constant, quantities per tier differ, or the total is not across the full consecutive set.

Transfer rule: If total selling amount, quantity, and profit per unit are given, then compute selling price per unit first and subtract profit per unit to get cost per unit.
Error pattern: Mixed up total and per-unit quantities, causing an inflated result from skipping unit normalization.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write SP/unit = total SP ÷ quantity; then verify CP/unit + profit/unit = SP/unit.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss or rate problems where one value is total for many items and another is stated per item.
Boundary: Ignore when all figures are already per unit, or when profit is a percentage rather than a fixed amount per item.

Transfer rule: If a counting question asks whether repeated pairings can coexist, then model participants as a one-to-one matching and test feasibility before computing totals.
Error pattern: I treated a constraint-satisfaction setup like an arithmetic puzzle, skipping the structure imposed by exclusive pairing.
Diagnostic check: Represent each side as nodes with degree 1; if any statement requires one node paired to two distinct partners simultaneously, reject all numeric choices.
Use when: Apply this to pairing, matching, handshake, seating, or dance problems with exclusivity between two groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when multiple partners are explicitly allowed over time, across rounds, or by the problem’s rules.

Transfer rule: If asked for a command that creates a saved configuration backup, then choose the syntax that copies the active configuration to persistent storage.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the task to standard command structure instead of relying on abbreviations or malformed variants.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify the command has a valid source, a valid destination, and uses the platform’s canonical full syntax.
Use when: Apply this on networking CLI questions about saving, backing up, or persisting device configuration across reloads.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about exporting to remote locations, vendor-specific aliases, or nonstandard operating systems.

Transfer rule: If one number divided by another gives a quotient and remainder plus a known difference, then set larger = quotient×smaller + remainder and subtract smaller to form one linear equation.
Error pattern: I likely guessed from choices or combined conditions loosely instead of translating both statements into equations and enforcing the remainder rule.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compute smaller = (difference − remainder) / (quotient − 1); verify it is a positive integer and the remainder is less than the smaller.
Use when: Apply this to word problems involving two numbers, a division result with quotient/remainder, and a stated difference or sum.
Boundary: Ignore this when the relation is not standard Euclidean division or when variables represent rates, ratios, or non-integers.

Transfer rule: If converting minutes to hours, then divide the total minutes by 60 and verify the unit changes to hours.
Error pattern: Confused the conversion operation or matched an option without performing the full unit calculation.
Diagnostic check: Compute minutes ÷ 60, then multiply your result by 60 to see whether it returns the original minutes.
Use when: Relevant in time-unit conversions, especially multiple-choice questions involving minutes, hours, or mixed unit rates.
Boundary: Ignore when the units are not time-based or when the problem asks for a different representation, such as remaining minutes only.

Transfer rule: If several expressions are all equal to one value, then set each variable by dividing that common value by its coefficient before multiplying.
Error pattern: I treated linked equalities too loosely and skipped explicit variable isolation, causing an arithmetic relationship error.
Diagnostic check: Write x for the shared value; solve each variable separately from coefficient·variable = x, then substitute and compute the target expression.
Use when: This applies to algebra problems where multiple scaled variables are chained as equal and a product or combined expression is requested.
Boundary: Ignore this when the statements are inequalities, proportions without a shared fixed value, or variables are related by sums instead of direct scaling.

Transfer rule: If motion combines your own speed with a moving surface, then compute ground speed by adding/subtracting relative velocities before finding times or averages.
Error pattern: Treated a relative speed as the total trip speed and ignored that different trip segments can have different ground speeds.
Diagnostic check: Write speeds relative to ground for each segment, find each segment’s time from distance ÷ ground speed, then verify average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Use when: A traveler moves on a conveyor, river, escalator, or other moving medium, especially when they later stop or change behavior.
Boundary: Ignore when all given speeds are already ground-frame speeds or when no moving reference frame affects displacement.

Transfer rule: If a formula says “add p% of X to the average of A and q% of X,” then compute the average first: (A + qX)/2, then add pX.
Error pattern: Misdistributed the averaging step, especially failing to halve both the constant and variable parts inside the mean.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite all percentages as decimal or fractional coefficients, expand parentheses, combine like terms, and verify the constant term was divided by 2 if it was inside an average.
Use when: The expression mixes percentages of a variable with an arithmetic mean, average, or “sum divided by 2” wording.
Boundary: Ignore when no averaging operation applies or when the constant/variable term is explicitly outside the mean.

Transfer rule: If items must be shared equally after keeping some back, then compute the total’s remainder upon division by the number of recipients; keep exactly that remainder.
Error pattern: I matched an appealing nearby value instead of enforcing the divisibility condition precisely.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, subtract your proposed kept amount from the total and verify the result divides evenly by the recipient count with remainder zero.
Use when: This applies to “divide equally,” “share evenly,” or “keep some so the rest can be split” problems involving whole items.
Boundary: Ignore this when fractional sharing is allowed or when recipients need unequal amounts or extra constraints.

Transfer rule: If an arithmetic expression has grouped sums and products, then evaluate each parenthesis first and multiply all resulting factors sequentially.
Error pattern: I likely skipped or distorted one grouped total, causing a cascade multiplication error despite using the right overall operation structure.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite the expression as factor × factor × factor, compute each factor separately, then estimate the final size before matching any choice.
Use when: This applies to multi-step numerical expressions with parentheses, several addends inside a group, and only multiplication between groups.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task depends on algebraic identities, variables, unit conversions, or hidden operation precedence beyond simple grouped arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If an arithmetic progression has fixed first and last terms, then set last−first = (number of gaps)×common difference and count factor pairs with gaps ≥ 2.
Error pattern: Treating the common difference as almost arbitrary instead of enforcing exact endpoint alignment causes massive overcounting; a lucky guess can still match.
Diagnostic check: Compute the endpoint difference, list its positive divisors, and count only those gap counts at least 2; each such gap count gives one progression.
Use when: A sequence is arithmetic, endpoints are fixed, terms must lie in an integer set, and the question asks how many such sequences exist.
Boundary: Ignore when endpoints are not fixed, noninteger steps are allowed, or the sequence type is not determined solely by equal consecutive differences.

Transfer rule: If asked for divisors with a structural restriction, then factor the number first and generate only divisors meeting that restriction from allowed exponent patterns.
Error pattern: I matched an answer by rough intuition instead of systematically enumerating valid restricted divisors from the prime-power form.
Diagnostic check: Write the prime factorization, list permissible exponents for each prime under the restriction, form every qualifying divisor once, and add them.
Use when: This applies to divisor-sum, divisor-count, or subset-of-divisors questions involving conditions like square, cube, even power, or parity.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is about all divisors with no restriction or when a direct formula already exactly matches the requested set.

Transfer rule: If counting groups with “at least one” from distinct categories, then partition into mutually exclusive cases or use total minus none, but do not subtract unless overlap exists.
Error pattern: Inventing double-counting in disjoint casework after an already complete, nonoverlapping count.
Diagnostic check: List each case definition and verify no valid group can satisfy two cases; if cases are exclusive, sum them directly and stop.
Use when: Selection/counting problems involve category membership, “at least one,” and combinations split by how many come from each category.
Boundary: Ignore when order matters, restrictions create overlapping cases, or the counting method is permutations rather than combinations.

Transfer rule: If two delay scenarios change only the reduced-speed segment, then equate the delay difference to extra distance × (1/reduced speed − 1/original speed).
Error pattern: I treated total lateness as enough by itself instead of comparing scenarios to isolate the unknown speed cleanly.
Diagnostic check: Compute the added affected distance between scenarios, convert delay gap to hours, form one equation from “extra slow time minus extra normal time,” and verify units.
Use when: A journey has an interruption point shifted along the route, with the same fractional speed reduction after that point and different lateness values.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple speeds change, stoppage time is added separately, or the later scenario alters route length or schedule.

Transfer rule: If a total-rate problem mixes subgroup percentages, then convert each group to counts and use weighted totals before subtracting.
Error pattern: I treated percentages without anchoring them to subgroup sizes, causing a mismatch between group composition and overall composition.
Diagnostic check: Compute each subgroup count from the total, apply each literacy rate to its own subgroup, then verify subgroup-literate counts sum exactly to the stated overall literate count.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with totals split by categories and one or more subgroup rates plus an overall rate.
Boundary: Ignore when every option can be eliminated by direct algebraic simplification without needing subgroup count reconstruction.

Transfer rule: If a security’s payout rate is quoted on face value but bought above/below par, then compute yield as annual payout ÷ market price × 100.
Error pattern: Confusing nominal rate with actual return on amount invested; failing to adjust for premium or discount.
Diagnostic check: Write face value as 100, calculate payout from the quoted rate, divide by purchase price, and compare the result against nearby choices.
Use when: Percentage-return questions involve stocks, bonds, debentures, or similar assets with a quoted rate and a separate buying price.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks only for stated coupon/dividend rate, or when extra factors like taxes, brokerage, time fraction, or capital gain are included.

Transfer rule: If an approximation problem mixes division and a squared term, then estimate each term separately, preserve operation order, and compare the sum to choices only at the end.
Error pattern: Underestimating a dominant nonlinear term by rounding too early or not evaluating the square carefully.
Diagnostic check: Compute rough bounds: first term from nearby easy numbers, second term using (near-integer)^2, then verify the total lies in the same hundred-range as your choice.
Use when: Expressions contain decimals close to whole numbers, exponents, and multiple operations with answer options spaced by moderate gaps.
Boundary: Ignore when exact arithmetic is required, answer choices are extremely close, or no term clearly dominates the total.

Transfer rule: If a solid’s width is given as diameter, then convert to radius before using any formula and keep units consistent.
Error pattern: Misreading a given measure and substituting it directly into a formula causes a systematic scale error.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list known quantities as “radius/diameter/height,” rewrite any derived value needed, then estimate whether the result’s magnitude matches the shape’s dimensions.
Use when: This applies to geometry problems involving circles or cylinders, especially when formulas require radius but the prompt may provide diameter.
Boundary: Ignore this when the needed formula uses diameter directly or when all required measures are already explicitly in formula-ready form.

Transfer rule: If a rate problem gives equal distances per different counts of steps and also counts of steps per equal time, then compute speed as (distance per step) × (steps per time) before comparing.
Error pattern: Mixing stride-length ratios with step-frequency ratios incorrectly, or treating one ratio as the final speed ratio.
Diagnostic check: Set one runner’s step length to a convenient unit, derive the other’s from the equal-distance statement, multiply each by its step count over the same time interval, then simplify.
Use when: Running, walking, gear, machine-cycle, or work-rate questions combine per-move size with moves taken in a shared time.
Boundary: Ignore when all quantities already use the same base unit of speed or only one factor varies.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is tied to one part of a ratio, then find the scale factor from that part and apply it to the other part before choosing.
Error pattern: Misread or inverted ratio-part mapping, treating the larger given group as if it corresponded to the wrong side.
Diagnostic check: Write ratio parts as variables, match the known count to its exact part, compute one-part value, then multiply by the target part and compare units.
Use when: Relevant for part-to-part ratios, recipes, map scales, class composition, or any question giving one group's count and asking for the other.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio is already converted to totals, percentages, or when the question asks for the same group's count.

Transfer rule: If two discount rates are linked by a known sum and a total savings amount, then define variables, write one savings equation plus one sum equation, and solve simultaneously before choosing.
Error pattern: Likely arithmetic/translation slip from not enforcing both constraints together or not back-substituting to verify the candidate rate.
Diagnostic check: Compute total savings as (unit price × quantity × rate) for each item, substitute rate2 = given-sum − rate1, solve, then plug the result back to confirm the stated total savings exactly.
Use when: Apply to mixture or shopping problems with different base prices, quantities, percentage rates, and a combined condition.
Boundary: Ignore when discounts are sequential, compounded, or applied to changing bases rather than fixed regular prices.

Transfer rule: If comparing total profit targets, then compute unit profit for each side, set required units = target total profit ÷ unit profit, and recalculate the division carefully.
Error pattern: Correct setup but arithmetic execution failure in the final quotient after converting a decimal divisor.
Diagnostic check: Replace decimals with cents, divide using whole numbers, then multiply the result back by the smaller unit profit to verify it reaches the target total.
Use when: Relevant in word problems about break-even or matching profit/revenue where per-item margins and a known sales quantity are given.
Boundary: Ignore when totals are asked directly, or when fixed costs, percentages, or nonconstant per-unit amounts change the linear relationship.

Transfer rule: If a shape has two parallel sides and a perpendicular distance between them, then use area = average of the parallel sides × the distance.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the correct geometric formula and applying arithmetic in the right order.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, compute (side1 + side2) ÷ 2 first, then multiply by the height, and verify the result has square units.
Use when: This applies to trapezium/trapezoid area questions that give both parallel side lengths and the distance between them.
Boundary: Ignore this when the given measure is not the perpendicular height or when the figure is a different shape/formula case.

Transfer rule: If a 3D measurement asks for volume in a different unit, then convert each length to the target unit before multiplying, or multiply the original volume by the cube of the scale factor.
Error pattern: Success came from handling dimensional conversion correctly instead of applying a linear factor to a cubic quantity.
Diagnostic check: Write units beside each dimension, note the scale factor once, cube it for volume, and compare the resulting magnitude to the unconverted volume.
Use when: Dimensions of a box-like object are given and the answer requires area or volume in a different unit system.
Boundary: Ignore this when units already match, the quantity is not multi-dimensional, or a direct formula without unit conversion is requested.

Transfer rule: If a total mixes a fixed per-unit service fee and a variable usage fee, then compute each separately and add only once per relevant unit.
Error pattern: Confusing additive cost components, especially treating the fixed fee as scaling with quantity like the variable charge.
Diagnostic check: Write a two-term expression with labels: (number of units × service fee) + (number of units × capacity × per-amount price); verify dimensions and arithmetic.
Use when: Word problems involve repeated items, a flat charge per item, and a consumption cost based on capacity, distance, weight, or volume.
Boundary: Ignore when fees are bundled, discounted, waived, or when the variable amount is not the full stated capacity.

Transfer rule: If two independent uniform integer draws come from the same finite range, then compute P(second > first) by symmetry and subtract only the tie probability.
Error pattern: Overcounting favorable outcomes by ignoring equal-value pairs or failing to use first/second symmetry.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify P(second > first) = P(first > second) and both sum with P(tie) to 1; for range size n, each strict inequality should be (1 - 1/n)/2.
Use when: Sequential comparisons of two random picks from the same discrete set, especially “greater than” versus “at least.”
Boundary: Ignore when draws are from different distributions/ranges, are dependent, or the comparison is not strict.

Transfer rule: If one selling price is tied to a gain and another asks for a loss, then derive cost price with exact fraction/ratio first and compute the new price from that base.
Error pattern: Converted percentages to rough decimals and accepted an approximate option instead of enforcing exact arithmetic through both steps.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite each percent as a fraction, keep values symbolic until the end, then compare by reversing: does the derived price reproduce the stated gain/loss exactly?
Use when: Relevant in chained profit-loss, markup-discount, or percent-change problems where one unknown base is inferred from another rate.
Boundary: Ignore when the same base value is directly given, or when the task asks only for an estimate rather than an exact matched choice.

Transfer rule: If a question asks “how much save” from a sale, then compute original price minus sale price.
Error pattern: I matched an option without performing the required subtraction, causing a basic arithmetic selection error.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write “savings = usual − sale,” subtract the two given prices, then verify the result appears exactly among choices.
Use when: Apply this on word problems about discounts, savings, price drops, or comparisons between an original amount and a reduced amount.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for final cost after discount, percent change, tax-inclusive totals, or involves multiple items.

Transfer rule: If a formula contains an unknown constant, then determine it from a simple valid case before substituting the target input.
Error pattern: Skipping parameter identification and plugging in values too early causes structurally wrong arithmetic.
Diagnostic check: Substitute the smallest allowed input into the given expression, solve for the constant, then verify the formula on one more small input.
Use when: A problem gives a general expression with an unspecified constant or coefficient and asks for a later numerical evaluation.
Boundary: Ignore this when all parameters are already fixed or when the task is purely conceptual rather than computational.

Transfer rule: If an operation is defined by substituting the current value into a formula, then compute repeated applications step by step, feeding each output back in.
Error pattern: Success comes from respecting function composition; failures usually come from treating the symbol like ordinary arithmetic or skipping the second substitution.
Diagnostic check: Write f(t)=given rule, compute y=f(input), then compute f(y); simplify carefully and verify each sign and constant term.
Use when: This applies to custom unary operators, recursively applied transformations, or any question asking for a symbol-defined operation used multiple times.
Boundary: Ignore this when the operator has extra constraints, is multivalued, or composition is not actually being requested.

Transfer rule: If combining equal amounts of two concentration mixtures, then average the target percentages first and convert to the requested complement only after.
Error pattern: Success came from using equal-weight averaging instead of adding percentages or averaging the wrong quantity.
Diagnostic check: Assume 1 unit of each; compute target amount in each, sum, divide by total units, then subtract from 1 if asked for “not target.”
Use when: This applies to mixture, concentration, percent-content, or ratio-blending problems with equal-volume or equal-mass parts.
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut when parts are unequal, units differ, or concentrations are given in incompatible bases requiring weighted averaging.

Transfer rule: If items come in two prices with a fixed total count and cost, then set one variable for one type, use count to express the other, and solve the resulting linear equation.
Error pattern: I guessed from price intuition without enforcing both constraints algebraically.
Diagnostic check: Let x be discounted items and total minus x be regular items; compute total cost symbolically, solve, then substitute back to verify both count and cost exactly.
Use when: This applies to mixture or purchase problems with two unit prices, a known total quantity, and a known total amount spent.
Boundary: Ignore this when prices vary item-by-item, totals are approximate, or more than two independent unknown categories exist.

Transfer rule: If a figure is formed by two families of parallel lines, then count shapes by choosing 2 lines from one family and 2 from the other, and multiply.
Error pattern: Treated a combinatorial selection problem like a simple product or grid-cell count, undercounting larger shapes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does every target shape correspond uniquely to selecting boundary lines?” If yes, compute combinations for each family.
Use when: The diagram has multiple parallel lines in each of two directions, and the shapes are bounded by pairs of lines.
Boundary: Ignore when boundaries are curved, families are not parallel, or shapes require extra constraints beyond line-pair selection.

Transfer rule: If a geometry question asks for an area fraction after adding a parallel segment inside a symmetric figure, then assign convenient coordinates and compute areas directly.
Error pattern: Chose a visually plausible expression instead of enforcing parallel-line constraints and area relationships with a concrete model.
Diagnostic check: Set side length to 1, place vertices on axes, encode the parallel condition with equal slopes, find intersection coordinates, then divide computed polygon area by total area.
Use when: A diagram involves triangles or quadrilaterals, shading, parallels, and answer choices are simple fractions or radicals.
Boundary: Ignore when lengths/areas are given numerically already or when the figure is not fixed enough for a unique coordinate setup.

Transfer rule: If your computed result is absent from the choices, then pause and test for formatting ambiguity or a likely key/printing issue before selecting.
Error pattern: I relied on one valid procedure and committed without reconciling the result with the answer set.
Diagnostic check: Compute once with standard precedence, then scan whether that value appears; if not, recompute using only allowed alternate conventions and compare all outputs to the choices.
Use when: This applies to short arithmetic multiple-choice items where notation could be interpreted differently or the options constrain what the test expects.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is open-response, explicitly states the convention, or includes parentheses that remove ambiguity.

Transfer rule: If a prime is constrained by another primality condition, then first list allowable residue classes of its last digit and eliminate any making the derived expression divisible by 2, 5, or 3.
Error pattern: I jumped from possible prime endings to multiplying too many candidates without filtering them through modular divisibility of the companion number.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate units digit, compute the derived number’s units digit and value mod 3; reject any class forcing compositeness before taking the product.
Use when: The problem asks for possible last digits of primes subject to an added linear expression also being prime.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on full factorization or non-decimal representations rather than residue-class screening.

Transfer rule: If a group’s overall average lies between two subgroup averages and one subgroup size is known, then use weighted-average balancing (distance ratio or equation), not guessing.
Error pattern: Misapplied average-combination logic by not enforcing that total excess above the lower average equals the known subgroup’s excess.
Diagnostic check: Set baseline at the lower subgroup average; compute overall excess × total count, and verify it equals known subgroup excess × known subgroup size.
Use when: One average for the whole set and two subgroup averages are given, with one subgroup count known and the total count unknown.
Boundary: Ignore when averages are not for disjoint groups, or when rates/percentages are mixed without a common unit.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is repeatedly reduced by “half the current amount plus a fixed part,” then work backward from the final remainder using the inverse step.
Error pattern: Chose by forward intuition/option matching instead of modeling each transfer as a recurrence and reversing it exactly.
Diagnostic check: Let next remainder be r; compute previous as 2(r + fixed part). Repeat for all rounds, then verify by simulating forward with no fractions appearing.
Use when: Multi-step give-away, take-away, or depletion problems where each round removes a fraction of what remains plus or minus a constant.
Boundary: Ignore when each round removes a fixed number only, percentages vary by round, or totals need not stay whole-number feasible.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate result is approximate and choices are approximate days, then compare the raw quotient directly to options before imposing whole-day or divisibility constraints.
Error pattern: Treating a continuous time/rate question as requiring exact integer completion caused unnecessary rounding away from the nearest option.
Diagnostic check: Compute each worker’s daily rate, sum rates, divide total work by combined rate, and ask: “Does the prompt require an exact whole day, or only an approximate duration?”
Use when: This applies to joint-work, unit-rate, and “approximately how many days” multiple-choice problems with scaled workloads.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task explicitly demands whole days, discrete batches, or minimum full periods to finish.

Transfer rule: If a mixture question gives two component prices, a target average price, and total weight, then solve both equations and match the asked component before choosing an option.
Error pattern: Correct algebra but failed answer selection by not mapping the solved values to the quantity actually requested.
Diagnostic check: After solving, write “asked for = ___”; substitute each solved amount into total-weight and total-cost equations, then verify the chosen option names that exact variable.
Use when: Two-item mixture, weighted-average, or system-of-equations problems where answer choices could match either component or another derived quantity.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem asks only for an equation setup, a ratio, or when labels are unambiguous and no option corresponds to multiple solved quantities.

Transfer rule: If two constant travel speeds give opposite early/late times for the same route, then equate distance as speed × time and use the total time difference between arrivals.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling a shared distance with variable scheduled travel time instead of averaging speeds or comparing speeds directly.
Diagnostic check: Let scheduled time be T; write d=v1(T+late) and d=v2(T−early), convert minutes to hours, solve, then verify both expressions match exactly.
Use when: Apply to one-route word problems with fixed distance, two speeds, and stated lateness/earliness relative to the same deadline.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ, delays include stops or changing speeds, or timing is not referenced to a common schedule.

Transfer rule: If groups contribute different output shares and defect rates, then compute the overall defect chance as a weighted average using each group’s share times its rate.
Error pattern: Success came from translating verbal production/defect data into proportions before combining them, rather than averaging rates directly.
Diagnostic check: Convert every percentage and “x out of y” statement to decimals, verify the group shares form a sensible whole, then sum share × defect-rate terms.
Use when: Apply this to mixture, factory, source, or population problems where subgroups have unequal sizes and different event probabilities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a conditional subgroup probability or when subgroup shares/rates are not all referenced to the same total.

Transfer rule: If a full container has equal amounts removed and refilled repeatedly, then track the original substance by multiplying by (1 − removed/total) for each cycle.
Error pattern: Treated repeated replacement like simple subtraction or mixed up remaining fraction after each step instead of compounding it.
