Error pattern: Confusing the reference population with the whole set, then using approximation or ignoring one group; sometimes the omitted part contributes nothing, but that must be shown, not assumed.
Diagnostic check: Write “base count = ?”, calculate each group’s per-person share from that base, multiply by each group size, and verify whether any term is exactly zero or nonzero.
Use when: Word problems split people into categories and define payouts as percentages of a specified count.
Boundary: Ignore this when percentages describe probabilities, changing totals over time, or percentages of different quantities per group.

Transfer rule: If operator meanings are reassigned, then first rewrite the entire expression with substituted operations before calculating.
Error pattern: Confusing original symbols with remapped meanings or applying order of operations before completing the translation.
Diagnostic check: Make a two-column map symbol→actual operation, rewrite every symbol once, then evaluate using normal precedence on the rewritten form.
Use when: A problem defines nonstandard meanings for arithmetic signs, logical connectors, comparison symbols, or similar operators.
Boundary: Ignore when symbols keep their usual meanings or when the task asks for direct computation without any remapping.

Transfer rule: If a comparison gives both step frequency and step length, then compute speed as (steps per time) × (length per step) for each side before comparing.
Error pattern: I matched one ratio directly to speed and ignored that speed depends on two multiplicative factors, not just leap counts.
Diagnostic check: Set a common time window, convert the stated leap-count ratio into counts, convert the stated leap-length relation into per-leap lengths, then multiply and simplify.
Use when: Apply this on motion/work problems where counts, rates, strides, or cycles are compared along with an equivalence between unit sizes.
Boundary: Ignore this when all units are already the same and only one factor varies, or when the asked quantity is not a product of rate and size.

Transfer rule: If a word problem asks how many you have now after collecting more, then combine the starting amount with the added amount.
Error pattern: I focused on the most recent quantity mentioned and ignored the initial total, causing a part-for-whole mistake.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each number as start, change, or result; if the change is an increase, verify the result is greater than each individual amount.
Use when: This applies to simple arithmetic word problems with an initial quantity and an action like got, found, bought, picked, or received.
Boundary: Ignore this when the action removes items, replaces amounts, compares groups, or asks only for the amount added.

Transfer rule: If asked for an average annual increase over years, then compute total change and divide by elapsed years, not by the number of listed values or endpoints.
Error pattern: Success came from translating a verbal growth description into a rate-of-change calculation with units checked.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, calculate end minus start, calculate later year minus earlier year, divide, and confirm the result’s unit is “amount per year.”
Use when: Apply this to time-span word problems involving averages, growth, decline, production, population, sales, or any quantity measured at two dates.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for percent change, compound growth, median, geometric mean, or gives many yearly data points needing a different average.

Transfer rule: If two travelers move at constant speeds with a delayed start, then compute head start distance = slower speed × delay and catch-up time = head start ÷ relative speed.
Error pattern: Confusing elapsed-time offsets with speed differences, causing an overestimate of the meeting time.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write three quantities with units—delay in hours, lead distance, and relative speed—and verify that distance = rate × time gives a plausible catch-up time.
Use when: Applies to pursuit problems with same route, constant rates, and one mover starting later from the same reference point.
Boundary: Ignore when speeds change, routes differ, stops occur, or the question asks for position rather than catch-up time.

Transfer rule: If a series ends when one side reaches a target, then count all terminal sequences of lengths below the maximum, not just one endpoint.
Error pattern: Stopping-count bias—treating only the shortest sweep cases or missing valid early-ending paths with mixed wins and losses.
Diagnostic check: Enumerate allowable final lengths; for each length, require the winner has target−1 wins in prior games and wins the last, then sum both teams’ counts.
Use when: Equal-likelihood, independent game sequences with an absorbing stopping rule, such as best-of-n contests ending once a threshold is reached.
Boundary: Ignore when game probabilities differ, ties/pushes exist, or the contest is forced to play all scheduled games regardless of early clinching.

Transfer rule: If a two-person transfer problem gives two relational statements, then write both post-transfer equations and solve by substitution/elimination before choosing.
Error pattern: Algebra setup was fine, but the simultaneous-equation solving step was inaccurate, producing an unsupported value.
Diagnostic check: After solving, substitute the result into both original transfer equations and verify each balances exactly; if either fails, recalculate.
Use when: Amounts change after one person gives money to the other, and the conditions compare the resulting amounts by multiples.
Boundary: Ignore this when relationships are not linear transfer comparisons, or when constraints involve percentages, totals, or more than two unknowns.

Transfer rule: If two people’s relative order is stated and counts are given before one, between them, and after the other, then total = before first-mentioned-later person + between + after earlier person + 2.  
Error pattern: I misassigned which person the “after” count belongs to and effectively counted from the wrong endpoint.  
Diagnostic check: Draw two ordered slots for the people, place the earlier one left, the later one right, attach each count to its stated side, then sum fixed groups plus both people.  
Use when: Ranking or queue problems give separation counts and a condition about who is earlier or later.  
Boundary: Ignore when counts overlap ambiguously, positions can vary, or the order condition is missing/contradictory.

Transfer rule: If discounts begin only after thresholds, then price each tier separately and apply every eligible prior discount to later tiers unless the wording says they replace earlier ones.
Error pattern: Misread cumulative tiered discounts as mutually exclusive, so the last segment got only the newest discount instead of the combined effect.
Diagnostic check: Build a segment table with quantity, base price, active discounts, net multiplier, and subtotal; verify later segments inherit earlier qualifying discounts.
Use when: Relevant for piecewise pricing, bulk purchases, tax brackets, commissions, or any “after the first/next” threshold language.
Boundary: Ignore when discounts are explicitly noncumulative, retroactive to all units, or stated as a single final rate per segment.

Transfer rule: If given pairwise completion times for three workers, then convert each to rates, add the three pair rates, and halve the total to get the combined rate.
Error pattern: Success comes from using work-rate algebra instead of averaging times or treating times as directly additive.
Diagnostic check: Compute 1/t1 + 1/t2 + 1/t3, divide by 2, then invert; verify the result is faster than every pair time.
Use when: This applies to work problems involving three agents where each statement gives the time for a different pair working together.
Boundary: Ignore this when outputs are nonconstant, tasks differ, or the data are individual times rather than pairwise times.

Transfer rule: If two people cover the same total distance in different times, then convert times to a speed ratio and compute each halfway time from that ratio.
Error pattern: Treated “running toward each other” as if it affected reaching a fixed midpoint; confused meeting-time reasoning with midpoint-time reasoning.
Diagnostic check: Let total distance be 1; assign speeds from full-trip times, compute each midpoint time as (1/2)/speed, then subtract and compare with choices.
Use when: Two movers start simultaneously from opposite ends, and the question asks about a fixed location like the halfway point rather than where they meet.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when speeds change over time or the target point depends on both runners’ motion.

Transfer rule: If adding decimals, then align place values and perform digit-by-digit addition, carrying from right to left before matching any option.
Error pattern: Premature rounding or choosing a “nice” whole-number-looking result instead of executing the exact decimal computation.
Diagnostic check: Write both numbers vertically, verify equal decimal lengths, add each column with carries, then compare the full sum to choices.
Use when: Relevant for arithmetic with decimals, near-whole numbers, or options that include rounded-looking distractors alongside precise values.
Boundary: Ignore when the task explicitly requests estimation, rounding, or a justified approximation rather than an exact sum.

Transfer rule: If converting scientific notation with a positive exponent, then move the decimal right by that many places and append zeros if needed.
Error pattern: Success came from applying place-value conversion directly instead of estimating or matching by appearance.
Diagnostic check: Count decimal shifts, rewrite as an integer, then verify the result has the original significant digits and total magnitude near the stated power of ten.
Use when: This applies to notation of the form coefficient × 10^n, especially when choosing among similar-looking whole-number options.
Boundary: Ignore this when the exponent is negative or when the task asks for rounding, comparison, or arithmetic beyond simple expansion.

Transfer rule: If a power-plus-term expression is divided by a modulus, then reduce the base modulo that modulus first and use parity/cycle patterns before adding.
Error pattern: Success came from modular reduction and recognizing a short residue cycle instead of estimating the huge power directly.
Diagnostic check: Replace the base by its residue mod the divisor, compute the first few powers to detect a cycle or parity rule, then combine remaining terms and reduce once more.
Use when: The problem has very large exponents, a small divisor, and asks for a remainder of a sum involving repeated powers.
Boundary: Ignore this when exact values are required, or when the modulus/base relationship prevents a simple cycle check from being efficient.

Transfer rule: If an age problem gives a current difference and a future ratio, then define current ages, add the same time shift to both, and solve the two equations before answering any later-time question.
Error pattern: I jumped from one relation to an answer choice without fully validating the algebraic setup and time translation.
Diagnostic check: Let older = younger + difference; write the future equation with both ages increased equally; solve, then substitute into the asked time and verify both original conditions.
Use when: This applies to word problems involving ages, fixed age differences, future or past time shifts, and multiplicative comparisons.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are not simultaneous ages or when the difference/ratio does not refer to the same pair at one time.

Transfer rule: If a fraction of a mixture is removed and replaced, then write a weighted-balance equation using amount of target substance, not just percentage differences.
Error pattern: Treated the change as a simple average/linear shift without accounting for the unchanged portion that stayed from the original mixture.
Diagnostic check: Assume total mass 1; compute target mass left after removal, add replacement as removed_fraction × unknown concentration, and verify the final concentration exactly.
Use when: A problem involves replacing part of one mixture with another and asks for the concentration of the added mixture.
Boundary: Ignore this when nothing is removed/replaced, or when concentrations change through evaporation, reaction, or unequal total mass.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then compute a weighted average using total sum = (group count × group average) for each group, then divide by total count.
Error pattern: Arithmetic conversion failure with mixed numbers and totals; the setup was right, but fraction multiplication/addition and simplification drifted.
Diagnostic check: Convert each mixed average to an improper fraction, multiply by its group size, verify each product is reasonable, add totals, divide by total items, then confirm the result lies between the two group averages.
Use when: Relevant for grouped-average, shipment, class, batch, or multi-day mean problems with unequal group sizes.
Boundary: Ignore when all groups have equal size or when the question asks for a median, rate, or unweighted summary.

Transfer rule: If two travelers start at different times and you need distance difference at meeting, then write separate distance expressions using each traveler’s own travel time before comparing.
Error pattern: Mixing up time offset with speed difference, causing an unjustified shortcut from rates directly to distance gap.
Diagnostic check: Define the later traveler’s time as t; set total distance = v1(t + delay) + v2t, solve t, then compute and compare each distance explicitly.
Use when: Opposite-direction motion, staggered starts, meeting/pass events, and a question asks “how much farther” one traveled.
Boundary: Ignore when both start simultaneously or when the asked quantity is only meeting time or combined rate without comparing individual distances.

Transfer rule: If an object fully clears another object, then use total distance = both lengths combined and convert speed to m/s before dividing.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/setup slip in standard rate–distance problems, especially unit conversion or using only one length.
Diagnostic check: Compute speed in m/s, add all required lengths for full crossing, divide, then estimate whether the time is near total-distance/20 to catch mismatches.
Use when: Relative-motion questions ask for complete crossing, overtaking, passing a platform, tunnel, pole, or another moving body.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks for partial entry/exit timing, acceleration effects, or gives speed already in consistent units.

Transfer rule: If a simple-interest question gives principal, amount, and time, then compute interest = amount − principal and rate = (interest × 100) / (principal × time).
Error pattern: Arithmetic/formula misuse—choosing a plausible percentage without fully converting the increase over the given years into an annual rate.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify units by recomputing amount from your rate using A = P + (P×R×T)/100 and confirm it matches the stated total.
Use when: Apply this on simple-interest multiple-choice items that provide starting sum, final sum, and duration, especially when options are close.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for compound interest, changing principal, or when fees, installments, or non-annual rates are involved.

Transfer rule: If containers have different capacities, then convert each amount to the same base unit before adding and compare the total to the target container’s full capacity.
Error pattern: I added fill fractions directly across unequal-sized containers instead of weighting each fraction by container size first.
Diagnostic check: Set the smaller capacity to 1 unit, express every contents amount in those units, add volumes, then divide by the receiving container’s capacity.
Use when: A word problem combines partial fills from containers with different sizes and asks for a resulting fill level or concentration.
Boundary: Ignore this when all fractions already refer to the same whole or the capacities are explicitly equal.

Transfer rule: If one moving object fully passes another object, then compute speed using total relative distance = sum of both lengths divided by the given time.
Error pattern: Success came from modeling “crosses” as full clearance, not partial overlap or single-object travel.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sketch start and finish positions and verify the front must cover both object lengths for complete passing.
Use when: Apply to motion problems with phrases like crosses, overtakes, passes, or clears another object or platform in a stated time.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks only partial crossing, same-point meeting, or gives direct speed-distance data without full-clearance wording.

Transfer rule: If a problem gives simple and compound interest for the same principal, rate, and two years, then use 2-year identities to isolate principal from their difference.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping verbal interest data to standard formulas instead of testing answer choices or mixing amount with interest.
Diagnostic check: Verify that compound interest minus simple interest equals principal × (rate^2/10000); first derive rate from SI = principal × rate × time / 100.
Use when: Apply this on time-and-interest questions with equal rate, same principal, and a short fixed period, especially exactly two years.
Boundary: Ignore this when rates differ, time is not two years, compounding frequency changes, or amounts rather than interests are being compared.

Transfer rule: If each term is obtained by the same multiplicative change from the previous one, then extend the sequence by applying that same factor once more.
Error pattern: Success comes from checking for a constant ratio rather than guessing from familiar fractions or repeating recent terms.
Diagnostic check: Compute consecutive term ratios; if they match, multiply the last shown term by that common ratio and compare with the choices.
Use when: Apply this to ordered number sequences, especially when values shrink or grow proportionally and include fractions or decimals.
Boundary: Ignore this when consecutive ratios differ or another clearer pattern appears, such as constant differences, alternating rules, or digit-based transformations.

Transfer rule: If a code maps letters to digits from examples, then build a letter→digit table from all given words and encode the target strictly by letter order.
Error pattern: I inferred the target code by pattern-matching digits instead of verifying each character’s mapped value and position.
Diagnostic check: List every unique letter from the examples, assign its digit, then rewrite the target one letter at a time and compare the full sequence to choices.
Use when: Relevant in substitution-style coding questions with repeated letters across example words and options differing mainly by digit order.
Boundary: Ignore when the examples suggest arithmetic, positional transforms, reversals, or non-fixed mappings rather than one consistent symbol substitution.

Transfer rule: If a simple-interest discount problem gives present worth and true discount, then first recover the amount due as their sum, derive the rate-time factor from true discount/present worth, and compute banker’s gain from the discount-method difference.
Error pattern: I jumped to a familiar-looking formula/result without reconstructing the shared factor linking true discount, banker's discount, and present worth.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify these identities numerically: amount due = present worth + true discount; factor = true discount/present worth; banker's gain = amount due × factor²/(1+factor).
Use when: This applies to commercial-math questions comparing true discount, banker's discount, present worth, and gain under simple interest.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem uses compound discounting, fees beyond discounting, or already provides banker's discount directly.

Transfer rule: If a price is marked up by p%, then recover the base by dividing the final price by (1 + p/100), not by subtracting p% of the final price.  
Error pattern: Percentage-change problems are solved well when converting markup language into a multiplicative factor and reversing it with division.  
Diagnostic check: Write “final = base × factor”; compute base = final/factor, then verify by multiplying the result by the factor to recover the given final price.  
Use when: The prompt gives an original amount changed by a stated percent increase or decrease and asks for the starting amount.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the percent is applied repeatedly, conditionally, or to a different reference amount than the unknown base.

Transfer rule: If a problem defines a special notation, then rewrite every expression using that definition before doing any arithmetic.  
Error pattern: I treated symbolic expressions as ordinary powers/sums instead of applying the newly defined operation to each term.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, substitute the definition into the endpoints, evaluate them exactly, and verify the interval’s values are what I’m counting over.  
Use when: Relevant in counting, number theory, or interval questions that introduce factorial-like notation or any custom symbol definition.  
Boundary: Ignore this when notation is already standard and explicitly interpreted, or when the task does not depend on evaluating symbolic endpoints.

Transfer rule: If pricing depends on visit order within a period, then count customers at each visit level and total revenue by tier, not by customer type.
Error pattern: Success pattern—translated overlapping repeat-visit counts into separate paid visit tiers and summed without double-counting or omission.
Diagnostic check: List counts for first, second, third, etc. visits; verify later-visit counts are subsets of earlier ones; compute each tier’s revenue and compare tier totals.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with monthly/reset periods, repeat visits or purchases, and different charges for initial versus subsequent events.
Boundary: Ignore when prices are flat per event, counts are already nonoverlapping totals, or revenue includes fees beyond the tiered visit charges.

Transfer rule: If a quantity rises “x% more than” a stated rate each year, then add the percentages first and compound from the original value for the stated years.
Error pattern: Misread a relative-rate phrase, substituted an unrelated smaller rate, and mixed simple yearly increments with compound-growth language inconsistently.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write the effective annual rate in one expression, compute one-year value, then square/multiply for later years and confirm the result exceeds the base appropriately.
Use when: Percentage-growth word problems mention inflation, markup, “more than,” annual change, and multi-year future price or value.
Boundary: Ignore when “more than” refers to absolute points, one-time change, nonannual periods, or when the problem explicitly uses simple interest.

Transfer rule: If a motion problem mixes km/h with seconds, then convert speed to m/s first and use distance = speed × time.
Error pattern: Unit-conversion failure leading to a plausible but wrong arithmetic result in a basic rate-time-distance question.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write the converted speed, multiply by the given seconds, and confirm the distance magnitude is reasonable for the object.
Use when: Relevant for objects crossing a point or pole, where the full object length equals distance traveled during the stated time.
Boundary: Ignore when all quantities already share units or when the object crosses another moving object, platform, or tunnel requiring relative speed or extra length.

Transfer rule: If a grouping problem changes group size, then compute total = old size × old groups and new groups = total ÷ new size; do not adjust an exact quotient.
Error pattern: Arithmetic was initially right, then overturned by unjustified option-chasing and invented corrections after seeing a mismatch.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify units and divisibility: total count stays constant, quotient × new size recreates the same total, and any remainder means partial group handling must be explicit.
Use when: Relevant for rows, boxes, teams, batches, or any fixed-total repartition from one group size/count pair to another.
Boundary: Ignore when totals change, some items are excluded, or the problem states uneven final groups/leftovers matter.

Transfer rule: If all items are to be ordered in every possible way, then use permutations of the full set and multiply by the moves required per arrangement.
Error pattern: Confused choosing with ordering and then mixed time-unit conversion, causing an unsupported final value.
Diagnostic check: Compute item count first; ask “Does sequence matter?”; if yes, compare 1, n!, and nCr sizes, then convert the resulting quarter-minute total directly to minutes.
Use when: Relevant in word problems about arranging or sending identical-sized groups, especially with phrases like “every possible arrangement/order/combination” plus a per-move time.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is only selecting subsets, items are indistinguishable, or no exhaustive ordering is required.

Transfer rule: If a fixed job is shared by identical workers or machines, then keep total work constant and divide by the new worker count.
Error pattern: I treated a work-rate change too loosely instead of enforcing the inverse relationship between workers and time.
Diagnostic check: Compute worker-hours from the original setup, then recalculate time with the new count; more workers must produce less time, not equal or more.
Use when: The problem gives identical agents, one unchanged task, and asks how time changes after the number of agents changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when workers differ in speed, setup delays matter, or the total job size also changes.

Transfer rule: If a tank fills slower because of a leak, then compute rates: leak rate = normal fill rate minus net fill rate, and emptying time = 1 ÷ leak rate.
Error pattern: Treating times as directly interchangeable instead of converting each scenario into per-hour work rates causes lucky guesses and contradictions.
Diagnostic check: Let capacity = 1; calculate the normal rate, the slowed net rate, subtract to get the leak rate, then verify net + leak = normal.
Use when: Apply this to pipes, cisterns, pumps, leaks, or workers where one process helps and another opposes completion.
Boundary: Ignore this when all processes act in the same direction or the problem asks only for combined time without any loss process.

Transfer rule: If a total covers mixed groups and one group’s average is known, then subtract that group’s total from the grand total and divide the remainder by the other group’s count.
Error pattern: Misallocated the known subgroup cost or skipped the leftover-total step, causing an inflated per-item value.
Diagnostic check: Compute known-group total = count × average; remaining total = overall total − known-group total; verify remaining total is positive, then divide by the remaining count.
Use when: A word problem gives a combined total, counts for two categories, and an average or unit price for one category.
Boundary: Ignore when all categories share one common average or when ratios/percentages, not additive totals, drive the setup.

Transfer rule: If counts are linked by phrases like “more than” or “times as many,” then write direct variable equations for counts first and substitute them into the value equation.
Error pattern: Mis-translating verbal relationships into algebra and not enforcing all constraints simultaneously before selecting an option.
Diagnostic check: After deriving expressions, plug them into the total-value equation in cents and verify the chosen counts also satisfy each count relationship exactly.
Use when: Word problems give multiple quantity relationships plus a total, especially with coin values, ages, or item counts.
Boundary: Ignore this when choices can be answered by pure estimation or when relationships are not exact algebraic constraints.

Transfer rule: If multiple agents work simultaneously on one whole job, then convert each time to a rate, add the rates, and invert once at the end.
Error pattern: Treated completion times as directly combinable instead of using a common “job per hour” unit.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write each worker’s fraction of the job per unit time, sum them, and verify the total rate exceeds the fastest single rate.
Use when: Relevant for pipes, workers, machines, or taps filling or emptying one shared task together.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are sequential, capacities differ by amount not rate, or the task asks for output over a fixed time instead of total completion time.

Transfer rule: If an equation has a variable base raised to a variable exponent equal to 1, then first test all standard ways a power can equal 1 and check domain limits.
Error pattern: I overfocused on a tempting zero/exponent shortcut and failed to systematically enumerate all valid cases for powers equaling 1.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, list cases base=1, exponent=0 with allowed nonzero base, and special parity/sign cases; reject any that make the expression undefined.
Use when: Apply this to exponential equations with variable bases/exponents, especially when the right side simplifies to 1 or another identity value.
Boundary: Ignore this when logs, complex numbers, or non-real conventions change the admissible cases for powers.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is averaged over time-varying rates, then compute total distance and divide by total time, then match that result to the chosen option.
Error pattern: Arithmetic/reasoning was correct, but final selection mismatched the computed result due to answer-choice transcription failure.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, compare the boxed value, units, and selected option; they must all be identical and correspond to the same choice.
Use when: Problems ask for average speed or average rate across multiple travel segments with different times or rates.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when all segments cover equal distances, where a specialized rate average may be faster than distance-summing.

Transfer rule: If one component is added to a mixture, then keep the other component constant and set constant part = target complement × new total.
Error pattern: Treated the total volume as unchanged after adding liquid and switched equations midstream without preserving invariants.
Diagnostic check: Write initial amounts of both components; mark which amount stays fixed; replace total with original plus added amount; verify target percent equation uses the new total.
Use when: Percentage-mixture problems where only one ingredient is added or removed and the question asks for a new concentration.
Boundary: Ignore when components react, evaporate, are both changed, or the percentage refers to something other than share of total volume.

Transfer rule: If a rate problem asks for travel time, then compute effective speed first and divide distance by that speed, keeping units unchanged throughout.
Error pattern: Arithmetic breakdown after setting up the right formula; simplifying and converting units without checking plausibility led to a nonsensical result.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, verify distance = speed × time with your candidate and confirm the time scale is reasonable for the given distance and rate.
Use when: Applies to motion questions with still-water or base speed modified by current, wind, or another additive/subtractive rate.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is not a distance-rate-time calculation or when rates vary over time instead of remaining constant.

Transfer rule: If a quantity changes by +p% and then −p%, then multiply factors (1+p)(1−p), set them equal to the stated net factor, and solve.
Error pattern: Treated opposite percentage changes as canceling or used the final percent incorrectly; missed that percentages compound multiplicatively from different bases.
Diagnostic check: Use a base of 100, compute both factors explicitly, verify the target final amount, and confirm the net loss equals the stated overall change.
Use when: Two or more sequential percent increases/decreases are applied across time or stages, especially when the later percent is based on a changed amount.
Boundary: Ignore when changes are additive in absolute units, or when all percentages are explicitly relative to the same original base.

Transfer rule: If a selection says certain items are “must,” then include them first and choose only the remaining required items from the optional pool.
Error pattern: Mixed up combinations with permutations and invented inclusion-exclusion without a stated overlap or exclusion condition.
Diagnostic check: Translate into “total chosen = required fixed items + extra items”; then compute choose(optional pool, extra needed) and ask whether order ever matters.
Use when: Relevant for counting problems with mandatory selections, exact totals, and wording like choose/select varieties/items without sequencing.
Boundary: Ignore when the task asks for arrangements, rankings, repeated choices, or any explicit order-sensitive process.

Transfer rule: If one new data point changes an average by a stated amount, then model totals before and after with the count n and use change-in-average × n = deviation of the new point from the new average.
Error pattern: Treated the average-change statement too locally and skipped a total-sum equation, causing an off-by-one/count mistake.
Diagnostic check: Before choosing, write old total = old average × (n−1), new total = new average × n, subtract them, and verify the difference equals the added value.
Use when: A problem says a single added result raises or lowers an average and asks for the number of items.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple values change, weights differ, or the “average” is not arithmetic.

Transfer rule: If a statement gives a chained inequality, then split it into separate inequalities, solve each, and intersect the resulting solution sets before testing claims.
Error pattern: Treating one derived bound as sufficient while failing to combine all constraints from the chain.
Diagnostic check: Rewrite as left<middle and middle<right, isolate the variable in both, compare which bound is tighter, then plug a sample value from the intersection into each statement.
Use when: The prompt has compound inequalities and asks what must be true among several candidate statements.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions are disjunctive, involve absolute values/cases, or “must” depends on unstated domain restrictions.

Transfer rule: If one measurement is stated as a fraction of another, then write an equation equating the full formulas with that fraction before simplifying.
Error pattern: Dropped a variable-containing quantity and then guessed from choices, treating a derived non-integer as something to round.
Diagnostic check: Define both formulas, substitute the relationship as perimeter = fraction × area, cancel common constants carefully, and verify the resulting value reproduces the statement exactly.
Use when: A geometry word problem relates boundary length to enclosed area for the same figure, especially circles or similar shapes.
Boundary: Ignore when the relation is approximate, dimensions use different unit systems, or the problem explicitly requests estimation.

Transfer rule: If a ratio and an absolute difference are given, then set quantities as common multiples of the ratio parts and match the stated difference.
Error pattern: Mixed up part-to-part ratio with totals, creating an invalid equation and then guessing from choices instead of deriving.
Diagnostic check: Let the quantities be a·k and b·k from the ratio; compute |b−a|·k and verify it equals the given difference before choosing.
Use when: Relevant for word problems comparing two categories with a fixed ratio plus a stated numerical gap.
Boundary: Ignore when the ratio refers to rates, probabilities, or includes a total amount rather than a direct difference.

Transfer rule: If a total is made from two ticket prices and one category’s spending must be minimized, then solve the value equation in nonnegative integers and choose the smallest spending that makes the remainder divisible by the other price.
Error pattern: Treated the task as simple subtraction or nearest option matching instead of enforcing divisibility and feasibility constraints.
Diagnostic check: Let spending on the higher-priced category be h; verify total − h is a nonnegative multiple of the lower price, and compare all feasible h values to find the minimum.
Use when: A total cost comes from exactly two fixed unit prices and the question asks for minimum or maximum spending/count in one category.
Boundary: Ignore when prices vary, additional constraints change feasibility, or the prompt asks for just any possible combination.

Transfer rule: If a middleman’s commission/profit is stated as a percent of selling price or cost, then write an equation tying sale price, retained fraction, and supplier cost before calculating.
Error pattern: Mixed up markup on cost with commission/profit taken from the final sale price, causing the base for the percent to be wrong.
Diagnostic check: Let selling price be s; compute distributor take using the stated base, set supplier payment plus required gain equal to s, and verify the resulting margin matches the wording.
Use when: Relevant for pricing, commission, markup, margin, reseller, and “price observed by buyer” word problems.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem explicitly gives a direct additive fee or all percentages clearly use the same base.

Transfer rule: If a container’s “wet surface” is asked, then total the wetted base plus all side walls up to the liquid depth; do not use full height or top area.
Error pattern: Misread the geometric phrase and omitted or miscomputed one or more wetted faces in a rectangular-prism surface-area setup.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write dimensions as L, W, d and verify wet area = L×W + 2(L×d) + 2(W×d); check units are all converted consistently.
Use when: Rectangular tanks, cisterns, troughs, or boxes ask for wetted, inside, or contact surface area with a partial fill depth.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks for volume, capacity, external area, full surface area, or includes non-rectangular geometry.

Transfer rule: If a percent describes one group and all remaining subgroup counts are given, then sum those subgroups to get the complement and divide by its percent.
Error pattern: I mixed categories from different partitions and invented an unsupported relationship between passing and course-taking.
Diagnostic check: Write a two-part partition table, place every given count in exactly one cell or margin, and verify the subtotal equals the stated complement before using percentages.
Use when: Relevant in word problems combining a whole-group percentage with counts only for the “not” group or another complement.
Boundary: Ignore when counts overlap ambiguously, categories are not exhaustive, or an extra assumption is required to link rows and columns.

Transfer rule: If two purchases share one identical item, then subtract the totals first to isolate the repeated item’s unit price before scaling.
Error pattern: I treated a mixed-cost system too loosely and skipped the elimination step, causing an unsupported guess.
Diagnostic check: Write paired equations, subtract them to remove the common item, verify the remaining difference equals one unit, then multiply as asked.
Use when: Relevant for word problems with two transactions containing the same extra item and different counts of another item.
Boundary: Ignore when the shared item is absent, quantities are inconsistent, or prices vary across transactions or include discounts/taxes.

Transfer rule: If dimensions are given as chained multiples and volume is known, then define one base variable, express all dimensions from it, form the product, and solve algebraically before checking choices.
Error pattern: I likely matched an option from intuition or weak arithmetic instead of carrying the ratio-to-equation setup through exactly.
Diagnostic check: Let breadth = x; write height and length in terms of x, compute the volume expression, isolate x, then substitute back to verify the original volume.
Use when: This applies to word problems about rectangular solids with multiplicative relationships among dimensions and a total volume.
Boundary: Ignore this when dimensions are independent, units are inconsistent, or the shape is not a simple rectangular prism.

Transfer rule: If a quantity is “increased by p%,” then replace it with original × (1 + p/100) before forming the new ratio.
Error pattern: Misreading percentage increases as add-ons to the fraction or not scaling numerator and denominator separately.
Diagnostic check: Write symbolic originals n/d; convert the stated changes to multipliers, simplify the resulting ratio, then solve for n/d and verify by substitution.
Use when: A ratio or fraction’s numerator and denominator are changed by different percentages, especially in multiple-choice settings.
Boundary: Ignore this when changes are absolute amounts, percentages apply to the whole fraction only, or values are not multiplicative percentage changes.

Transfer rule: If two travelers cover the same distance with speeds in ratio a:b, then set times in inverse ratio b:a before using any time difference.
Error pattern: I matched faster speed with smaller time only intuitively, but skipped the explicit inverse-ratio setup that prevents option-driven mistakes.
Diagnostic check: Let times be bk and ak; subtract to match the stated time gap, solve for k, then verify the slower traveler’s time exceeds the faster’s.
Use when: Applies to same-distance rate–time questions giving a speed ratio and a difference between arrival times.
Boundary: Ignore when distances differ, the given ratio is of times instead of speeds, or extra constraints change the direct inverse relationship.

Transfer rule: If quantities are linked by “is twice” and “is half of,” then express all values from one variable before using the average/sum.
Error pattern: Misread directional comparison and skipped consistency between stated order and ratio relationships.
Diagnostic check: Let the middle quantity be x; derive the ordered triple symbolically, then verify each sentence against the triple before matching choices.
Use when: Word problems define several numbers by pairwise multiplicative relations and ask for their order from an average or total.
Boundary: Ignore when relationships are additive, approximate, or the problem directly gives equations for each quantity.

Transfer rule: If a work-rate problem has phases, then convert each phase to rate × time = work and solve using only the work from that phase.
Error pattern: Mixed total work with a later phase, causing double-counting and an equation that ignores the staged timeline.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, make a two-row timeline table; verify each row’s acres sum to the total and each equation uses the correct phase subtotal.
Use when: Multi-step constant-rate problems where one worker starts alone, others join later, or a remaining amount is completed together.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities are not additive work units over time or rates are not constant across phases.

Transfer rule: If total selling price of x items equals total cost price of y items, then compute per-item SP/CP = y/x and convert gain or loss % from that ratio.
Error pattern: Misread a total-price equivalence as a direct percentage instead of first normalizing to one item.
Diagnostic check: Let CP per item = 1 unit; derive SP per item from the given total equality, then verify whether profit = SP − 1 and % = profit/1 × 100.
Use when: The statement compares prices of different quantities of identical items and asks for gain, loss, or markup percentage.
Boundary: Ignore when quantities refer to different goods, extra costs are included, or the question asks only for a price ratio.

Transfer rule: If two objects cross each other, then use relative speed as difference for same direction and sum for opposite direction, with crossing distance equal to total lengths.
Error pattern: Confusing which motion uses sum versus difference, then mixing in unnecessary unit conversions or invented intermediate distances.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write two mini-cases: “same direction = slower closes gap” and “opposite direction = both close gap”; verify the larger relative speed gives the shorter time.
Use when: Relative-motion questions involve crossing, chasing, equal or known lengths, and a time given for one direction setup.
Boundary: Ignore this when objects are not interacting by relative motion or when acceleration/changing speeds matters.

Transfer rule: If profit is given as a percent of cost and cost changes while selling price stays fixed, then convert to ratios from cost, update cost, and recompute profit as a fraction of selling price.
Error pattern: Success came from translating verbal percentages into algebraic relationships instead of comparing percentages directly.
Diagnostic check: Let original cost be 1; write original selling price and profit, apply the stated cost multiplier, then verify new profit = fixed selling price minus new cost and divide by fixed selling price.
Use when: Relevant in profit-loss or markup questions mixing “percent of cost” with “percent of selling price” after a change.
Boundary: Ignore when both cost and selling price change, or when all percentages already use the same base quantity.

Transfer rule: If combining groups with different averages, then compute each group’s total exactly and divide the combined total by the combined count.
Error pattern: Replacing exact fraction arithmetic with rough decimals and then forcing a nearby mixed-number choice causes weighted-average mistakes.
Diagnostic check: Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions, multiply by each group size, add totals, divide by total items, and verify the result lies between the two group averages.
Use when: A problem gives separate counts and average values for multiple groups and asks for one overall average.
Boundary: Ignore this when groups are equally sized or when the task asks for a sum, difference, or median instead of an overall mean.

Transfer rule: If an age word problem gives relations at different times, then define present ages as variables and translate each sentence by shifting both ages equally before solving.
Error pattern: I likely matched an option from intuition or arithmetic shortcuts instead of enforcing both time-based constraints simultaneously.
Diagnostic check: Write two equations from the stated past/future conditions, solve, then substitute back into both original sentences and verify the requested present-age ratio.
Use when: Apply this to age-comparison problems involving phrases like “years ago,” “years hence,” multiplicative relations, and age differences or ratios.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic for single-time ratio problems or when no past/future shift creates a system of equations.

Transfer rule: If a probability asks for outcomes of two independent dice with a sum condition, then enumerate ordered pairs or count complement cases before choosing.
Error pattern: I likely guessed from an intuitive fraction instead of systematically mapping the sample space and valid outcomes.
Diagnostic check: List totals satisfying the condition, count combinations per total, sum favorable cases, and verify favorable plus unfavorable equals all equally likely outcomes.
Use when: This applies to paired-dice, equally likely outcome grids, or any small discrete sample space with threshold conditions like greater than or at least.
Boundary: Ignore this when outcomes are not equally likely, dice are biased, or the event depends on non-sum rules needing different counting.

Transfer rule: If asked how much greater one period’s gross profit is than another’s, then compute each gross profit as quantity × (selling price − unit cost) and subtract once.
Error pattern: Correct setup followed by unjustified post-hoc adjustment to force a listed option.
Diagnostic check: Before committing, verify the final value equals “later profit minus earlier profit” directly, with no extra scaling, doubling, or closeness-based changes.
Use when: Relevant in word problems comparing profits, revenues, costs, or totals across groups or time periods with different quantities and margins.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt explicitly asks for a ratio, percent change, combined total, or multi-step transformed comparison.
